09eb9ad6985b.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press By — Rio Yamat, Associated Press Rio Yamat, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/faa-approves-boeings-737-max-10-for-passenger-service Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FAA approves Boeing's 737 Max 10 for passenger service Nation Oct 20, 2026 5:56 PM EDT Boeing's 737 Max 10 airliner has been approved for passenger service after years of delays, the Federal Aviation Administration announced Tuesday. READ MORE: Boeing won't face criminal charge over 737 Max crashes that killed hundreds The Max 10's certification represents another milestone in Boeing's efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers. "After extensive safety reviews – including thousands of hours of test flights – the team at the FAA is ready to approve this critical aircraft for sale," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement. "This is a major win for American manufacturing and our nation's status as a global aviation powerhouse." Duffy is expected to speak about the decision later Tuesday during a visit to Boeing's manufacturing plant in Everett, Washington. The Max 10 — the largest version of Boeing's bestselling 737 family — is an important piece of the company's effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face. Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said in a statement that "completing the certification program clears the path for us to deliver a Boeing airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation." The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8. The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification. Boeing said in its 2020 annual report that it expected to make the plane's first delivery in 2023. The company now expects to begin deliveries in 2027. The delays have held up a key part of Boeing's business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog. Major customers for the Max 10 include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more. Boeing's struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing's manufacturing and safety practices. The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus's A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10. Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses. The Max 10's certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the smaller Max 7 for airline operations in August. Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10's design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers. In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. "I think that would be overstating it," he said, noting that 50% of Tesla shareholders would need to approve the deal, which he called a high hurdle. Of note: Any combination would be massive: SpaceX has a market cap of more than $2 trillion, while Tesla's is nearly $1.5 trillion. Tesla reports its quarterly results on Wednesday. WATCH: Fraternity culture under scrutiny in wake of Cornell allegations The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket's international platform. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to "activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law." "Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time," a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. "This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market." Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract. Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities. Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird. Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization. A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James. A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren't involved. Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company. Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform. When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket's international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket's international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading. "We've never, until now, seen this deluge of policies that have been direct attacks on international students to this level," said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an agency that promotes international education. READ MORE: Trump said he's pro legal immigration, his policies say otherwise The restrictive policies have had detrimental effects on international students and universities, experts told PBS News. A preliminary analysis by NAFSA in August estimated a drop in international student enrollment by 111,000 in 2026, which would result in up to $3.4 billion in lost revenue. Here's what to know about the Trump administration's policies targeting international students, the effect the potential changes are expected to have and how they compare to other countries. Why is Trump targeting international students and foreign workers? The Trump administration has given an array of reasons for its policies targeting international students and workers. In its proposed rule published on Oct. 8, the Department of Homeland Security said requiring universities to pay $70,000 per international student to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT), a program that lets foreign students temporarily work in the U.S. after graduation, was necessary to "place the United States' interests first and protect American workers." The administration gave a similar justification for its proposed rule to impose a filing fee exceeding $100,000 for companies to hire highly skilled workers on H1-B visas and to suspend certain tech companies from using the program altogether. WATCH: Vance says Microsoft is being suspended from green card program for H-1B visa workers The administration also cited fraud and abuse in its justification for the rules increasing fees for international students and workers. DHS did the same in a July rule requiring student visas to be awarded for a fixed four-year period rather than until students complete their programs. A federal judge temporarily blocked the rule before it went into effect. The administration has also cited national security and the country's best interest in its restrictions, including a State Department mandate to vet applicants' social media accounts. In January, the State Department announced on X that it had revoked 8,000 student visas "for individuals who had encounters with U.S. law enforcement for criminal activity." For months, international students reported receiving notices that their visas had been revoked without being given a reason. Many visas have been restored following court challenges. Why does the U.S. rely on international students and workers? Historically, the U.S. has been considered a "preeminent destination for the world's best and brightest," Aw said. Watson described a "pipeline by which we take a really talented, highly educated group of people, and we bring them into our labor force." The route begins with international students getting their undergraduate or more advanced degrees at universities and then working for one year or longer under the OPT program, depending on their field of study. U.S. companies then sponsor highly skilled workers' H1-B visas and eventually those employees may go on to become permanent residents and U.S. citizens. Most of the more than 1 million international students in the U.S. pay full tuition at colleges and universities, which in turn helps subsidize American students' education, said Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education. "There are more spaces in colleges and universities than there are students, there are more opportunities for researchers

A Â£3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.
The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.
At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.
It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the Â£3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.
The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year.
Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other.
Louise Beardmore, chief executive of United Utilities, told the BBC the proposals were a "100 year solution for this lake".
"In the UK we invest in five year periods and so we come along all the time and we do a bit, then we go away and we come back and do a bit more. This is saying we need to do something differently," she said.
Beardmore said she was excited that a broad coalition including her company, regulators, the local authorities and environmental campaigners had come together to draft this proposal which is called "Only Rainwater into Windermere" (ORiW).
Perhaps the unlikeliest member of the group is activist Matt Staniek. He called today's proposal a "milestone".
"For me this is a plan on a piece of paper. It is not definitive action and that's what I want to see." he said. "This is the beginning, and the end of this is the moment that sewage stops entering Windermere."
It will now be up to the government to decide whether the plans are developed further, and if so how.
At present the sewage network around Windermere is fragmented, with homes served by a mix of public wastewater treatment works and privately owned treatment facilities and septic tanks.
When treatment works are overwhelmed, such as during heavy rain, they spill raw sewage. The rest of the time they emit a continuous stream of treated effluent which, while cleaner than raw sewage, can contain high nutrient levels.
On several occasions in the last five years the high nutrient levels and warm temperatures have combined to cause algal blooming turning parts of the lake a lurid green.
The ORiW proposal would see 12,800 people connected to the sewage network for the first time with up to 86 miles (138km) of new sewage infrastructure and a single wastewater treatment works built to serve them at the end of a 4m-wide sewage tunnel.
Two slightly different plans are being put forward. Both have the tunnel at their heart but one would see the treated effluent discharged into the River Leven, the other into the Irish Sea at Ulverston.
The report highlights two options for paying for the project.
One would see the cost passed on to United Utilities' customers and would -depending on the route chosen - add up to Â£3.17 to their monthly bills.
People like Nigel Wilkinson from Love Windermere group, which is linked to many local businesses, would like the cost to be spread nationally, increasing all bills in England by up to 35p a month.
"We believe Windermere is of such national significance and international significance that it is justifiable to treat this as a national asset and fund it accordingly," he says.
Much now depends on the government's enthusiasm for following through on promise made then Environment secretary Steve Reed in March 2025 to stop all sewage going into Windermere.
"We share the public's determination to protect this iconic lake." a Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs spokesperson said, stressing that further work needed to be done to test alternative options.

Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (Â£1.1bn) and SpaceX at $2tn (Â£1.5bn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
How likely is the merger?
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.
The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.
Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.
But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.
Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.
He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.
But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.
"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.
What would it mean for customers?
Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.
In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.
Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.
Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.
Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.
"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.
The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.
The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.
What does Musk get out of it?
The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.
The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.
A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.
"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.
However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.
The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.
Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.
"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.
The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.
To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".
But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.
This story contains some distressing details
Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024.
He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.
Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.
TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.
Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces.
But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.
Bel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation.
He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed.
His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor.
The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case. ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death".
"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case.
In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation.
Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag.
"He went twice to the ICE facilitiesâ¦ begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him."
In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight.
In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year.
Ohio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings.
At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield.
"You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers.
The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer.
"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."
In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY".
The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to.
The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning.
The signs of decades of economic decline are still visible in Springfield, through shuttered factories and boarded up homes.
This part of the American Midwest was hit badly by last century's de-industrialisation, when those laid off from its once prolific factories sought work on the coasts or migrated to warmer, southern states.
Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000 strong arrived in the town. Many fled the devastating earthquake in 2010. Others left Haiti in 2021 during the violence and unrest that followed President Jovenel Moise's assassination.
It meant Springfield's population increased rapidly. With their legal status under TPS, many Haitians took on low-paid jobs in factories and distribution warehouses.

"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"
Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped her and her friend to ask what they thought of what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."
But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, YaÃ«l Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.
French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.
French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.
A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections.
The mass looting of what's said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?
Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. President Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.
Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts has lead former French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.
Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's Interior minister Bernard Quintin, warned of the 'TikTokisation' of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liege on "known far left groups".
In France, Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu and his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire," said Nunez. On Tuesday Mr Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he'd accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader, Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.

7f832356396e.text: In the race to fend off AI-enabled cyber threats , security teams are confronting a new problem: The AI models they rely on to investigate attacks can suddenly refuse to help. Why it matters: While AI giants race to build AI tools that can respond quickly to hacking or other malicious online threats, strict guardrails on their most powerful models lock out defenders mid-investigation, leaving them scrambling for alternatives at critical moments. What's happening: OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, said it was compromised over the weekend, allowing attackers to obtain API keys belonging to some customers, including keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google services. OpenCode said the breach was "related to a large scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users." OpenCode co-creator Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting its systems continuously for 48 hours, forcing the company to keep its own AI agents running around the clock to respond. OpenAI , Google and Anthropic have said they worked with affected customers to revoke exposed API keys and address unauthorized usage charges. Zoom in: Raad said on X that frontier AI models initially helped investigate the breach but then "started refusing." The models' safety restrictions reportedly began blocking requests as the investigation turned to potentially malicious code, even though OpenCode was trying to defend its own systems. OpenCode then gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted cybersecurity defenders access to models with fewer restrictions. "We definitely need to be more proactive and we've made so many improvements over the last few days," Raad wrote on X Monday. The big picture: The incident underscored a dilemma facing cybersecurity teams trying to figure out when to use powerful proprietary AI models, which come with built-in restrictions, or open-weight alternatives that offer greater control over how they're deployed. When Hugging Face discovered suspicious activity on its systems that it later linked to OpenAI's own agents, its security team turned to a Chinese open-weight model to help investigate after encountering restrictions on frontier models. Yes, but: AI companies maintain that they need to gate access to their most powerful models to ensure that malicious actors can't abuse their cyber capabilities. Between the lines: Cybersecurity teams will have to figure out how to balance the need for faster AI-powered defenses with restrictions designed to keep those same capabilities out of attackers' hands, Chris Jones, chief technology officer at Nightwing, told Axios. "We're all going to have to figure out how that race gets modulated over time," Jones said. "That's a big piece here." Go deeper : Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

ea09eb5e8cc7.text: By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/florida-puts-77-year-old-man-to-death-carrying-out-its-18th-execution-of-the-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Florida puts 77-year-old man to death, carrying out its 18th execution of the year Nation Oct 20, 2026 8:20 PM EDT STARKE, Fla. (AP) — Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis ' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the September 1986 shooting death of Indian River County sheriff's deputy Richard Raczkoski. READ MORE: Florida executed a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence. It's the state's 17th execution of the year The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time with Reaves already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last words, he replied "No, I do not." The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves' shoulders and shouted his name, but there was no response. A medic was called in a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later. Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation's aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a year, and it's poised to tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled. DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said he wants justice to be delivered to victims' families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be imposed. Marc Raczkoski, the deputy's brother, briefly told reporters after witnessing the execution that his brother finally got justice. But Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who was also on hand, said at a post-execution briefing that he saw the execution as closure, not justice. "Would we all be so lucky to be 77 years old and to die so peacefully," Flowers said. "That's not justice in any way in my opinion." Reaves struggled with the deputy after dropping a gun Raczkoski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store on Sept. 23, 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store. While the two men talked, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. They then struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. Raczkoski died later that day from his wounds. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and newly sentenced to death in 1992. Subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves' 11th-hour appeal without comment. Lawyers challenged lethal injection procedure The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves' appeals seeking to spare his life. His attorneys challenged Florida's three-drug lethal injection protocol. All Florida executions are carried out via injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld the protocol against similar challenges. Florida's method differs from the single-drug injection used in states such as Tennessee, where condemned inmate Christa Pike was rushed to a hospital last month after surviving two doses of pentobarbital. READ MORE: Christa Pike's attorneys say she is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt Reaves' attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never told the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated the Army veteran as 100% disabled because of post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 military veterans appealed to DeSantis to halt the execution in a letter Monday, citing those factors. Florida close to tying its 2025 record of 19 executions A total of 47 people were executed in the United States in 2025. Florida led the nation that year with 19 executions and has accounted for more than half of the 32 U.S. executions — Reaves included — carried out thus far in 2026. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, becoming the first state in nearly a decade to do so. On Nov. 5, Jesse Guardado, 64, is scheduled to receive a lethal injection in the same Florida death chamber. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a 75-year-old woman while stealing items on a crack cocaine binge in 2004. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. ac8dbdb013ff.text: By — Ope Adetayo, Associated Press Ope Adetayo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/nigeria-confirms-ebola-case-in-its-capital-as-woman-who-arrived-from-uganda-tests-positive Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Nigeria confirms Ebola case in its capital as woman who arrived from Uganda tests positive World Oct 20, 2026 8:06 PM EDT LAGOS, Nigeria (AP) — Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the Health Ministry said. The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria. READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. "We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had," he said. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus. Uganda's Ministry of Health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo's eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality. "Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has "no confirmed active Ebola cases." Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the latest outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that "we are facing an extremely serious threat," with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases. "This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa," he said. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country's preparedness for a potential outbreak. "These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers," the agency said. Nigeria established an Ebola task force in June following the outbreak in Congo in mid-May. "We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat." The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people. The latest outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa's regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said. Nigeria was one of the countries affected, recording 20 cases before the outbreak was declared over in the country after three months. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. ed81b69d85ee.text: Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is pouring $4 million into a bombshell ad in which his opponent's estranged mother attacks her daughter — doubling down on the message despite fierce bipartisan backlash, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Ramaswamy is gambling that the deeply personal attack by Amy Acton's mother — who Acton has said sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted Acton when she was 12 — will resonate with voters. After the ad began appearing Tuesday on social media, many fellow Republicans urged Ramaswamy to distance his campaign from it. They warned it could backfire at a time when the controversy over the Epstein files has elevated the sexual abuse of children as a national campaign issue. Driving the news: Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed to Axios that it produced the ad, which began circulating on social media late Monday without language identifying its sponsor. Sources close to Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with "persuadable" voters, prompting the decision to launch a $4 million statewide campaign that began streaming Tuesday night. Catch up quick: The minute-long commercial features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. "She lies about her past," Arthur says. "She's lied her entire life." Arthur also disputes Acton's account of experiencing homelessness as a child. The other side: Acton, a physician, has said she was sexually abused at age 12 by her stepfather, who faced criminal charges, and that her mother sided with him. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. According to her brother, their mother remained married to Acton's alleged abuser until his death. Acton, 60, has said she hasn't seen her mother since childhood. In a statement posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Acton said that "between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me." "I've always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it's sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain." Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, called Ramaswamy's ad "disgusting." What they're saying: Despite bipartisan criticism, Ramaswamy's campaign continued to treat the mother's statements as campaign gold. "This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton. The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing told Axios. Several prominent Republicans and conservative commentators blasted the ad, arguing that it could generate sympathy for Acton. Republican strategist David Urban on CNN drew a parallel to the Epstein controversy, warning that voters are especially sympathetic to victims of sexual assault and that the ad could backfire. "It seems crazy to me one would assume this would work and not backfire," conservative commentator Mary Katharine Ham posted on X. Yes, but: Some conservatives defended the commercial, including Donald Trump Jr., who urged Ohio voters to "watch [it] and think about what it means." By the numbers: A mid-October Marist survey showed Acton leading Ramaswamy 50% to 43% among likely voters. What's next: Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted are set to campaign with Vice President Vance in Cincinnati on Wednesday.

Has Washington's long-standing policy of isolating the military regime in Myanmar now changed?
The revelation that a top official in the Trump administration met its leader Min Aung Hlaing last month, and the removal of some business figures from the US sanctions list, suggests that it has.
Until now, the US had had very little official contact with the regime following the 2021 coup, when Myanmar's military ousted democratically-elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. More recently, it had applied a series of targeted sanctions against those judged to be supporting the junta.
The meeting on 15 and 16 September was with US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, and it took place in Myanmar's capital Nay Pyi Taw. Its ostensible focus was to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen who had been detained in June over a dispute with the local American Chamber of Commerce.
But Vance was the most senior US official to meet Min Aung Hlaing since he seized power, and they almost certainly discussed other matters of mutual interest.
Vance is also known to have met Burmese officials in Tokyo in June, again in Tokyo this month, and to have met representatives of the groups opposing military rule.
Signs of a shift in US policy towards Myanmar, though, go back to July last year, at the height of President Donald Trump's tariff war.
That was when Min Aung Hlaing, along with other leaders in the region, received a personal letter from the US president informing him that his country's shattered economy was about to be hit by, in Myanmar's case, 40% tariffs.
Other countries reeled in shock at the punitive levies imposed on their vital trade with a country they had once seen as a friend and ally.
But Min Aung Hlaing was delighted.
He replied immediately to express his "sincere appreciation for this encouraging invitation to continue participating in the extraordinary Economy of the United States, the Number One Market in the World", mimicking Trump's hyperbolic phrasing and eccentric capitalisation.
"It is with great esteem that I wish to acknowledge Your Excellency's strong leadership in guiding your country toward national prosperity with the spirit of a true patriot."
This was not just a dictator's hunch that flattery might be the best way to win favours from Trump. Min Aung Hlaing's coup, and the civil war it ignited, had turned him into an international pariah.
His regime was largely unrecognised. He was accused of being a war criminal, with cases lodged against him at the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Aside from Russia and, more recently, China, he was shunned by other governments.
Yet here was the US president addressing him just like any other president or prime minister, as "Your Excellency. There was no mention in Trump's letter of the appalling human cost of Min Aung Hlaing's power seizure; of a democracy crushed and leader Aung San Suu Kyi jailed.
That same month the regime signed a $3m (Â£2.3m) contract with DCI, a long-standing Washington lobbying firm which had been used by a previous Burmese military regime in 2002 to try to improve its image.
Since then the military government has also hired Roger Stone, a controversial lobbyist and confidant of President Trump, at a fee of $50,000 a month.
Also around the same time Adam Castillo, a former US marine and Trump supporter who had just stepped down as president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Yangon, was in Washington trying to persuade Vice President JD Vance's team that it was time to re-engage.
Castillo believed that the US reliance on sanctions to isolate the junta had failed.
"Myanmar mattered to America not only as a morality play but as a strategic interest," he wrote in his book Finding Our Voice: A Story of Leadership in Crisis and the American Spirit Abroad. He discussed with the vice-president's team how the US "could engage Myanmar without war or isolation, loosen China's grip on critical minerals, and align peace with American interests".
Castillo was pushing at an open door.
The US dependence on rare earths from China had been exposed when China blocked them in retaliation against Trump's tariffs in April. The administration began prioritising finding alternative sources. Myanmar happens to have large reserves of rare earths which are currently being exploited solely for China's use.
At almost exactly the same time, the state department issued new guidance to US embassies around the world on what to say about elections. From now on, it said, "messages should avoid opining on the fairness or integrity of an electoral process, its legitimacy, or the democratic values of the country in question".
So, when Myanmar held its much-criticised general election in December and January, allowing Min Aung Hlaing to turn himself from coup leader into a notionally civilian president, the US did not, like most Western governments, condemn it as neither free nor fair.
For decades the US has consistently pronounced judgement on other countries' elections. Now the US had nothing to say.
Washington's decision to lift sanctions on some of those targeted by the Biden administration seemed only to confirm the new direction of US-Myanmar policy.
"For years, the US approach toâ¯Myanmar has been defined by isolation, sanctions, and distance," wrote the lobbyists DCI in a recent newsletter. "That era is overâ¦ thankfully, President Trump has the courage to try something different."
The tone is certainly different, but not so much the substance of US-Myanmar relations.
"In practice less has changed than the headlines suggest," says Richard Horsey, Myanmar adviser for the International Crisis Group, adding that Min Aung Hlaing is still sanctioned. "What is new is the level of contact and the location. Senior US officials have now been to Nay Pyi Taw, which is exactly what Min Aung Hlaing wanted. What he wants next is sanctions relief, and that will be harder."

"Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.
It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.
But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.
Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.
Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief â at home, and beyond its borders.
Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."
Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too.
"Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.
Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".
Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south â in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.
The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls.
"I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."
For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.
In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" â even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.
He didn't have to.
And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer â including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.
But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast.
"Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto.
"Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.
An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets â a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.
At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.
After Monday's vote, Carney â the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance â pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials.
"Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.
At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.
Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.
The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union.
"I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.
For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home â including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.
And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".
The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth.
"Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of it

Travel disruption and damage to buildings are expected when Storm Austen, the first named storm of the autumn, hits south Wales later this week.
The Met Office said the storm will bring a spell of strong winds up to 70mph (112km/h) overnight on Thursday and into Friday, mainly in coastal areas.
The yellow warning, external for Wales was issued on Wednesday morning, with periods of heavy rain also expected. The Met Office said injuries and danger to life from flying debris are possible.
Some roads and bridges may close, and longer journey times and cancellations to public transport are possible.
The weather warning is in place between 00:00 and 14:00 BST on Friday.
Gusts of wind about 50 to 60mph are likely to hit areas such as Cardiff, Swansea and Merthyr Tydfil.
Some coastal or exposed areas could see about 70mph gusts of wind, the Met Office said, adding winds will slowly ease during Friday afternoon.

The barn owls have become one of Richard Peace's favourite sights on the farm.
As dusk falls near the woods edging his land outside Nuneaton in Warwickshire, the birds emerge to hunt over fields he has spent years managing.
This year he wanted to do more to help them thrive.
To encourage the owls, Richard planned to leave some crops unharvested near the woodland where they live.
"Obviously that will bring some of the wildlife out of the woods, like voles and mice, and I was hoping that the barn owls would then thrive even more than they are already," he said.
But leaving part of a crop in the ground comes at a cost.
The government offers support to farmers carrying out environmental work through schemes that pay for so-called public goods, from improving habitats to boosting biodiversity.
For Richard, accessing some of the Â£310m funding from the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) scheme seemed straightforward enough. All he had to do was submit an application.
What he did not realise was that he was entering a race against thousands of other farmers for that limited pot of cash.
"We looked at 8am and it wasn't live. I had things to do so I went to work on the farm," he said.
"Checked again at lunchtime, it was live and I started. We had a few errors but I did get to the end of the form and submitted it.
"I was minutes too late and the scheme had been subscribed. The money pot was exhausted."
Richard is among thousands of farmers who missed out after funding was snapped up within hours.
He believes smaller family farms may have been at a disadvantage.
While some larger businesses could dedicate staff to monitoring the application process, Richard spent the morning carrying out day-to-day work on the farm before returning to complete his submission.
The National Farmers' Union (NFU) had already warned that demand could outstrip the available funding.
Helen Fisher, who farms near Atherstone and is deputy regional chair of the NFU Midlands, said: "The scheme opened and closed in six hours. Nobody had anticipated that level of demand.
"We had been warning Defra there would be high demand and 12,000 farmers just couldn't get their applications in in time."
Richard believes a first-come, first-served system is the wrong way to allocate support.
"It should be available to everybody, those applications should then be evaluated," he said.
"If the scheme is oversubscribed the larger payments should be scaled back so that smaller farmers can get a slice of the larger pot."
Farmers in the Midlands often operate on a smaller scale than elsewhere in England, although regional data showing who ultimately benefited from the scheme is not publicly available.
Stories like Richard's have become increasingly familiar, and ministers have acknowledged concerns about the way applications were handled.
Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: "I know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be deeply disappointed not to have secured an agreement during Window 2, particularly given the challenges the sector has faced this year.
"I have heard those concerns and am determined to work closely with farmers as we learn lessons from this year and shape SFI27, including exploring alternatives to a first-come, first-served application process."
For Richard, the hope is that by next year the system will be fairer and allow more farmers to access support for projects that benefit wildlife.
If that happens, the barn owls he enjoys watching over his farm may have an even better chance of thriving.

d55c6fa04e54.text: Executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file workers to trust AI over their own judgment, per a survey out Wednesday morning. Why it matters: It's a worrying development. Leaders are hired for their experience and knowledge. Outsourcing that to AI raises the risk of making decisions that don't line up with reality, which then reverberate across companies and beyond. By the numbers: 32.8% of executives said that they trust AI more than their own judgment, according to the survey from Charter, a workplace research and media company. That's twice the rate for workers, or individual contributors. Just 16.3% of individual contributors said the same. The divide shows up at the level below executives — 34.8% of managers said they trust AI more than their own judgment. Zoom out: "Cognitive offloading" is a term for using tools like AI to reduce mental effort. "Executives—despite having the most experience—are doing it more than anyone," the report's coauthors wrote. By the numbers: Charter in August surveyed 5,002 U.S. office workers, at companies with at least 100 employees, who said they use AI at work, including 2,952 individual contributors, 1,547 managers and 503 executives — including vice presidents, C-suite executives, owners and founders. Between the lines: Most executives are under a lot of pressure to know the answers to a lot of questions really quickly — and AI can help with that at least in the short term, says report coauthor Brian Elliott, a former Slack executive who is now executive-in-residence at Charter and co-wrote the report. AI "lends itself very well to the 'seldom wrong, never in doubt' tendency that some executives have," he says. "If you feel like you have to fake it until you make it as an executive, then AI is certainly going to feed those tendencies because you can appear to be really smart, really quick." Zoom in: He described tech executives who use AI to build product prototypes over a weekend, then expect their teams to quickly turn those into functioning products — without appreciating the more complicated work involved. "AI is really good at giving you the executive summary. It's not necessarily as good at giving you the very specific answer to the problem you've got today, which is more often what an individual contributor faces." Reality check: The Charter survey measures executives' self-reported trust in AI, but not whether they actually follow its advice when making consequential decisions. The report's findings were overall positive about AI's potential in the workplace. 42.7% of AI users said it improved both their work and personal lives. Friction point: A key tension for workers is the threat of AI job loss, the researchers observed in separate qualitative interviews with 91 more workers. The better workers become with AI, the more they realize how much can be done without them, the survey found. There's a "persistent tension." The bottom line: Executives are mostly free from that tension, says Elliott. "The odds that an AI CEO shows up and takes over a company are excruciatingly low."

President Vladimir Putin says Russia has agreed to release a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, state media is reporting.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said, during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
Hubbard, a former teacher originally from Michigan, was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024.
Prosecutors had accused him of serving in a defence unit in the eastern city of Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine two years earlier.
The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard as "wrongfully detained", and on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said that he had raised his case with Putin.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused â on âHubbard".
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
Russian state media reported that Witkoff had thanked Putin for Hubbard's release and, on Trump's behalf, for the deal struck with Washington earlier this month to import Russian diesel.
The first shipment under the agreement will leave Russia "in two to three days", Putin said during the meeting, as quoted by state news agency TASS.
The diesel deal has infuriated Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and seen diplomatic relations between Kyiv and Washington further deteriorate.
During Wednesday's meeting in St Petersburg, Witkoff was filmed by Russian TV saying the deal was an example to Ukraine of what could be achieved by working together.
"Your decision to remove export controls on diesel oil from Russia, not just to the US but also to the world at large in the midst of an economic shock, I think that was really important that that happened," he said.
"I know [President Trump] is deeply grateful for it."

15a774e6f7f6.text: Republicans and Democrats are flooding the midterm airwaves with explosive TV ads accusing their opponents of protecting pedophiles and child sexual abusers. Why it matters: The advertising blitz underscores the lingering power of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal , which has fueled distrust of powerful figures and pushed allegations of child sexual abuse to the forefront of national politics. The controversy over the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files — including allegations that officials sought to protect powerful figures by not releasing all of the files — has kept the issue in the headlines. The midterm ads that have followed have been bipartisan and are playing out in state and federal races. By the numbers: Since Sept. 1, candidates and outside groups have aired at least $70 million in TV ads mentioning pedophilia, Epstein and allegations related to child sexual abuse, according to AdImpact. Of the 118 ads identified, 63 were sponsored by Democrats, 52 by Republicans and three by independents. Driving the news: The issue has become a flashpoint in the competitive Senate race in Kansas, where Democrats unveiled three ads Tuesday attacking Republican Sen. Roger Marshall over his initial vote against a measure to force the Justice Department to release additional Epstein files. Meanwhile, the conservative Club for Growth has been airing an ad accusing pastor Adam Hamilton, Marshall's Democratic opponent, of mishandling sexual abuse allegations involving a church camp volunteer. The allegations date to 2005, when church leaders initially investigated accusations involving boys at the camp rather than immediately contacting police. Hamilton has released a commercial in which he denies a cover-up. The Club for Growth's ad closely resembles promotional materials for the new movie "Primetime," which is inspired by the former NBC TV series "To Catch a Predator." In Texas, Democrats backing Senate candidate James Talarico have spent more than $8 million on ads attacking his opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), over his office's initial offer of a plea deal calling for just one day in jail for a man accused of sexually abusing a child. Paxton says he agreed to the deal to spare a child abuse victim from having to testify in court a second time. In North Carolina, meanwhile, Democrats have aired four ads accusing Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley of appointing a convicted sex offender to a state GOP committee. Whatley has denied hiring the man. "It's an issue that goes to character and judgment," said John Anzalone, a veteran Democratic pollster who's advising Whatley's Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Behind the scenes: Private GOP polling in Kansas, provided to Axios, illustrates why strategists believe the attacks can resonate. After hearing allegations about Hamilton's handling of the church camp incident, 69% of Kansas voters surveyed said they were less likely to support him, strategists found. State of play: Republicans' embrace of the attacks marks a striking turn for a party that spent months on the defensive over the Trump administration's resistance to releasing additional Epstein files. Some GOP strategists see the attacks as a way to put Democrats on defense as Republicans struggle to sell voters on Trump's agenda. Democrats have spent much of the campaign hammering Republicans over high prices. But with voters' views on the economy largely set, attack ads are increasingly focused on issues of character and judgment. What they're saying: "Epstein reinforced the suspicion that powerful people protect each other and operate under different rules," Republican pollster Chris Wilson told Axios. "Allegations involving children are especially visceral, and [the collapse of trust in institutions] gives them added resonance."

The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for strong winds as Storm Austen is forecast to sweep across parts of the UK.
The warning - the second-highest tier that the Met Office issues - is valid for Cornwall and parts of west Devon from 03:00 until 10:00 BST on Friday.
Wind gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) are expected around exposed coasts, with 60-70mph gusts elsewhere.
Flying debris could lead to injuries or a danger to life, with the risk of power cuts and damage to buildings.
A broader yellow Met Office wind warning covers large swathes of southern England and south Wales with some travel disruption possible.
When will Storm Austen arrive?
Storm Austen is currently developing in the Atlantic and will continue to deepen as it approaches the UK.
It will move close to south-west England on Thursday night with the strongest winds expected to arrive early on Friday morning.
The very windiest conditions are expected on coastal headlands in north and west Cornwall - exposed to the north-westerly gales - but gusts of up to 70mph could occur even in inland areas.
According to the Met Office there is a high risk of 'significant' disruption with possible delays to road and rail transport.
Air and ferry services could also be affected.
Injuries and danger to life are likely from flying debris and large waves along the coast. Some power cuts are also possible.

9203dcaed0dc.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy. Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips. The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models. If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky. Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin. In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand , that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush. In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church. In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days. In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance." Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants. In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa. For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative. Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts. Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining. What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating. His Berlin keynote offers another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet. The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company.

0d5453566113.text: Anthropic's impending IPO will test a jittery Wall Street , but investors say the timing isn't optional. The reason is simple math: the AI giant has grown too big for private fundraising. Why it matters: Top AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are racking up 12-figure spending commitments, straining the financial system's ability to keep up with a buildout that rivals America's railroads or interstate highways. With private borrowing costs spiking, tapping the massive liquidity of the public markets is the best way to fund the next phase of the AI arms race, investors say. State of play: Anthropic's computing commitments could reach $750 billion in the coming years, according to a draft IPO prospectus seen by The Wall Street Journal . The company already faces more than $600 billion in future infrastructure costs and is negotiating additional deals that could add another $150 billion. While Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the company also disclosed an $80.7 billion net loss over the same period, though most of that is tied to accounting charges related to fundraising, per the WSJ. Zoom in: That math points to a numbers problem that can only be solved by public markets, investors tell Axios. OpenAI's most recent fundraising round — the biggest in history — is a case in point. It took the company months to secure more than $120 billion in financing, a historic feat that is unlikely to be repeated in this market climate. While demand for Anthropic shares is absurdly high — just ask the guy who offered up his near $5 million home to get some — the souring market climate significantly raises the stakes for a public listing. If it goes well, it could help reset investor angst about the stability of the AI boom. Public markets will provide a deeper pool of financing as Anthropic expands beyond traditional venture capital. Follow the money: The pool of cash on the private markets side is getting harder to tap. Anthropic is offering Blackstone a yield exceeding 10% on $9 billion in junior debt as part of a record $60 billion chip-financing package, according to the Financial Times . That's above the 8.5% rate on an earlier financing deal, suggesting private investors are demanding greater compensation for taking on AI-related risks. Between the lines: Private markets have done the heavy lifting on AI investing long enough, and they're ready for somebody else to carry the load. Anthropic was widely expected to go public in September before one of its researchers quit and a raft of safety incidents brought new public awareness to AI safety concerns. Now, Anthropic is expected to IPO before Thanksgiving . Zoom out: The IPO follows anxiety on Wall Street regarding the AI trade, especially as companies specializing in renting computing capacity and building data centers confront market skepticism. Nvidia-backed Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned IPO amid market volatility. South Korean AI cloud provider Elice saw its shares plunge 32% in their trading debut despite rapid revenue growth. Meanwhile, concerns about AI infrastructure debt have pushed borrowing costs for CoreWeave sharply higher, with yields on some of its bonds approaching 15%. Reality check: Anthropic isn't just any AI startup. One Anthropic investor told Axios the company is simply ready to go public given its size and maturity. The investor also described Anthropic's latest financial results as "spectacular," pushing back on concerns about slowing revenue growth. The bottom line: Anthropic may have to go public in less than perfect conditions, but investors see an IPO as the best way to put the AI boom to the market's ultimate test.
