States Are Forcing Hospitals To Offer More People Financial Aid. In Oregon, It’s Working.
Four years ago, Oregon hospitals were under fire from state authorities and patient advocates. Hospitals, critics said, had made it too hard for patients to apply for and receive help paying their bills.
Within months, the state enacted a sweeping law that required hospitals to proactively screen patients and give financial aid to those who qualify for it. Oregon’s new rules, which took effect in July 2024, required hospitals to skip applications for nearly all patients — a rarity among hospitals nationwide.
“They will be told up front, Hey, we got you,” said Democratic Oregon state Sen. Lisa Reynolds, who introduced the legislation. “You are here at a very scary time in your life because of illness or injury, and we got your back.”
The law worked.
Oregon Health & Science University’s hospital, one of the largest in the state, saw 64% of its patients automatically qualify for financial assistance in the early months of the new law, up from 12% previously.
In their first full fiscal year under the law, spending by Oregon hospitals on financial assistance more than doubled, on average, according to federal financial reports from about two-thirds of the state’s hospitals. That’s compared with their last full year before the change.
For patients, the switch meant direct relief from high healthcare costs, advocates said.
“They don’t have to have the late nights being like, how am I going to afford my mortgage? How am I going to afford these medical bills?” said Adam Zarrin, a director of state government affairs for the advocacy group Blood Cancer United.
Hospitals in the state have pushed back on the requirements, saying they need better screening tools, and they face added financial strain from the Trump administration’s domestic policy agenda. Millions of people are projected to lose health insurance in coming years under cuts to Medicaid pushed through by Republicans in Congress.
Oregon’s early success is the first big test of a new approach that more states are turning to, known as presumptive eligibility. Hospitals skip the applications and screen patients automatically to determine if they qualify for aid.
North Carolina this year expanded its screening requirement to include patients with income up to triple the poverty line. California and Delaware are requiring hospitals to automatically grant financial aid by July 2027.
A Promising Tool To Prevent Medical Debt
As many as 100 million adults in the U.S. have healthcare debt, according to a KFF Health News analysis. That financial burden can alter people’s lives, forcing them to skip prescriptions and follow-up care to avoid further bills.
Hospitals are a major source of that debt, and they have faced growing scrutiny over their prices and billing practices.
Policymakers have focused specifically on nonprofit hospitals, which account for about half the sector. Nonprofit hospitals typically don’t pay taxes, in exchange for providing benefits to their communities — a vaguely defined standard under federal law. Many hospitals meet this requirement by providing free or discounted care to low-income patients.
That financial assistance, however, can be difficult to get. Applications can be onerous and confusing. Congress and state officials have spent years testing policies to promote the help and make it easier to receive, with mixed results.
Research finds hospital financial aid spending varies, as does the degree to which hospitals benefit by not paying property, sales, or income taxes.
“Hospitals have been on the winning side of this deal for a long time,” said Reynolds, the Oregon lawmaker. “They enjoy millions and millions and millions of dollars in tax breaks, and that money is supposed to be then spent on poor people who can’t afford their care or even their copayments. It has not penciled out.”
Reynolds pressed for Oregon’s screening requirement, she said, to hold hospitals “accountable for what they should have been doing all along.”
Early evidence suggests the law is doing what Reynolds hoped. Oregon hospitals’ spending on free and discounted care increased to 2.7% of all operating expenses, on average, from 1.4%, among the roughly two-thirds of hospitals with available federal data.
That brings hospitals in Oregon closer to the national average for nonprofit hospitals, which from 2021 to 2024 was about 2.4%, according to an analysis by Johns Hopkins University researcher Hossein Zare, who studies the industry.
More Help for the Insured
Among those in Oregon who started to get more help: patients with health insurance.
OHSU’s spending on help for insured patients reached about $39 million in the first year under the law, federal data shows, about five times as much as in previous years.
Lawrence Furnstahl, then OHSU’s chief financial officer, said in a public meeting in January 2025 that, before the law, insured patients often didn’t apply for help and instead paid their share of the bills. The new automatic screening often wiped out or reduced what they owed — including for large deductibles that patients have to meet out-of-pocket before insurance will kick in.
Patients who pay hospital bills often still carry medical debt, surveys show, because many use credit cards or loans from family, friends, or banks to afford their care.
A 2025 survey from the Commonwealth Fund found that 1 in 3 adults with private insurance have medical debt.
“It defies the purpose of health insurance coverage, which is to enable people to get healthcare when they need it and protect them from serious costs,” said Sara Collins, an economist and senior scholar with the Commonwealth Fund.
‘A Very Different World’

New Arrivals in the ER? Georgia Gears Up To Solve Rural Maternal Health Crisis
LAVONIA, Ga. — It had been a decade since Kara Holden last had a baby. But as the former obstetric nurse prepared for her fourth child, her head was swimming with contingency plans.
The labor and delivery unit where she used to work in this rural northeastern Georgia community is no longer open. So, she asked former co-workers to be on standby around her anticipated due date. She and her midwife mapped out emergency rooms along the more-than-50-mile trek to the hospital in Greenville, South Carolina, where she planned to give birth. And, to prepare for a worst-case scenario, she curated items to keep in the car in case she went into labor en route.
“That’s a horrible place to put a pregnant woman in,” said Holden, who on Oct. 11 made the painful, hourlong trip to Greenville Memorial Hospital to deliver her son Tucker.
Holden lives roughly midway between Athens and Greenville, two of the nearest cities with labor and delivery units. Owing partly to Medicaid cuts from President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, St. Mary’s Sacred Heart Hospital in Lavonia stopped providing obstetric services nearly a year ago. Its closure is part of a trend touching rural communities nationwide. From South Dakota to Alabama and from Ohio to California, low Medicaid reimbursement and dwindling birth rates are pushing hospitals to shutter these services. Today, fewer than half of rural hospitals offer labor and delivery services.
In Georgia, only 36% of rural hospitals have a labor and delivery unit, and four have closed since 2020, according to data from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform.
To address the challenge the closings pose to patients seeking care, the state — which ranks among the worst in the nation for maternal health outcomes — has turned to federal money from the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. This fund was created by congressional Republicans to offset concerns about the outsize fallout Trump’s signature legislation would have in rural communities.
More than $12 million — out of the nearly $219 million approved for Georgia in the program’s first year — will be allocated toward placing obstetric carts in 43 rural hospitals without labor and delivery units. The carts will be outfitted with supplies needed for a birth or obstetric emergency. For example, they’ll have neonatal resuscitation tools, thermal blankets, and essential medications such as oxytocin, which stimulates contractions, and magnesium sulfate, used to treat seizures in pregnant people with high blood pressure.
The delivery carts sound fine, in theory, said Justin Peterson, an OB-GYN who practices in southern Georgia and has seen the pressures rural health institutions face providing maternal care.
Like Holden, Peterson worries that the carts, while helpful, will put supplies in the hands of ER doctors lacking extensive obstetric experience. Instead, he wants the state to fill coverage gaps by investing more to prevent the closure of labor and delivery units in rural areas.
“You’re putting a band-aid on a hemorrhage,” he said.
‘Can’t Practice Scared’
Brittany Mitchell was about seven months pregnant when Sacred Heart’s labor and delivery unit closed. She was reassigned to an OB-GYN in Athens, even though the nearly 50-mile drive from Lavonia was stressful and inconvenient.
That OB-GYN wanted to see Mitchell weekly after finding high levels of protein in her urine — a warning sign of preeclampsia, which can cause organ damage, seizures, and other complications. To make it to those prenatal appointments, she routinely gave up a day of work as a home health aide, a job she said already didn’t pay much.
But if Mitchell were to have another baby, she said, she’d still prefer to drive to Athens to see an OB-GYN than be treated by an ER doctor. When she had her first child nine years ago, the local OB-GYN had to act quickly when her daughter briefly lost oxygen.
“If they were in that situation,” she wondered of ER doctors, “would they know how to do all that?”
In written responses to KFF Health News, Lauren Williams, director of communications for the Georgia Department of Community Health, said that training ER medical staff is the main goal of the obstetric cart initiative. The rollout will include simulation drills, during which ER staff will practice high-risk procedures.
The Georgia Hospital Association will procure and distribute the carts. When exactly that will happen is unknown, but the grant funding must be spent by Sept. 30, 2027, said Anna Adams, the organization’s chief government relations officer.
The concept of obstetric carts is great, said Justin Law, an emergency doctor with SouthlandMD, a physician-owned and -operated healthcare management and staffing company. Most items planned for the carts are already available in ERs. But having them in one organized spot will be helpful, he said.
Still, while ER doctors are more frequently positioned at the front lines as labor and delivery closures persist, advocates argue that they shouldn’t be used as a stopgap in obstetric care.
In the decade he’s worked across rural Georgia, Law said, he’s never delivered a baby in the ER even though he’s trained in emergency obstetrics and has experience delivering babies as a paramedic. When a mother needs an emergency cesarean section or has another high-risk complication, she would likely be transferred to a hospital with labor and delivery capabilities, Law said.
Holden, the former obstetric nurse, said familiarity with obstetric delivery practices and procedures is essential because some complications can’t wait for a transfer. “You’re not going to save anybody’s life just because you got access to some equipment,” she said.

Over the past year, boats have plied the waters around Hinkley Point C, a nuclear power plant under construction along England’s Somerset coast, laying and testing a network of ultrasonic speakers across the seabed.
This technology, set to drive fish away from the plant’s deadly cooling pipes, is expected to save fewer than one salmon, fewer than one sea trout, six river lamprey, 18 Allis shad and between approximately 100 and 528 twaite shad each year.
This is one of three protections for fish in the nearby Severn estuary, built into the plant’s original planning and environmental approvals, set to cost French-owned EDF Energy, which leads the project, more than $926 million.
For some of nuclear’s proponents, the price tag reflects an exacting regulatory system that has slowed nuclear development and channeled huge sums toward site-specific mitigation where it could be better used to deliver broader benefits for nature. This argument was put forth in the 2025 Fingleton Review, a government-commissioned examination of the regulatory barriers facing nuclear projects, which called for “radical reforms.”
Embracing the premise, the government is now pursuing an innovative funding strategy to usher in a “golden age” of nuclear power to strengthen energy security, meet its 2050 net-zero target and supply the growing electricity demands of data centers. Britain is betting over $22 billion through 2030 on what it calls its “most ambitious nuclear new-build programme for a generation.”
Based upon so-called Environmental Delivery Plans, the new approach would anticipate projects’ environmental impacts, set out conservation measures deemed sufficient to address them, and calculate costs aimed at securing “environmental uplift.”
Developers would make single payments into a Nature Restoration Fund managed by Natural England, the government’s environmental regulator, discharging their relevant obligations without the need for project-specific environmental surveys and old-school mitigation efforts. The Nature Restoration Fund was first introduced in the 2025 Planning and Infrastructure Act to help unblock housing development.
The government says Natural England could pool those payments to deliver “conservation measures at scale” and maximize the outcome for the environment, with ministers calling it a “win-win” for nature and development.
Much of this work will be contracted to private-sector organizations, such as habitat banks and ecological consultancies, or environmental non-governmental organizations.
Not everyone is impressed. Alexa Culver, an environmental law and policy specialist, calls the approach “ecologically illiterate,” echoing a sentiment expressed by many others in the broader environmental community, who say traditional regulation is being scapegoated for nuclear’s time and cost overruns, with selective examples used to make the case for rolling back environmental protections.
The Case for Conservation at Scale
Natural England’s new chief executive began his tenure Oct. 1 by endorsing the shift from “site-by-site mitigation to work at scale.” Still, the push toward landscape-scale conservation, which the Environmental Delivery Plans could advance, is not new.
In 2010, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs commissioned a review led by ecologist Sir John Lawton to assess whether England’s wildlife sites were capable of responding to climate change and growing demands on land.
Its conclusion: “The essence of what needs to be done to enhance the resilience and coherence of England’s ecological network can be summarised in four words: more, bigger, better and joined.”
The idea helped give rise to England’s Nature Improvement Areas, which offer an example of what landscape-scale conservation can look like in practice.
The Birmingham & Black Country Nature Improvement Area, a partnership of more than 50 organizations, covers some 60,000 hectares across one of England’s most heavily urbanized regions.
Its work spans creating more habitat, new woodland and species-rich grassland and meadows, on sites such as capped landfills, linking them to existing core ecological areas. These efforts improved the quality of existing habitat by reintroducing appropriate land-management techniques, clearing invasive plant species and introducing those sourced from remaining old woodland or ancient meadows. Wildlife corridors, or “linking areas,” were also improved where they had been degraded, narrowed or broken by development. In one project, a heavily engineered stretch of river was freed from pipes and widened to allow it to flow more naturally.
Jeff Ollerton, an ecologist and environmental consultant, sees an opportunity for EDPs to advance landscape-scale restoration if done well. “The devil will be in the details,” he said.
Richard Cowell, a professor of environmental policy and planning at Cardiff University, also acknowledged potential benefits of the approach.
“You could do more strategic, large-scale mitigation, where the problems in conservation are that a lot of pepper-potting and small areas may not help achieve greater nature reversal in the ways we might want.”
But he cautioned that the approach would require both institutional capacity and land that can realistically be restored.
“Natural England needs to have the time and capacity to do it,” Cowell said. “Plus, we are a full country. The idea that there’s space enough to easily recreate large areas of habitat where existing interests exist is problematic.”
Despite Natural England’s public support for the Natural Restoration Fund and EDPs, internal emails obtained by Greenshank Environmental through a Freedom of Information request show that staff at the agency and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have raised concerns that developer payments may not “come in fast enough to take forward sufficient conservation measures.”

The share of Americans who believe the federal government is effective at improving their lives has dropped significantly since last year, a warning sign for Republicans struggling to assuage votersâ cost of living concerns and keep control of Washington.
Forty-three percent of US adults say the federal government is effective at bettering peopleâs lives, down from 51% in 2025, according to a new Bentley University-Gallup survey.
In comparison, 58% say state and local governments improve their lives, while 56% say the same of businesses and 77% of charitable and advocacy groups.
At the same time, more than nine in 10 Americans say the federal government has the power to make a positive impact on society â suggesting many believe the current administration is not making use of that power.

Design It For Us, a youth-led group that advocates for guardrails on Big Tech companies, is releasing an ambitious 2027 AI policy platform, shared first with Semafor. Its top goals: Prevent catastrophic risk, allow states to pass their own laws, protect against digital fakes, and focus on design that helps and protects people.
The platform is based on feedback from 700+ members across 40 states, co-founder Zamaan Qureshi said. He added that Anthropicâs recently leaked bill falls short and said the group is calling on Congress to pass a bill by the end of 2027, âbecause itâs our future on the line.â
The group says itâs shaped several must-haves by taking lessons from Washingtonâs failure to regulate social media. Among them: The government should be able to block the deployment of dangerous models; large AI companies should be required to have independent testing and meet minimum standards for capabilities; companies should be liable for their projects injuring people; and states should have leeway to regulate AI.
âThe decisions about AI today will define the world we inherit,â the groupâs policy platform states. âWe cannot afford to be excluded. Those who build and regulate AI systems must be accountable to the generation that will live with these consequences the longest.â
Design It For Us has played an active role in debates on Capitol Hill over kidsâ online safety bills, often influencing lawmakers to draft stronger legislation â but one of its key legislative goals, the Kids Online Safety Act, has yet to pass Congress. However, if Democrats focus on AI safety after winning control of one or both chambers of Congress next month, the groupâs work on AI issues leaves it well-positioned.

The Scene
The cozy Capitol Hill restaurant â and favorite MAGA clubhouse â Butterworthâs is closed on Friday mornings, so Nick Solheim let me in through a side door.
American Moment, the group he cofounded in 2021, was leading a training upstairs for a group of earnest young right-wing political staffers, 17 men and one woman. When I poked my head into the room, they were listening to one of the heterodox economists orbiting the Trump White House explain what is wrong with traditional notions of free trade.
These young conservatives are the vanguard of a new class in Washington that you encounter at the junior levels of federal agencies and congressional offices. It left me wondering: Where did all these very nice, very young, and very MAGA kids come from? When I worked as a reporter in Washington during the George W. Bush and Obama administrations, the ambitious young conservatives were involved in Republican politics at Penn or writing for the conservative student newspaper at Dartmouth. They would go on to become the so-called neocons â many of whom still occupy positions of power in conservative Washington, though their politics have shifted to better match President Donald Trumpâs.
The members of this new generation are more likely to have grown up outside a city like Columbus, Ohio, and to have gone to state school or Christian college. Solheim, a compact, blond 29-year-old who is American Momentâs CEO, boasts heâs never admitted an Ivy League alumnus to his organization. In their jobs in the Trump administration and Republican congressional offices, American Momentâs fellows do a lot of answering the phones, and they always politely take a message and call back âÂ sometimes with an outrageous Trumpian statement or hardline defense of ICE arrests to pass on.
âI came of age politically when it was really important to have sharp elbows, and I just donât see that in these young conservatives,â said Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts, who calls American Moment âone of the most important organizations in the conservative movement today.â
Solheim started American Moment with Jake Mercier and Saurabh Sharma, the latter of whom left the organization for a senior role in Trumpâs presidential personnel office. The group, which had a $2 million budget in 2024, hasnât sought or gotten much publicity: Sharma said on American Momentâs podcast in 2023 that if he had his preference, âthis would be a completely dark-arts project, almost like a glacier. Youâd see a tiny 10% poking out over top, and the rest of it would happen without any attention whatsoever.â
By then, he said, theyâd trained about 1,500 young conservatives; that number, Solheim said, is now several thousand. (Earlier this month, Solheim would only let me in for a brief, off-the-record peek at the training.)
Their goal has been to bring the Trump generation of young people to Washington. That has partly meant broadening the pipeline beyond those with elite credentials. The program has clear ideological tests: Applicants should oppose immigration, free trade, and foreign adventures.
âOur goal is to create 10,000 Stephen Millers,â Solheim said on the podcast last September. He told me the hardline Trump aide is a model not only for his effectiveness, but also âbecause his career trajectory perfectly tracks what weâre attempting to achieve with our young people. From junior Senate staffer to assistant to the president, and everything in between.â
Much of their training is practical: The group takes in 15-30 paid fellows each semester in its most intensive, paid program, and teaches them to tuck in their shirts, shower daily, and network relentlessly. The training includes mock networking happy hours and credit cards with $100 to take people out to coffee. (Solheim himself favors Butterworthâs Vesper martini.)
The project is well-regarded inside the Trump administration, including by Vice President JD Vance, who was an adviser to American Moment in its early days. Vanceâs former national security adviser, Andy Baker, is joining the group as a senior adviser.Â
âWhen people hire a fellow from American Moment, they know they are getting someone who has had ideological and intellectual formation with whom the principal may agree,â said Rachel Bovard, the vice president of programs at the Conservative Partnership Institute and a member of the groupâs board. âAnd they know the standards of how you should behave.â
American Momentâs critics on the left and the right accuse the group of flying too close to the racism and nihilism of the online right. The groupâs podcast guests have included Jeremy Carl, a Trump administration official whose confirmation faltered because his views on anti-white racism were seen as too extreme. In the spirit of Vanceâs relationship with Tucker Carlson, Solheim and his allies avoid criticizing allies to the right.
But in the taxonomy of the young American right, there are degrees of difference. People involved in American Moment insist they screen for extremist tweets, telling their fellows to stay off the internet and avoid edgelord politics.
âYou havenât seen the Paul Ingrassia types come through American Moment,â said one Trump administration official, referring to a colleague who noted his own âNazi streakâ in leaked text messages.
White supremacist Nick Fuentes, meanwhile, groups American Moment on his enemies list with âneoconsâ and âZionists.â He once delivered an extended racist rant directed at Sharma and the group.
âIf you are at all adjacent to Nick Fuentes or anything he says, you are not getting in,â Bovard said. Instead, the group recognizes that âespecially for young men, thereâs this toxic stew of nihilism and Andrew Tate out there that can be attractive if you have nothing else. Some of the American Moment project is taking young men like that and giving them purpose.â

The Gambia will use funds received from the US from the forfeiture of long-time ruler Yahya Jammeh's property to pay victims of his rule, authorities have said.
The Gambia's Reparations Commission said it received $2.5m (Â£1.86m) from the sale of a mansion in Maryland owned by former leader of the West African nation.
The US had in 2022 secured the right to sell the property on grounds that it was acquired through "criminal proceeds and misappropriated Gambian public funds".
Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years after taking over in a coup in 1994 - a time marked by allegations of human rights abuses forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.
On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.
It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".
Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.
He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.
Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.
In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.
A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.
There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.
Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.
A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.
Phil Haines said the"horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.
Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.
Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.
"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."
He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.
"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.
Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.
He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.
Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.
"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."
Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.
Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.
Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".
The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.
Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.
"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.
"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.
Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.
Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.
The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.
In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.
There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.
Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.
Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.
Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.
Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".
"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.
"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (Â£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.
Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.
He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.
Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.
According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.
US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.
The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.
Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.
If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

A nature reserve manager has finally dismantled a large wasps' nest in her office after the insects made it their home for four months.
Eilish Rothney, a nature reserve manager for the Trinity Broads at the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, found wasps buzzing around the room in June, when she returned from conducting surveys.
The wasps had made their home on the shelves of the Ormesby St Michael office, wrapping around binders and other items. They left the nest a few weeks ago.
Rothney said: "It's kind of a fitting tribute that we've welcomed what many, many people see as a pest...and we've helped them survive, which will help this whole ecosystem that we rely on."
Rothney said that when she first saw the size of the nest in June it was about the size of a paperback book.
She added: "There was just like constant [wasps] coming and going, probably 10s, 20s in and out all the time."
Rothney started dismantling the nest on Tuesday and said that she knew in the autumn, it would be time for them to leave.
When she hadn't seen any wasps for a number of weeks she decided to explore by cutting away at the nest.
She said that she was "amazed" to peel back a number of layers before reaching the shelves. She added that it was not until she got closer to the ring binders that she could see "hexagonal cells where the larvae would have been".
Rothney said she'll miss her office colleagues, but she knows they'll be back and added: "I think if they do come back in here next summer they will be welcome".
Rothney said it was important that we make space for nature. She added: "Although people don't like them [wasps] are part of nature.
"They have a really, really important role to play, as do all the insects, even mosquitoes, which are not my favourite."
She said she thought the wasps struggled because of the warm summer. Due to her office being near a pond and a meadow, the wasps were able to get food and water.

Add ‘post-AI’ encryption to your to-do list
OpenAI’s trove of 400+ math results suggests traditional encryption may be at risk.
Even as federal agencies move their most sensitive systems to new forms of encryption following an order from the White House in June, the release this month by OpenAI of new results to theoretical math problems has sparked concern about whether even proposed post-quantum encryption will be safe from increasingly capable AI models.
Encryption is what keeps online data secure; encrypting a message means applying mathematical equations to disguise its contents to an attacker. But new math techniques could let an attacker decipher encrypted messages without a key: the equivalent of a safecracker using the click of pins in a lock to find the right combination. If existing encryption algorithms fall, huge swaths of the internet would be at risk of attack.
Plans for post-quantum encryption may need to incorporate stronger multi-layered defenses—and move forward more quickly than the White House anticipated—to protect data that hasn’t yet been collected.
Encryption works now because, in practice, there are ways to make it very easy for someone with the key to apply some math and reveal the original message, but not to find the key or solve the equations by brute force in a reasonable amount of time. But the encryption techniques currently in widespread use haven’t been proven theoretically safe; they’re trusted because nobody has been able to crack them so far. So if new math is discovered that makes solving encryption schemes much easier, the foundations of the internet’s security would be at risk.
AI systems have been churning out math discoveries at an unprecedented rate. In May, an OpenAI model disproved the Erdős unit distance conjecture, a well-known problem in a subfield of math called discrete geometry. And in September, the company announced its AI had a solution to the Navier-Stokes equations. The equations make up one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, some of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
“It just solved 400 problems, any of which, if a human had solved it, that could have been the highlight of their career, that could have been their tenure case,” Scott Aaronson, author of Quantum Computing Since Democritus and Chair of Computer Science at UT Austin, said in an interview.
Omer Reingold, computer scientist and co-winner of the Gödel Prize in 2009, wrote before the latest release that, “The world of mathematics, including theoretical computer science, is in turmoil. Even the Millennium Prize Problems…are no longer beyond the reach of LLMs.”
The OpenAI papers showed new results, “in just about all areas of math, but with this very conspicuous exception that there was nothing in cryptography. And that can't possibly be an accident,” Aaronson said.
Justin Drake, a security researcher at the Ethereum Foundation, wrote that he believes there was “backroom interventionism.”
“I've witnessed first-hand the U.S. government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case,” he said.
Regardless of whether OpenAI redacted encryption results from this particular release, the flood of new results has prompted fears that AI systems could find weaknesses in existing encryption algorithms. The cryptocurrency industry, which depends on encryption to safeguard its digital currencies, has been particularly alarmed.
As part of the way cryptocurrencies function, many crypto accounts expose some information about themselves when they send money. On X, formerly known as Twitter, Drake wrote, “Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for ‘bunker mode’. My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses.”
A “fresh address” is one that has never been used to send money to another account, limiting the ways future attackers might break its security.
Other cybersecurity experts are skeptical that AI will have much of an effect on concrete security issues. “Cryptographers are incredibly conservative... we put a lot of buffer into [secure encryption], an enormous amount,” said Bruce Schneier, security guru and author of the bestseller Applied Cryptography.
His concern is more on implementation questions in cybersecurity than the possibility of breakthroughs in theoretical math.
“Computer security is so bad. That's the worry. Finding vulnerabilities in code, hacking into systems. Those are the worries, not the math ... Of all the security things going on, math is the strongest we have,” Schneier added.
Emily Wenger, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at Duke University, who has used machine learning to test the security of post-quantum encryption methods, said she doesn’t think “advanced large language models are going to break all encryption.”
“But when you make practical implementation choices... we found in the past that certain instantiations of these algorithms are insecure,” she said. “There's kind of two ways to break these things. You can either prove something about the math problem, or you can look at implementation choices.”
Aaronson noted that undermining the math behind widely used encryption algorithms like RSA would have sweeping consequences. “These mundane vulnerabilities, you can play the game of whack-a-mole. As soon as you find one, you patch it. Whereas if there's a break of RSA ... if all of our public key crypto systems were broken, then we would really have a problem, the way that we have constructed the internet.”
Dan Boneh, a cryptography expert and professor of computer science and electrical engineering at Stanford, said in a video that losing current forms of encryption “would affect the entire internet... it affects the entire digital world. So, home banking, healthcare, government communications, everything [would be] impacted by such a break.”

A country house and farming estate in one of England's driest and most nature-depleted areas has an "abundance" of wildlife with more than 5,000 species recorded, the National Trust has said.
Rare species, including barbastelle bats, great crested newts and corn buntings, have been spotted at the Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire in the last six years.
General manager David Hassall said the number was "remarkable in any landscape, but particularly here in Cambridgeshire, where wildlife is facing the combined pressures of habitat loss and increasingly hot, dry conditions".
The government said the East was one of seven UK areas in drought, external, with hosepipe bans in force across parts of the region.
The charity said 5,242 species were recorded across the estate's parkland, farmland, woodland and wetlands.
Hassall said the number "reflects five decades of careful stewardship and shows that nature can flourish alongside farming, public access and heritage conservation".
Since 2021, the National Trust said it had planted 125,000 trees and created 35 hectares of woodland and 52 hectares of wood pasture, with another 77 hectares of tree planting currently being designed.
Species recorded also included a tiny pygmy ant, which the charity said was recorded at only one other UK site.
Ben McCarthy, head of nature conservation at the National Trust, said: "Across the UK, wildlife is under immense pressure from habitat loss and fragmentation as well as climate change, making the need to restore nature more urgent than ever.
"Places like Wimpole demonstrate the value of taking a long-term approach to nature recovery.
"By creating and restoring habitats across whole landscapes, we can provide more space for wildlife and help reverse decades of decline."

For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual.
"Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday.
But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social.
Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".
The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city.
Yardan described a potential shuttering, even if temporary, as a "huge dent" in DC culture that could change the heart of the space.
Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".
But courts will need to mediate the dispute between the White House and the community before Trump can realize his plans.
The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. A lawsuit from the DC Preservation League and two golfers from the course asks the court to stop Trump's planned renovation.
"Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves," Democracy Forward, the group representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement on social media.
The legal fight intensified this month after the government began large-scale tree removal on the course without giving the court or plaintiffs notice.
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop its redevelopment plans until at least 26 October.
Despite the work stoppage, Trump took to social media on Sunday to announce that the course will be closed for 15-months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.
"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote in his post on Sunday.
While golfer Thomas Snow, who is not part of the suit, conceded the course could use a "facelift", he thinks the president's description of the course is a "gross overstatement".
Currently, East Potomac does not offer the manicured experience one might find at the luxury, private golf courses the president is known for building. The public course is open to all and does not require a membership to access.
The facilities at the DC course are more modest, offering food court-style dining rather than amenities such as white tablecloth restaurants and upscale locker rooms.
Golfers like Snow and Yardan who regularly play the courses at East Potomac, told the BBC it offers a rare combination of affordability and proximity to the city.
"You start to clear everything out and it just starts to become an empty plot of land that you just hit golf balls on; I think it gets rid of the culture of the golf course," Yardan said.
As a 70-year-old golfer, Snow pays $29 (Â£21.65) for 18 holes when he visits East Potomac.
"There's no place in the whole DMV (the metropolitan region including DC and its Maryland and Virginia suburbs) that you can play a nice 18 holes for that price point," he said.
Snow worries that if Trump's proposal moves forward, people will be priced out.
Yardan, the twice-weekly golfer, echoed those concerns.
"Anytime you hear about big league, big golfers, that also includes big prices," he said. "The biggest thing that I like about this golf course .. is that it's affordable," he said.

The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the decision, which could see the first gas produced by the end of this month, would help heat millions of homes and protect hundreds of jobs.
The government also said it would create a new energy wealth fund, using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, to invest in "green transition".
But environmental campaigners have reacted angrily to the decision, arguing it would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. Once imports are taken into account that equates to about 2% of national demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing â known as a tie-back in industry terms â before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect jobs and add Â£2.9bn to the economy.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".
"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.
The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank
The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund, with an initial Â£2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.
"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.
He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".
Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."
Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.
But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.
The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.
In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.
"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects i

French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.
Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.
Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".
It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.
Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.
Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.
The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.
Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.
Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders...
"We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."
On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".
He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.
Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.
"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."
"Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.
According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.
It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.
Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.
David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".
France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.
BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.
The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.
The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.
Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.
The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.
It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.
While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.
Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

Nestled within a rebuilt inkjet printer, droplets of ink hang suspended above a page. Seen through a microscope, the droplets reveal how an inkjet printer produces crisp, uniform letters.
Ole Bielfeldt, a design student in Cologne, Germany, has been photographing the microscopic world since about 2021. His interest began as a quarantine hobby, when an old school microscope from his attic gave him a way to explore while stuck at home during the pandemic.
His printer image won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. To capture the winning photo, he built a custom rig that moved the paper instead of the printer’s ink nozzles, keeping the nozzles stationary and in focus.
The mini side of ‘macro’
Ole Bielfeldt created this custom rig to catch impossibly fast ink droplets midflight. The contraption is only a bit larger than his head. Swipe through to see what word the printer was spitting out ink to spell.
Bielfeldt estimates that the droplets traveled at nearly 20 meters per second — too fast for even his best slow-motion camera to resolve. To freeze their motion, Bielfeldt worked in darkness, illuminating the scene with a single brief flash. He instructed the printer to repeatedly spell out “macro,” a nod to his social media handle, macrofying.
Before this project, a printer was “like magic,” Bielfeldt says. Photographing its inner workings helped him understand how it operates.
Bielfeldt no longer takes the magic printers spit out for granted. “It’s so, so advanced technically, but at the same time it’s so, so common,” he says.
His photograph is one of 86 images recognized in this year’s competition, whose winners were announced October 21. Here are some of our other favorites.
Did you capture my jumping side?
This pollen-dusted jumping spider offers a close look at the bristling hairs and some of its eight eyes that are easy to miss with the naked eye.
John-Oliver Dum’s fascination with spiders began as a childhood fear. Dum says he suffered a particularly painful arachnid-inflicted bite when he was young. Several years ago, when he was inspired to study the movements of a curly hair tarantula (Tliltocatl albopilosus), Dum became passionate about capturing their beauty.
Preparations for his photographs can begin years before he submits them to a competition. His wife grows plants selected for their pollen, which Dum uses in his images.
“The biggest challenge was finding a spider like this on the right plants, with the right pollen attached to it, at exactly the right time of year and at exactly the right moment,” he says. “You need to understand not only the spider’s behavior, but also the surrounding insect and plant life and their seasonal rhythms.”
Dum hopes the photograph, which won second place, encourages viewers to look more closely, too. “We first have to see the beauty of this largely unknown world before we can truly understand what we may be destroying,” he says.
Seeing a mouse eye in a new way
It’s not a leaf and it’s not a flower. This cross section of a mouse eye is crisscrossed in fractals of blood vessels and tethered by the optic nerve.
Cell biologists Sinem Karaman and Satu Paavonsalo at the University of Helsinki visualize vascular networks, like blood vessels, to study how they work within tissues. The arrangement, Paavonsalo says, could even point to mechanisms underlying how these systems stop working in obesity and diabetes.
Paavonsalo says the duo set out to capture a mouse eye in 3-D, different from the flattened retinas typically used in her research. After meticulous mounting which required several attempts for an arrangement she was satisfied with, Paavonsalo still didn’t know for certain the image would turn out right.
“I had to hope that the sample was correctly positioned and that the staining was detected throughout the sample,” Paavonsalo says, which made her excitement upon seeing the image even more pronounced. The image won 19th place in the competition.
A tardigrade Easter egg
A water bear emerges from its shed cuticle, and oh! What’s that left behind? This egg will be protected by its mother’s discarded skin.
The tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is one of nature’s toughest creatures, able to survive space by going into a state of suspended animation. This species, emerging from its former skin, is only about two-and-a-half times as wide as a strand of hair. Evolutionary developmental biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas captured the image during his studies of these tiny wonders at the University of Montpellier in France.
In the tardigrade life cycle, “egg laying is closely synchronized with molting,” says Quiroga-Artigas. Tardigrades can lay up to about a dozen eggs at once, and the moment one sheds its old cuticle happens quickly enough that it’s easy to miss.
Snapping this image demanded painstaking mounting and imaging of many specimens. Quiroga-Artigas chose this particular one, which won 12th, because “the egg looks almost like a precious gem being left behind by its mother.”
The stretch of a slime mold
This slime mold (Hemitrichia sp.) was found in the heart of Brooklyn, N.Y., sprouting from a decaying log in Prospect Park. The image features the mold’s gelatinous fruiting bodies, which release spores as part of reproduction. To bring the delicate structures into sharp detail, Eric Epstein stacked 240 images.
First, Epstein searched local parks for slime molds to photograph, carefully cutting pieces of waterlogged wood free without disturbing his subjects. “In this liquidy state, any touch would demolish” the fruiting bodies, he says.
One species of slime mold closely mirrors the cosmic web of gas and dark matter connecting galaxies, which helps scientists to more accurately map the cosmos. Another species has fascinated researchers for its ability to pack a store of bacteria to feed the next generation, when it’s near death.

The Russian leader has agreed "in principle" to resume the talks after Nov. 10, Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters following a meeting in St. Petersburg between Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff. READ MORE: Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard after over 4 years in prison, during a visit from U.S. envoy Witkoff The trilateral talks will focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends," Ushakov said. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted only a summit of leaders can break the impasse. The two armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes. Representatives of the three countries held three rounds of trilateral negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February. WATCH: Tightening sanctions on Russia is 'the way to end this war,' says David Kramer However, there was little progress beyond exchanges of prisoners of war as Moscow and Kyiv stuck to their basic demands. The discussion in St. Petersburg lasted about three hours, the Kremlin said, and came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo. Witkoff's meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to U.S.-led peace efforts, more than 4½ years after the war began. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion Wednesday of an imminent high-level breakthrough. WATCH: Trump says U.S. has gotten 'nothing' from Ukraine other than 'high diesel,' urging deal Zelenskyy says that freezing the conflict in Ukraine was the "minimum" required from Russia to bring about an end to the war. "Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war," Zelenskyy said in an interview broadcast Wednesday on Fox News. Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts Witkoff and Putin met at St. Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link, Ushakov said. Before the meeting, Witkoff said that "there is some degree of momentum" in talks. He thanked Putin for lifting Russia's ban on diesel exports, which angered some U.S. lawmakers, adding that it would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers. Putin said that he was ready to consider prospects for the restoration of U.S.-Russia economic ties, adding that he's also prepared to discuss the U.S.-led conflict with Iran. Moscow is ready to use its special relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said. Russia on Wednesday released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, Witkoff said, in what appeared to be a goodwill gesture by the Kremlin after Trump asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard. Putin also met Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St. Petersburg for talks with other Russian officials, the Kremlin said. Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a U.S. proposal for U.N. experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran. Norway's prime minister sees a possible 'new phase' in talks Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. "I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday. Zelenskyy was still in Oslo early Wednesday, where he visited Norway's parliament and met with lawmakers. Zelenskyy said Tuesday that on the agenda of the latest contacts were future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction and the possibility of a ceasefire. Trump said Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks on energy infrastructure. But Russia has kept hammering Ukraine's power grid and Kyiv has hit Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two leaders have soured again. "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss." If that doesn't happen, "I think it's going to be a very bad thing," Trump said. The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.
Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.
Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.
There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing.
The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament).
Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology.
Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.
Apology means 'an awful lot'
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us".
"It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the missions that happened," he said.
He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions".
"So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report.
"And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it."
Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family.
"My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said.
"He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name."
Prior to the DÃ¡il proceedings, the Stack family held a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan.
'Utterly unacceptable'
In 2007 the Garda Commissioner directed a review of the case by the Garda Serious Crime Review Team. Over 200 recommendations were made relating to the cases.
This review led to "serious failings" being found as well as "the shortcomings in the management" of the earlier Garda investigation.
These failures, listed by Martin in the DÃ¡il, are: failure to keep a map made of the crime scene, a failure to keep a motorbike helmet found near the crime scene and linked to the crime, a failure to keep custody of material exhibits, including various fingerprints, samples and debris gathered during the investigation.
The taoiseach also said there was a failure to document some potentially important aspects of the original investigation, including whether Brian's colleagues at Portlaoise Prison were interviewed and whether prisoners at the prison were interviewed.
There was also a failure to interview the Stack family and to interview Brian's wider group of friends.
"It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda SÃochÃ¡na.
"It is admitted by An Garda SÃochÃ¡na that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation," Martin said.
He formally apologised to the Stack family for these failings.
Speaking in the Commons during Northern Ireland questions on Wednesday, Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he "warmly welcomed" the apology.
Asked about the matter by Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, Sir Chris said Dublin doing so was "entirely right and proper" and went to the heart of discussions MPs had been having this week as they debated the UK government's Troubles legacy bill.
He added that it was "incumbent on all of us to make fulsome and not mealy-mouthed apologies".
'Regret'
The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn FÃ©in's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander.
Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing.
A Sinn FÃ©in spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing".
"The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family."
The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception."
Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee also spoke during the State apology, she said: "The State failed you during their investigation into Brian's killing."
She said Brian was "targeted" by the Provisional IRA and said "they are responsible".
"To Sheila and to all of the Stack family, we are deeply sorry for all that you have endured, for the failures of the investigation and the additional suffering they have caused you, we are deeply sorry. I hope today's formal apology brings some measure of peace and comfort."
Donegal Sinn FÃ©in TD (member of Irish parliament) Pearse Doherty said the Stack's family "long search for answers deserves respect".
"No apology can restore Brian Stack's life or return the years spent seeking answers but it can recognise the wrong done."
He said the failures of the garda investigation "compounded" the suffering of the Stack family.
In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder.
