"I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I'm complaining about, who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse," she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio. She said Ramaswamy made similar personal attacks during his run for the Republican presidential nomination two years ago, calling it "a lifelong pattern." READ MORE: After taxpayer-funded ads glorifying Trump sparked backlash, he says his super PAC will pay instead Ramaswamy's campaign initially issued a statement that did not address whether he was responsible for the ad or knew who produced it. In the earlier statement, Luck said Acton "has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of." Democrats and Republicans condemn the ad Casey Putsch, a car designer and YouTube provocateur who competed against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for governor, said on social media that he would be voting for Acton in the wake of the ad's release. He called the video "pretty damn low." Acton's campaign released a statement from her brother, Philip Stearns, who said the two were removed from their mother Donna Arthur's custody as children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur, whose last known address was in Pennsylvania, since they were in a courtroom together in 1978. WATCH: Ohio becomes midterm battleground after years of Republican wins Later Tuesday, the Acton campaign released a video featuring Stearns, who recalls his older sister taking "the worst" of the abuse they faced as children in order to protect him and disparages Ramaswamy and his allies for exploiting the situation. According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died. High-profile Republicans who back Ramaswamy — including Donald Trump Jr. and influencer Laura Loomer — elevated the video in online posts. But others joined Democrats in condemning the ad. Meghan McCain called it "dastardly" and Dan Hauser, a strategist for Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, said he deleted his post sharing the video once he realized "the very serious accusations that caused their issues." The Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, described the spot as "disgusting" and said everyone — including his opponent, Sen. Jon Husted — should be willing to condemn it. Husted's campaign didn't respond to a request for comment. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A fuel leak in the River Taff which killed fish and sparked a warning for people to shut their windows has now stopped, official have said.
Officers from Natural Resources Wales (NRW) on Wedneaday the source of the pollution affecting the Taff in places such as Nantgarw, Treforest and Taffs Well since 16 October over.
GE Aerospace previously confirmed fuel got into the river while repair work took place at its site nearby, but NRW said it was working to determine how fuel entered the drainage system and reached the river.
NRW added it had found fewer than 10 dead fish and impacts to aquatic invertebrates as a result of the leak.
NRW said the source was identified at 19:30 BST on Friday, after kerosene spread down almost 2.5 miles (4km) of the river.
It added evidence was being compiled and reviewed as part of the ongoing investigation.
The environmental body also received reports of pollution affecting the Taff in Glan Y Llyn, Gwaelod-y-garth and Tongwynlais.
In an update on Sunday evening, NRW said due to the nature of the incident, identifying how the fuel entered the drainage system was difficult as it involved underground systems.
Specialist drainage and containment contractors had been sent to the site and were removing the fuel.
Eurig Thomas, a resident in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cyon Taff, told the BBC on Sunday: "It smelt like a petrol station, it hit you as soon as you came out."
Public Health Wales advised people living nearby to keep windows and doors closed, avoid any contact with the water and to call NHS 111 if they felt unwell.

Two leaders of the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been freed from jail a week after they were arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka walked out of Tihar jail hours after a magistrate ordered their release. They had been detained by police and jailed after they crossed barricades and climbed over the locked gate at Jantar Mantar.
The historic venue was recently removed from a list of designated protest sites.
The men, who denied wrongdoing, have been calling on India's chief election commissioner to resign. Critics accuse the commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit India's governing party, charges the commission rejects.
A special executive magistrate court in Delhi, passed their release order, legal news website Bar and Bench reported.
After bail was granted, Das told reporters from a police van: "Truth alone triumphs. Long live the revolution."
Das and Ranka are key leaders of the CJP, which began as an internet joke in May after India's top judge compared unemployed young people to "cockroaches".
The CJP is not a registered political party, but a collective which began by mobilising thousands of young people to protest over leaked exam papers.
By July it had emerged as a major force.
A march towards parliament that month ended in clashes with police, drawing wider attention to the movement and increasing pressure on the government. The unrest eventually led to the resignation of India's education minister.
The CJP has since shifted its focus to India's electoral system.
Along with opposition parties, students and other critics of the government, it accuses Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of revising electoral rolls, an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the allegation.
The SIR exercise has resulted in around 130 million names being removed from voter lists since last year.
Critics warn that the process could also exclude eligible voters, potentially denying them their right to vote, while the Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove ineligible, dead and duplicate entries.

Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing through on their way to regional wineries, or music lovers visiting its annual jazz and blues festival.
Instead, locals are fielding endless questions about their MP - and having to explain to strangers what it all means for the town's nearly 30,000 people.
They are clearly in shock about what police say was a targeted and deliberate attack on Helen Haines on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a car just outside her office.
"People are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy," Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who represents King Charles, said at a press conference on Wednesday.
The independent federal MP had to have both legs amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne. But the "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape", her husband Phil Haines said.
The MP isn't a divisive figure, locals tell the BBC, and no one can understand why she was allegedly targeted.
"Everyone knows Helen," says Jane Hill, who owns a party supply shop a few hundred metres down the town's main street from where Haines was hit.
"She is a such a good person in our community. She'd go to everything - celebrations, funerals, she's one of those genuinely kind people - and so are her family."
Local man Brendan Nugent, whose father has been good friends with Haines for decades, faces at least three charges over the alleged attack including intentionally causing harm and appeared in court on Wednesday. Police say they are considering further charges, including attempted murder.
MP 'thanked everyone' as she lay injured
First elected to parliament in 2019, Haines is best known for her years-long efforts to establish a national anti-corruption commission.
She was spurred by on a series of major political scandals which, in her words, saw "public money spent for political gain", disproportionate spending on "shiny infrastructure projects" in marginal seats and decisions benefitting big donors over ordinary people.
The commission finally opened in 2023 under Anthony Albanese's Labor government.
Haines has also helped to secure funds for housebuilding, railway improvements and health infrastructure in her region, which she argues has long been sidelined by policies favouring cities.
On a spring afternoon in Wangaratta, nobody seemed to have a bad word to say about the former nurse and midwife turned politician.
Local Mayor Irene Grant described her as "warm", "cheerful" and "committed", and pointed to her record on climate action and Indigenous rights.
In a police update on Wednesday, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said she'd given "wonderful support" to local police when two officers were shot dead in the nearby town of Porepunkah last year.
Bystanders who came to Haines' aid recalled how she thanked them even as she lay severely injured.
"It was incredible," Jacklyn Black told Nine Network's Today show. "We were having conversations, she was telling me about her grandkids."
"To be in that situation and be as calm as she could be in the moment, but also thankful to the aid that the community had given her... I could [not] speak any more highly of her in a moment like that," Cody Lepoidevin added.
"She just thanked everyone."
There's a large print-out of Helen Haines plastered onto the window of her office - anyone delivering flowers for her gets a big smile back as they look up and walk away.
Across the road on Tuesday, a man waved an Australian flag. On his T-shirt were the words "Wangaratta - this is not us!!"
It's clear that many feel that way in this friendly community where people look out for each other.
Next door to Haines' office is RickyChops barbershop, owned by Ricky Jefferies. When he heard the chaos unfolding outside, he rushed to help, pinning down the suspect.
"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him, and I told him that he can't leave," he explained after the incident.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way."
Some clearly disagree with Ricky. By Tuesday afternoon, he too had received a bouquet of flowers tied to his shop's door, and a small balloon with the words "thank you".
Down the road at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral, a vigil was held, attended by a couple of hundred people lining up to light a candle for Haines.
Some hugged the clergy, while others wore campaign T-shirts carrying the words "Team Helen Haines".
Her husband Phil said he had received "thousands upon thousands" of messages of love and support.
"I can only say how much of a difference that makes to all of us," he said. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter."
"Whether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community at heart so that's all you can really ask for; a politician that represents your community," said Austin Longfield who lives in nearby Albury.
"It's just something that you wouldn't expect in our community," he added. "You see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here."
With additional reporting by Simon Atkinson

The race to be Ohio's next governor has turned ugly amid uproar over one of the most viral attack ads of the midterm elections campaign.
Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy released an ad featuring his opponent's estranged mother urging Ohioans not to elect her daughter.
"She's lied her entire life," Donna Arthur says in the video.
But the ad leaves out that her daughter, Democratic candidate Amy Acton, alleged she was raped by Arthur's husband 40 years ago when she was just 12.
Acton's brother said turning alleged sexual assault into "a political talking point" was a "despicable low". Experts told the BBC that the jarringly personal nature of the political attack will likely backfire.
Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged in 1978.
That's when she last spoke to her mother, Acton said in an interview with The Vindicator, an Ohio news outlet. The Arthurs fled Ohio, and he was never prosecuted on the rape charge. He died in 2004.
Political attacks ads are not a new feature of US politics, but they have grown more coarse, experts say.
"They have become more intense, and the boundaries have stretched in terms of what one attacks about," said David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs.
Lublin also said it was not new for relatives to be used against a political opponent, mentioning family members who testified against Robert F Kennedy Jr before he was confirmed as health secretary.
"But this is of a different order," Lublin said. "They're estranged not over policy but over a rape allegation."
The BBC has reached out to Ramaswamy's campaign for comment. In a statement to the BBC's US partner, CBS News, a campaign spokesman reiterated assertions in the ad that Acton was untruthful, but conceded, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother".
When the ad was initially released to social media on Monday evening, it did not say who the video was paid for or authorised by. But Ramaswamy confirmed on Tuesday that it came from his campaign, and he later pledged to spend $4m (Â£2.9m) to further air it.
The move drew intense backlash from Democrats.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said on X it was "an abhorrent attack". Illinois governor and 2028 presidential hopeful JB Pritzker said Ramaswamy "has reached a new low by launching these vile and false attacks".
Acton's team released its own campaign ad on Tuesday, a video featuring her brother, Philip Stearns, recounting childhood abuse and saying "Amy always got the worst of it".
"Shame on Vivek," he says in the 30-second clip. "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio."
Some Republicans also criticised the ad. Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for president in 2024, said "he's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it".
Vice-President JD Vance, when asked by the BBC if he thought the ad was appropriate, did not say. "It's not really my concern," he said. "What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government."
Lublin said President Donald Trump's rhetoric and campaigns have helped act as a catalyst for the coarsening of American political discourse - he mentioned when Trump appeared to mock a reporter in Ohio who had a disability.
"We live in an age where certainly many candidates can appear mean and even inappropriate at times," Lublin said.
"The key purpose of attack ads isn't necessarily to convert the followers of your opponent, but more to depress their turnout," he said.
But Lublin expects the Ramaswamy attack ad to backfire. He said it could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favor in the increasingly competitive race for Ohio governor - even though a Democrat has not been elected governor there in over two decades.
Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has moved the Ohio governor's race from "leans Republican" to "toss up".

Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said.
Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg.
Ushakov said a new round could be held next month, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky later said he wanted this to happen as soon as possible. Kyiv and its European allies have long been pressing Moscow for resumption of the talks halted in February.
Russia has for months refused as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks.
Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Monday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after talks in Oslo that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.
Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine".
"This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Late on Wednesday, Zelensky told reporters: "We received feedback that Russia... supports a trilateral meeting between our teams. The American side is proposing to do this as soon as possible. We are in favour of it."
Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".
Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.
"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.
Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."
The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.
Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
He was heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".
That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.
Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.
Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".
Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions by the US satellite internet network Starlink which is owned by Elon Musk which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.
US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.
Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.
When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.
"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

Two members of the Bush family, the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, have backed Democrat James Talarico in the hotly fought race for a Senate seat in the Lone Star State.
Barbara Bush, daughter of ex-President George W Bush, has reportedly donated to Talarico's campaign, while her uncle, Neil Bush, says he backs the Democrat.
The Republican candidate, Ken Paxton, beat a primary challenge from Neil Bush's nephew, so the endorsement may be cast by critics as political sour grapes.
But the Bushes could potentially influence some disaffected Republican voters when it comes to next month's vote. No Democrat has won a Texas Senate seat since 1988.
Opinion polls show Paxton and Talarico neck and neck ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.
Neil Bush said he was opposing Paxton because of his efforts to help President Donald Trump deny his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden.
In a post on Facebook late on Tuesday, Neil Bush wrote that he had cast his ballot for Talarico as early voting began.
"My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton's record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico," Neil Bush wrote on Facebook.
A businessman who has never held political office, Neil Bush is remembered for his role as director of the Silverado Savings and Loan when it collapsed in 1988, costing taxpayers more than $1bn.
Meanwhile, Barbara Bush has donated to help Talarico, campaign finance records show.
Bush, the twin of US chat show host Jenna Hager Bush, reportedly gave $2,500 (Â£1,900) to a political action committee that supports the Democrat.
The BBC has contacted Barbara Bush for comment.
A survivor of several political scandals, Paxton was previously impeached by fellow Republicans in the Texas state legislature.
He also beat a primary challenge from the son of Jeb Bush, George P Bush.
The Bushes have had a complex relationship with Trump since he beat Jeb Bush, the former Florida governor, during the 2016 Republican presidential primary race.
Former President George HW Bush previously called Trump a "blow hard" and confirmed he had voted for Democrat Hillary Clinton in the 2016 race.
His son, George W Bush, whom Trump repeatedly lambasted for launching the US war in Iraq, has made thinly veiled criticisms of Trump.
But during his own political campaigns, George P Bush backed Trump.

e2eca65bbeb5.text: Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted a sortie on Monday, flying as far as the Iranian border, according to Israeli and U.S. officials. Why it matters: The operation, more than 800 miles away from Israel, took place a week before the Israeli elections and on the same day Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Israel's Ovda Air Base. The sortie wasn't connected to Hegseth's visit. While some Israeli and U.S. officials said the sortie wasn't unusual and that it was meant to deter Iran, it could have led to a miscalculation, triggering an Iranian response and reigniting the war. Behind the scenes: The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft, the sources said. It followed a flight path consistent with a potential strike against Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace. As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they turned around and returned to Israel, the sources said. The intrigue: U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the sortie. According to the sources, Israel notified the U.S. in advance and described the operation as a training exercise intended for "power projection" and aimed at deterring Iran from launching attacks against Israel ahead of the elections. However, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran. Fox News reported on Tuesday that the Israeli Air Force conducted a drill towards Iran. Driving the news: Last week, Axios reported that Netanyahu and President Trump discussed in early October the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections. Netanyahu told Trump he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir told Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine at the time that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Trump initially seemed to be inclined to resume attacks, but then grew hesitant and eventually decided against Netanyahu's proposal. State of play: An Israeli official said Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir will not allow any unjustified military activity that could undermine the Oct. 27 elections. What he's saying: On Wednesday Netanyahu said at a military graduation ceremony that Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei "has decided to follow in his father's footsteps" and allowed Iranian scientists to move forward with building a nuclear weapon. "He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death," Netanyahu said. "Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given to the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies," he added.

Data-center companies are ponying up to find out which communities will resist them the least. Startup Hamlet has parsed tens of thousands of city council meetings by scraping local governmentsâ video recordings, tagging comments as friendly or hostile to a potential project.
CEO Sunil Rajaraman told Semafor that a large fund that finances data centers and a data-center developer are among its paying customers, looking for whiffs of a moratorium.
âWhere there might be more favorable political viewsâ may well determine where future projects get built, Rajaraman said.
Investors backing these projects are also obvious customers for a real-time feed into Americansâ growing antipathy toward data centers.

Scientific papers may be getting a 21st century update.
A system called Paper2Agent lets scientists do more than read a new scientific study. When a paper comes with code, methods and data, the system packages these into a tool set that an AI assistant can use to work with new data, researchers report September 16 in Nature.
The system is essentially “a virtual author of the paper,” available around the clock, says James Zou, a computer scientist at Stanford University.
In tests, Zou and colleagues tried to convert 100 computational biology papers into working tool sets and succeeded with 74. The others had obstacles such as missing code or data, or software that wouldn’t run. With the papers that were converted, the Paper2Agent tool set could run analyses of the published work and answer questions about the results. It did so more accurately and also more than twice as fast as the same agent working from the original papers and accompanying code.
Making another scientist’s code usable can take substantial work, says Peter Clark, a senior research director at the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in Seattle who was not involved in developing Paper2Agent. Researchers already share code on platforms such as GitHub. But Clark says he often has to “grub around” for half a day to figure out how to get it running.
A general-purpose AI assistant such as Claude can help, he says, but it typically generates new code on the fly. Paper2Agent instead packages code associated with a paper into reusable tools, tests them against reference outputs and writes step-by-step instructions guiding an AI assistant on which tools to use and in what order. This streamlines and standardizes the process of using AI to interact with scientific research, Clark says. It’s “an exciting step” toward papers that actively help scientists.
To Zou, transforming scientific papers into agents seem like a natural next step for transmitting knowledge. We’ve already moved from stone tablets and papyrus to paper and then to digital formats, he says, and now it’s time to move from passive to active formats for human knowledge. A paper-agent can help one human scientist quickly use another’s code and methods. The tool can also search for paper-agents about similar topics with the aim of alerting their human authors about potential collaborations.
Zou says his team has already created “over 100 different paper-agents” from their own work and that these have already helped him find other scientists to collaborate with.
Clark notes that Paper2Agent specializes in helping scientists reuse methods and code, and not in answering general questions, like a true virtual author should be able to do. Also, he worries about what could happen if millions of low-quality papers get turned into agents capable of pestering scientists. That could make things “worse rather than better,” he says, recalling the days of Clippy, the much-maligned Microsoft Office assistant. But he’d love for a “non-annoying agent” to pop up and tell him about work that he should be paying attention to.
For more open-ended questions about a paper, Clark says he would still want to talk to the people who did the research. “The reason I would write to a corresponding author is for precisely the things they didn’t put in the paper.”

0eb618919f02.text:
Davidâs view
If Abdul El-Sayed wins Michiganâs Senate race next month, the Saturday clip of him admonishing a GOP activist about freedom of religion will achieve legendary status in his party.
âItâs you who need to understand the Constitution, not me,â El-Sayed told Thomas Teepell during an appearance in the small Michigan city of Caro. The candidate accepted Teepellâs challenge to âdisavow the Muslim Brotherhood,â then denounced the âdual loyaltyâ smear it seemed like the activist wanted to make.
If El-Sayed wins, Iâd expect Republicans to study that clip, too. Thatâs because the lesson conservatives can take isnât that the topic of El-Sayedâs religion is too hot to touch. Teepell struggled to follow up because he couldnât handle the moment.
From President Donald Trump on down, Republicans are very comfortable contending that Muslim immigration threatens America and that the liberal crusade for diversity is national suicide. They love running against El-Sayed, even in the 49 states where heâs not on the ballot. And they donât hold their tongues anymore for fear of political backlash.
âWhat excites him is this prospect of wielding the power of a country he hates,â Vice President JD Vance told Michigan Republicans about El-Sayed this month. âHe wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you.â
This isnât a swerve away from the GOPâs midterm message. It is the message: Foreigners are undermining America from within, and Democrats wonât stop them. (Never mind that El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills.)
Teepell was very much in line with the Trump-era Republican rhetorical strategy to demonize the âother.â Where he went wrong was, in part, failing to go toe to toe with one of the most skillful extemporaneous talkers in Democratic politics.
He was also working against a new reality: The Trump administrationâs border closure and shutdown of most asylum claims has made âimmigrationâ less critical to most voters. Casting El-Sayed as the enemy simply wasnât as easy as he might have hoped.
But the bigger context is more favorable to MAGA conservatives: With no Democrat running on a return to pre-Trump border policies, they see that topics once considered forbidden or offensive by media gatekeepers can win elections. The El-Sayed-Teepell moment happened as Paris was gripped by riots; Trump, his White House, and supportive media outlets warned that Democrats would bring the same migration-driven chaos across the Atlantic.
Those media gates of the past might not even be standing anymore.
They were sturdy in 2008, when Republicans campaigned more cautiously around questions of race and immigration. El-Sayed has indulged comparisons to Barack Obama, whose 2008 campaign convinced the young Muslim that he could one day run for office.
In his 2020 memoir, El-Sayed wrote that after he graduated from the University of Michigan, he brushed off the idea (floated by Bill Clinton, his commencement speaker) that he might have a future in politics. Of course not: His name was Abdulrahman Muhammad El-Sayed. But one year later, âsomeone whose father had immigrated from eastern Africa â someone who was marked by a funny name and dark skin,â won Michigan by 16 points.
The idea that something had changed, and that attacking Islam or a foreign name didnât work anymore, ran through El-Sayedâs 2018 campaign. At one stop, he was buttonholed by Laura Loomer, then a semi-cancelled independent muckraker, who asked how he could âreconcile your own personal practice of Islamic law with your Marxist, socialist political platform.â
Loomer was fairly easy for that campaign to brush off. Sheâs now one of the most influential conservative activists in America, with a direct line to the president.
Republicans in the Bush years, who briefly hoped to build a lasting multiracial coalition, were hesitant to attack Obama over his pastor, or to elevate rumors that he was a Muslim. (âNo, maâam.â) On the right, itâs widely believed now that this was a loserâs strategy.
Thatâs why Teepellâs biggest error, in the eyes of the right, was simply lacking a clapback. If Republicans lose big next month, thereâll be a brawl to assign blame â which consultants blew it, which ads wasted money, which issues didnât work.
The partyâs margins with non-white voters and first generation Americans, which improved in 2024, will get a harder look. But I wouldnât expect them to ditch tactics like the El-Sayed confrontation, tactics that the new media environment is built for.
Notable
- In Slow Boring, Matthew Yglesias wrote about the edgy conservative debate over âthe Indian question,â and whether Republican rhetoric about immigrants was hurting them. âYou either need to be willing to bite the bullet and say youâre eager to keep good people out or else you need to redefine good behavior as bad.â

The Satya Nadella I interviewed last week for Future Proof at Microsoftâs headquarters in Redmond, Wash., was a very different version of the CEO I saw there in 2023, who wanted to make Google âdance.â
Back then, generative AI was the exciting (and scary) new thing, and without Microsoftâs investment in compute, OpenAI wouldnât have been able to build ChatGPT, and the industryâs trajectory might have been very different.
Weâre now four years on from the launch of ChatGPT and, outside of software development, AIâs impact on the world has been incremental, not exponential. And Microsoft is less about making competitors dance than it is about getting down to the nitty-gritty of making AI work predictably and reliably â Nadella has gone back to being the CEO of a company that is building a sturdy dance floor.
âWe, as an industry, have to wake up to this,â Nadella said. âItâs not about the shiny object and FOMO.â
Wall Street is happy with the strategy. Microsoftâs stock is up 27% over the past six months and itâs valued at close to $4 trillion. But will it outpace the frontier labs and Nvidia in the long run? Nadella calls the frontier labs âmagical businesses,â but points to Microsoftâs remarkable 51-year history. âI look at them and say, hey, this is not an industry where your initial success means anything,â he said.

Critical flaws in ubiquitous website software draw urgent warning from NSA, FBI
Organizations should imediately update to the latest version of PHP or take systems offline, agencies say.
Two critical flaws in software widely used in websites have the NSA, FBI, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urging organizations to update their systems or take them offline immediately.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP, a programming language that works behind the scenes to run websites, process forms, and retrieve information. Hackers could exploit the flaws to run commands on an affected server without logging in, potentially allowing them to steal data, change a website’s contents, or take control of it, the agencies said Wednesday.
PHP powers run roughly 70% of websites whose underlying server-side programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs. It is a key part of popular website-building platforms, including WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.
Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said it identified more than 22.6 million internet-exposed instances that might be vulnerable.
“While CISA has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication, they pose a risk to organizations if left unpatched,” the cyberdefense agency said in a blog post.
A Nextgov/FCW analysis using Shodan, a search engine that catalogs internet-connected systems, identified roughly 900 results associated with U.S. federal, state and local government websites that showed signs of PHP use. Many listed older versions of the software, though it’s unclear if the records reflect the versions currently running on those systems, as Shodan may not yet have captured recent updates.
Governments in Europe have already been taking some websites offline to implement fixes.
“I’d expect a great deal of opportunistic exploitation: attackers don’t need to know what’s vulnerable before they start knocking on doors,” said Trey Darley, the founder of Proper Tools, a cybersecurity standards consultancy. “Meanwhile, defenders can’t reliably count what they need to patch and protect.”
“Right now, the priority is protecting the systems people actually have,” he added.
The U.S. government was involved in coordinating the response ahead of disclosure. OpenAI said it and its partners engaged the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to help security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services.
The flaws, collectively known as “php2shell,” affect the software beneath websites rather than a single website or application. That means an organization could have carefully secured its own code and still be exposed through the PHP software running it.
Cybersecurity company Wiz said it demonstrated successful attacks against WordPress, Drupal and Joomla installations. Researchers also showed they could read sensitive information from a server’s working memory, including passwords and access credentials.
PHP’s developers also said all installations handling web requests are at risk. Under certain setups, an attack can take place before the website’s own code even executes.
The discovery adds to evidence that AI is helping researchers find and exploit flaws in widely used software. OpenAI said security firm Calif identified a critical flaw using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the development and release of fixes.
PHP’s developers released updates Wednesday for supported versions of the software. They said organizations using Linux distributions or long-term support services should check their vendors for updated packages, including fixes adapted for older versions.
The warnings followed an early leak that accelerated plans to disclose and fix the vulnerabilities. A post on the technology forum Hacker News surfaced Tuesday morning and was subsequently removed, but screenshots spread across social media, according to cybersecurity firm Huntress. PHP’s developers then announced that fixes would arrive a day ahead of the planned disclosure, leaving website operators little time to prepare for updates.
Editor’s note: This story is breaking and may be updated.

8546e21a8403.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/supreme-court-rebuffs-trump-administration-restrictions-on-medical-care-for-transgender-inmates Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates Politics Oct 21, 2026 12:17 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce new medical restrictions for transgender people in prison. The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy. It was adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump, a Republican who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term. WATCH: Supreme Court upholds Tennessee law banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors The brief order did not detail its legal reasoning. Justice Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas would have allowed the policy to be enforced as the lawsuit played out in lower courts. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Supreme Court has previously allowed other policies for transgender people to move ahead for now, including restrictions on military service and passport sex markers. Trump's order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren't spent "for the purpose of conforming an inmate's appearance to that of the opposite sex." WATCH: Where trans advocates are focusing efforts after recent court defeats The new policy would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services. Attorneys for transgender inmates challenged the policy in court and U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered treatments to continue. Lamberth, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President Ronald Reagan, pointed out that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects like depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts. The Trump administration appealed, arguing that treatments raised security concerns and "could no longer be justified." A divided appeals court panel left the order in place. About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, the agency said in court records. Withdrawing care would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health, their lawyers said. The government has not detailed evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates over the 30 years it has been provided, they wrote. The conservative-majority Supreme Court has previously upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender youth, and restricting sports participation by transgender athletes in women's sports. The News
The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America is divided over whether the AI industry is a destructive capitalist force that could kill everyone, or merely an overhyped capitalist hustle.
The rift within the largest chapter of the left-wing organization centers on whether the New York DSA should acknowledge the possibility that AI could lead to mass automation and to systems that escape human control â the kind of warnings that gained traction after recent AI-powered hacks. Some tech leaders and Democratic politiciansÂ â including Americaâs leading socialist, Sen. Bernie Sanders âÂ have warned that without guardrails, thereâs a chance AI could lead to human extinction.
At the chapterâs convention on Nov. 14, members are expected to consider a resolution proposed in September by two graduate students and local DSA members: They warn that industry ânegligenceâ creates âthe potential for loss of control of AI agents to cause catastrophic harm.â
But the groupâs established Tech Action Working Group is not persuaded. Some in the self-described âtechno-skepticalâ committee that steers the chapterâs technology policy see things differently, arguing that dire warnings of doom are an attempt to inflate company valuations, and AI is already doing enough damage.
Members of the groupâs leadership proposed to amend that measure by removing clauses on automation, loss of control, and catastrophic risk: âAI alarmism and AI hype are the same story,â the group posted to Instagram in September.
The resolution also calls for âthe democratization and socialization of AI,â but the amendment deletes that phrase.
Know More
The socialist organization is now mired in procedural infighting. Alexei Gannon and Zachary Jones, who wrote the original resolution, accused the TAWG of presenting its leadersâ views as the groupâs official position, even though the group never formally voted on where it stands on AI risk. The TAWG, Gannon and Jones wrote in a Substack post, hasnât held a membership meeting since March.
âTo equate worrying about catastrophic risk with buying a Silicon Valley narrative is to lump hundreds of DSA comradesâ¦ and 60% of the American public into the same bucket as Sam Altman and Elon Musk,â they wrote.
Gannon and Jones declined to comment; the New York City DSA chapter and the Tech Action Working Group didnât respond to requests for comment.
The DSA is also grappling with how to use the technology itself: The local chapterâs tech working group voted in January to ban using generative AI text, images, and video for âany DSA purpose.â The national DSAâs tech committee this month adopted a policy that âneither endorses nor prohibitsâ AI coding tools for its own software.
J.D.âs view
The discourse in the DSA in many ways mirrors the broader debate confronting the American left over AI, as Democrats look to stake out a position on the issue ahead of the 2028 presidential election. How the DSA and other left-wing factions speak to voters about AI risk could shape what regulation looks like if Democrats retake Congress in the midterms, and which candidates win over the partyâs AI-skeptic vote.
I got a glimpse of how progressives are positioning on the issue at the Peopleâs AI Assembly on Monday, organized by the AI Now Institute and More Perfect Union. The event centered on the impacts of data centers, surveillance, and the concentration of power in a handful of companies. Sanders-esque warnings about AI threatening humanity werenât a focal point, suggesting the DSA camp thatâs more focused on mitigating present harms is setting the terms of the conversation, at least in New York.
âEven as we reckon with these larger societal questions, there are still rules that we can implement and hold these kinds of companies to account for,â New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a DSA member, told the crowd.
Room for Disagreement
It was clear at the Peopleâs AI Assembly that broad swaths of the left remain united on a number of AI-related fronts, including data centers, the concentration of corporate power, and the broader need for regulation and oversight.
Brian Romero, a DSA member and incoming state assemblymember who has worked with the chapterâs tech working group in the past, framed the debate as a complex, fast-moving issue that factions across the political spectrum are having.
âItâs not unlike any other policy issue,â he said. âThereâs going to be differences of opinion on the left.â As another attendee at the Peopleâs Assembly told me: âIt wouldnât be the DSA if there wasnât debate.â
Notable
- Sanders is facing pushback from some on the left over his doomerist AI rhetoric, WIRED reported. âSome of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened?â one NYC DSA member said.
- The broader DSA has no âconsistent line on what elected socialists should advocate for regarding AI,â Zhao Levi, a DSA member, wrote in Cosmonaut in September, proposing a national working group to draft one for the 2027 national convention.

The Scoop
Both OpenAI and Anthropic lobbied lawmakers on the ability of AI companies to share information with one another without running afoul of antitrust rules in the third quarter of this year, according to federal lobbying disclosures reviewed by Semafor.
Anthropicâs lobbying form lists the Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act, a bill that would allow labs to coordinate with each other on security risks, as a point of focus for the company on Capitol Hill. The legislation could make it into law as part of must-pass defense policy legislation, Semafor previously reported.
OpenAIâs lobbying form is less specific, listing âAI-security collaboration and information-sharing, including proposed antitrust protectionsâ as topics discussed in Washington. Lobbying forms donât say whether companies are arguing for or against the proposals discussed in meetings.
The antitrust lobbying is of interest given the talks around a coordinated AI development âslowdownâ pitched by AI leaders last month. The companies regularly lobby Washington lawmakers on proposed AI regulatory bills, as well as legislation on export controls and data centers.
OpenAIâs head of global affairs, Chris Lehane, has argued that an antitrust exemption specifically for model pacing would not be necessary. But Trump administration officials criticized AI leaders for calling for such a carve-out, saying they were capable of deciding to slow down among themselves without the governmentâs blessing.
Know More
Meta spent $5.9 million lobbying Washington lawmakers in the third quarter of 2026 â the most of any big tech firm during that period â as the AI race grew more competitive and high-profile hacks put pressure on the AI safety debate in Washington, according to Senate lobbying filings.
Meta often is the biggest lobbying spender among its Big Tech and AI counterparts, but OpenAI and Anthropic have been spending more and more each quarter, nearly doubling and tripling their spends in the first half of the year, respectively, as they navigate Washingtonâs discussions about containing their technology.
Google, Amazon, and Apple lagged behind Meta in spending but beat AI and chip companies, though Nvidia also posted its highest-ever quarter at $2.2 million as the chipmaker stays dominant and influential in the Trump administration. All three companies have built up massive lobbying portfolios on a range of tech policy topics including kidsâ online safety, immigration, taxes, education, and energy policy.

b144421b5a0a.text: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Traders are betting that oil prices will remain elevated for longer than they anticipated just weeks ago, threatening to prolong the inflationary pressures that businesses and consumers have weathered for months. Why it matters: Oil inventories have helped cushion the blow from disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, but much of that buffer has been depleted since the war began. The possibility of sustained price pressures into next year throws into doubt the logic that central banks traditionally rely upon to look through energy price shifts — that they represent a one-time shift in relative prices, not an ongoing inflationary process. That leaves the global economy more vulnerable to another energy price surge, with potentially more lasting consequences for growth, inflation and interest rates than energy shocks of yore. By the numbers: Oil futures for delivery in 2027 — contracts to buy or sell crude next year — have climbed to their highest levels since the Iran war began. Prices for January 2027 are up 17% since early September, to more than $97 a barrel. Markets still anticipate some relief next year, but considerably less than they expected just weeks ago. It's a reversal from late summer, when hopes of easing tensions with Iran and a recovery in Middle Eastern oil supplies briefly pushed futures lower. June futures have jumped 18%, to $88 a barrel, while December futures are up 13%, to about $81. State of play: Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, including shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, surpassed prewar levels in the week ending Oct. 18, according to the Wall Street Journal . But the costly workarounds enabling that recovery have their limits. Those include ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, where security risks have deterred some vessels. "You're coming up against limitations on actually how much volume you can move out of the Middle East, even with these processes," Christopher Haines, global head of oil at Energy Aspects, tells Axios. Restoring confidence among shipping companies and insurers that vessels won't be attacked will be "exceptionally hard," Haines adds. Zoom in: Economist Robin Brooks argues that oil prices reflect higher shipping costs and fears of further attacks more than actual shortages. Using earlier monthly data, he estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to 91% of prewar levels, with a "temporary fear factor" adding at least $20 a barrel. What to watch: The Trump administration is seeking to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterms, most recently by allowing more Russian diesel onto the market. But relief may be minimal: Ukrainian attacks have damaged Russian refineries, while sanctions complicate repairs, limiting additional exports, Haines says. The bottom line: "The market narrative has shifted from "transitory" to "new normal" right before our eyes," Bob Elliot, chief investment officer at Unlimited Funds, wrote Wednesday morning .

c5d9f2142f2d.text: By — John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press By — Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/chemical-tank-explosion-in-ohio-of-glycidyl-methacrylate-forces-evacuations-prompts-fears-of-another-blast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Chemical tank explosion in Ohio of glycidyl methacrylate forces evacuations, prompts fears of another blast Nation Oct 21, 2026 11:43 AM EDT TOLEDO, Ohio (AP) — A chemical tank exploded in Toledo, Ohio, forcing hundreds of residents to evacuate their homes or shelter in place due to fears of a toxic release, and the mayor warned Wednesday that it may still be explosive. A sheriff's deputy was injured when he responded to the explosion around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday and was able to drive himself to the hospital, Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said at a news conference Wednesday morning. READ MORE: Washington chemical tank was called unfit for service before deadly failure, investigators find MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate, which it described as "an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Kapszukiewicz said the chemical is liquid inside the tank but becomes a gas when released. Video from the area showed a large plume in the sky. "There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," the mayor said, adding that it can hold 5,500 gallons of the chemical in liquid form. He said officials don't know what caused the explosion. People who come into contact with glycidyl methacrylate may feel as if their eyes, nose, mouth and skin are burning, the city fire department said. Overexposure can lead to headache, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting. READ MORE: More than 30 lawsuits filed against aerospace company in California over damaged chemical tank "It's really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it," Karim Baroudi, director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department, said during the news conference. "Now we're trying to kind of determine how much of a toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance." Baroudi advised residents to close their windows and that those who "feel irritation in the eyes, heavily breathing, just take a shower for now." The fire department said those who experience symptoms should contact a medical professional. First responders, hazmat and safety teams are not approaching the tank because of the risk of more explosions, and will reassess conditions later Wednesday morning, Kapszukiewicz said. The city ordered people within a 1-mile radius of the explosion to evacuate their homes and businesses Tuesday night. More than 900 people live within the evacuation zone, and it was believed that all of them had left by Wednesday morning, the mayor said. A shelter-in-place order was issued for residents beyond the evacuation zone within a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius. It was very foggy early Wednesday in the city of about 265,000 people, hindering visibility and delaying efforts to use drones to monitor the site. Kapszukiewicz reassured residents outside the evacuation zone that the fog was unrelated to the chemical explosion. The National Weather Service said the fog was expected to lift by mid-morning. Arkansas-based MC Tank Transport said in a statement the company is working with the fire department and other emergency authorities. Company representatives were on their way to Toledo, Kapszukiewicz said. "Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees," it said. "Our immediate and overriding concern is the safety of area residents, emergency responders and our employees." McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire. - Published
Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use.
The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts.
Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so.
"Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity.
In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles."
"We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."
Google is one of several tech companies that signed contracts with the US military earlier this year to deploy AI across classified military environments. The US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority, saying the Trump administration will become an "AI-first warfighting force".
But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight.
After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said.
Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, external, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.
The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for.
Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns.
Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future."
"Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added.
In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities.
The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data.
Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up.
Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation."
However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year.
Google's contract with the Pentagon, which was signed earlier this year, allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control".
Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations.
As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war.
"AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team.
"When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."
Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company.
"In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".
Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."

edc13139eba8.text:
Drug overdose deaths unexpectedly took a nosedive in the United States a few years ago. But it doesn’t appear to be due to more people being revived than before.
At the peak in mid-2023, there were around 111,000 drug overdose deaths per year in the United States. By the end of 2025, the number had fallen to under 71,000 per year, and researchers are still piecing together why. One theory: The wider availability of naloxone, a medication that reverses opioid overdoses, made it possible to revive more people than before.
But a study of U.S. emergency medical services agencies found that emergency medical responses for nonfatal overdoses dropped along with deaths, and the use of naloxone also declined. That suggests that fewer overdoses overall occurred, not that naloxone stopped deaths more often, researchers report October 21 in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
“Naloxone still saves lives every day,” says Michael Barnett, a health services researcher at Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I. “But it doesn’t look like the reason for the sudden turn” in overdose deaths.
State policies, community distribution programs and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s approval of the nasal spray version of naloxone as an over-the counter drug have expanded access.
Barnett and colleagues analyzed nearly 186 million emergency medical service activations — an ambulance or other EMS response after a 911 call — nationwide that occurred from May 2020 through December 2025. Of 2.5 million responses for nonfatal drug overdoses, 40.5 percent involved opioids.
From May of 2023 onward, EMS activations for nonfatal opioid overdoses fell on average by about 6,000, or around 33 percent, below what was expected. Total administrations of naloxone dropped as well, by around 4,700 on average, or 21 percent below what was expected. The study suggests that naloxone was not used more often than before by bystanders prior to the EMS response, but did not include data on cases when a bystander provided naloxone and no one called 911.
Additional possibilities to explain the steep drop in overdose deaths — which followed a three-decade increase — include changes to the illicit opioid supply or with the population of people at risk for overdoses. “My own read is that a disruption in the fentanyl supply best explains how sudden and widespread the turn was,” Barnett says. “Underneath it, the population at risk has probably been shrinking for years.”
But “a supply-driven decline can reverse,” Barnett says, noting that the decline in overdose deaths slowed in 2025. Traffickers can adapt “by finding new chemical sources or turning to more potent synthetic opioids.”

ff40cd9fe105.text: Democratic groups sued the Trump administration Tuesday, accusing it of using unfounded voter fraud claims to muscle its way into how states run elections. Why it matters: The groups say the administration is issuing a stream of threats to intimidate and bully both voters and election officials. They're asking a judge to declare the administration's actions unlawful and block further interference. Driving the news: The lawsuit condemns the administration for targeting state voter rolls by insisting that local officials review federally compiled lists of alleged noncitizens on their voter rolls. The suit also alleges that the administration is improperly demanding that states deny ballots to registered voters based on those federal lists. The Democrat-aligned groups also claim the administration has attempted to intimidate state and local officials by threatening them with jail time or prosecution. Case in point: The lawsuit cites a Department of Homeland Security claim that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. The department later claimed that it had confirmed 185 of those people were noncitizens. State records later indicated that all 185 were citizens. The DOJ also demanded that California deny ballots to more than 20,000 people based on a federal list that flagged them as suspected ineligible voters, the lawsuit says. A preliminary investigation by Los Angeles County investigators found that more than 25% of those flagged listed a U.S. birthplace, and others already had their voter registrations canceled. What they're saying: "Department of Justice and DHS officials have sought to bolster their interference efforts through a persistent stream of threats and intimidation directed towards state and local election officials across the country," the groups' attorneys wrote. "Defendants' coercive threats of legal retaliation against state officials, including even potential imprisonment, for simply following state law and aiding registered voters in casting their ballots objectively intimidate voters and election officials alike, in violation of Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act." The suit, brought by Democratic organizations including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democratic leaders and a voter, names Trump, the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, and their respective heads as defendants. The other side: "The Justice Department enforces federal election law, and election integrity is a top priority," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement "Every action the Department has taken to protect the integrity of this year's elections is grounded in the law and being litigated in open court. Ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted is a requirement of federal law." "We notified California that noncitizens are likely registered to vote, and we asked the state to independently verify the citizenship of any ballots cast by people on a list that we provided. It refused to do so. Federal law doesn't permit this willful blindness." The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: The suit also argues that the president has no constitutional authority to decide who gets to vote or dictate how states count ballots. Investigations and audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud. Research shows noncitizen voting is rare, and there's no evidence it occurs on a scale that could swing elections. Go deeper: Trump sues California to prevent counting 20,000 voters' ballots

afb0d6cf8d23.text: House Democrats' campaign arm is instructing allied super PACs to promote minor candidates in several key House races, Axios has learned. Why it matters: This allows Democrats to steer outside groups toward siphoning votes from Republicans without violating laws against direct coordination. An Axios review of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "redboxes" — publicly available webpages laying out what PACs should say in ads and which voters to target — found references to minor candidates in five races. The DCCC included language on four of those pages promoting a third-party or independent candidate with language touting their conservative, pro-gun or anti-government bona fides. "Registered Republicans under the age of 55 need to see ads," the redbox for Colorado's 5th District says, "showing that ... Christopher Mitchell, a libertarian, is the true conservative running for Congress." The page for Virginia's 2nd District says white, college-educated men should see that independent J. Matt Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment" who will "defend our constitution." In Virginia's 5th District , the DCCC wants the same group of voters to know that independent Cooke Harvey "will fight for Virginia's farmers against big government." Republican women in Nevada's 2nd District should be informed that American Independent Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values," the DCCC says. Zoom in: In several cases, the redboxes urge super PACs to steer Democratic and left-leaning voters away from minor candidates who could siphon votes from the DCCC's recruit. The redbox for Alaska's at-large district — where Democrats are backing independent Bill Hill — says voters need to know Eric Hafner is a "fake Democrat" despite being listed on the ballot as one, noting he is an inmate in New York with no clear ties to Alaska . The page for Virginia's 2nd District urges PACs to ding the progressive credentials of another independent candidate, Geral D. "Bishop" Staten , a self-identified "Democrat Socialist." Black voters should hear that Staten "said that he would vote for Donald Trump in 2024 and said that President Obama is a quote 'puppet and a clown,'" the DCCC redbox says — though he has denied supporting Trump. Between the lines: In the post-Citizens United era, redboxes have emerged as a way for campaigns to give messaging guidance to cash-rich outside groups that often have less localized knowledge of their turf. The practice is so named because the websites often put a red box around the instructions. The NRCC has its own publicly available redboxes , though it shies away from encouraging PACs to boost spoiler candidates. The big picture: There have been several other isolated examples this year of both parties allegedly boosting spoiler candidates, including with redboxes. Democrats successfully sued last month to get a Green Party candidate who they alleged was a GOP plant booted off the ballot in Pennsylvania's 7th District. Republicans in Alaska tried and failed to do the same with unaffiliated candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who they allege is a spoiler for Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his race against Democrat Mary Peltola. It's even happened in party primaries: The campaign of Rep. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.) put language on its redbox promoting Republican Zachariah Wooden in the hopes of keeping progressive challenger Mai Vang out of the general election.

Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.
Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.
The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.
"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".
The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.
A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.
Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.
If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.
Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.
TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.
One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.
They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted
Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.
