Here's what happened Politics Oct 21, 2026 6:50 PM EDT A national polling organization revealed on Tuesday that the vast majority of its data had been fabricated, saying it was an "experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities" of the modern political polling industry. Wedgewood Polling, whose polls had been cited by national news outlets, released the statement after FiftyPlusOne, a polling and election analysis site, questioned the veracity of its results. "We wanted to test a simple hypothesis: How easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary?" Wedgewood Polling said on X. "The short answer: Far too easy." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. FiftyPlusOne and The New York Times had included Wedgewood Polling data in their databases aggregating results from various polls. The organizations have since removed the data. MS NOW, Newsweek, Decision Desk HQ and Mediaite had also cited Wedgewood's polls. "The ease with which unverified figures were absorbed into mainstream political narratives highlights a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation," Wedgewood said in its statement. Andrew Gelman, a professor of statistics and political science at Columbia University questioned Wedgewood Polling's statement that it had always been intended to be an experiment. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. "Maybe so, but it's kind of suspicious that they happened to release this statement on the very day that they got caught," Gelman wrote in a blog post. A day after Wedgewood's admission, Federal Communications Commission head Brendan Carr said in a statement on X that TV networks could violate their regulatory obligations by airing "fake polls." "Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations," Carr wrote. Without citing evidence or specific polls, he added that there had been a "significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls" during this election season. Here's what to know about the incident, Carr's response and how polling works. What do we know about Wedgewood Polling? In its statement, Wedgewood Polling described itself as a "fictional entity run by a small group of industry veterans." The organization's X account was opened in June 2026. Its website now displays an error message. FiftyPlusOne refuted Wedgewood's claim that its site and The New York Times had aggregated the polling data "without verifying the source, methodology, or underlying firm legitimacy." FiftyPlusOne and The New York Times said in their statements addressing Wedgewood Polling that before including the alleged data on their websites, the organizations had reached out to the polling firm with questions about the organization and its methods. According to FiftyPlusOne, the polling firm was run by Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. FiftyPlusOne wrote that it confirmed Sims had previous polling experience. "It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different," FiftyPlusOne said. Independent news organizations had previously raised alarms about Wedgewood Polling Several months back, Straight Arrow News and Urban Milwaukee published concerns about the veracity of Wedgewood Polling. Bruce Murphy, long-time editor and columnist for Urban Milwaukee, questioned the reliability of Wedgewood Polling in July and August, describing it as "a shady outfit." Murphy wrote that Wedgewood had published a poll showing Francesca Hong, a candidate for Wisconsin governor vying for the Democratic nomination, at 30%. Other polls, Murphy wrote, showed Hong with "far less of the vote." Hong lost the primary. Straight Arrow News pointed out that Wedgewood Polling's website didn't include employee names, a phone number or an address. The news organization said it reached out to the polling firm, which confirmed they were a "two-person shop" but declined to reveal their identities or appear on camera. "We understand that this decision can naturally raise skepticism," the firm reportedly told Straight Arrow News in a statement. It cited "recent concerns surrounding organizations such as Median Strategies." That fraudulent polling organization admitted in August that it had also faked results as a "short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification." Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Senate candidate in Michigan says fake polling hurt her campaign Mallory McMorrow, a Democratic state senator in Michigan, suspended her campaign to become a U.S. senator in July, about a month before the state's primary that progressive Abdul El-Sayed won. In an X post on Tuesday, McMorrow detailed what she described as the impact of Wedgewood's "experiment." McMorrow wrote that a Wedgewood poll in June showed her "plummeting into single digits (which was at odds with our internals)." As a result, she said "donations dried up" and "volunteers were devastated." "Sure, a point was proven. Polling is broken," McMorrow wrote. c1f96cc4c842.text: The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct recent stories about alleged staff drama, or it would suffer unspecified consequences. That deadline expires Thursday. Why it matters: The White House demand threatens to escalate already tense relations with Politico specifically and, more generally, the press corps that covers President Trump in Washington. Politico, CNN, and MS NOW are already banned from covering Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One because the president does not like their coverage. Trump blocked all three outlets from the White House grounds as well, but a judge on Oct. 13 restored their access. CNN threatened legal action Wednesday to regain access to Air Force One and the "pool" of television networks that accompany the president. Zoom in: In his letter to Politico, White House Counsel Will Scharf singled out three stories concerning White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles despite "on-the-record refutations" or contrary evidence supplied by senior staff and even the president. 1) Oct. 15: In a story headlined " Trump's ice maiden is under fire ," Politico Playbook reported that Trump was considering a replacement for Wiles. Trump called it "fake news." 2) Oct. 16: Politico Playbook wrote that the prior day's story had caused a "freakout" and that the president "blew up" over it. A White House spokesman called it "unbelievably stupid and false." 3) Oct. 16: In a story headlined " Susie Wiles helped set up Fox interview ahead of press secretary's exit ," Politico insinuated the chief of staff set up Katie Zacharia to fail in a Sean Hannity interview on Fox the night before. The White House and Fox News denied the reporting. And White House officials provided text messages to Politico before publication showing Zacharia — not Wiles — set up the interview, which the New York Post reported the following day. "Politico has not corrected or retracted its false reporting. Instead, a Politico reporter confirmed that Politico declined to remove Ms. Wiles from the story because she was the 'hook' for the story — a legally fraught and alarming admission to say the least," Scharf wrote. What they're saying: Scharf wrote that "freedom of the press is not a professional exemption from accountability. I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives." Otherwise, he wrote, the White House would conduct an "immediate review of Politico's relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies." A Politico spokesperson did not return a message seeking comment. White House officials fault the new management at Politico for pushing its reporters to engage in what Scharf called "gossip-peddling." The letter was addressed to global editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger. Zoom out: Trump has had an ongoing love-hate relationship with the press. He is available to reporters for far more question-and-answer sessions than any recent president, but he's quick to anger and threaten press bans for coverage he doesn't like. Early in his second term, Trump banned the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One access after it balked at calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. A federal judge reinstated AP's access months later. The New York Times reported this week that Trump has mused about removing the press entirely from the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room and building a swimming pool there. What's next: Scharf would not specify what consequences Politico faces, but a White House official said "all options are on the table" and described Trump's counsel as "uncharacteristically enraged." Trump is highly litigious with media organizations and, advisers say, his appetite for launching lawsuits hasn't diminished. Some advisers outside of the Trump White House noticed that administration officials may be telegraphing another avenue to attack Politico as a malign foreign influence because it's owned by a German company, Axel Springer. "Politico is a foreign-op designed to interfere in American politics and meddle in our elections with disinformation and misinformation," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote on X Saturday.

From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.
There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".
Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.
"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.
The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.
String of incidents
Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.
Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".
Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.
The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.
Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".
This was just the start of the problems.
Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.
In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.
Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.
"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.
"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."
'Overwhelmingly cheaper'
As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.
GL Events had won the 63bn yen (Â£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.
A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.
Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.
But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".
"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.
Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.
"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.
GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.
Hopes for the future
Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.
It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.
Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.
But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.
"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."
While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.
Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three

9aa0afa22e03.text: By — Stephen Whyno, Associated Press Stephen Whyno, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/nfl-welcomes-a-review-of-how-eagles-handled-jalen-hurts-blood-clots-roger-goodell-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter NFL welcomes a review of how Eagles handled Jalen Hurts' blood clots, Roger Goodell says Nation Oct 21, 2026 5:49 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The NFL welcomes an investigation into the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots after the players' union asked for one, Commissioner Roger Goodell said Wednesday. Goodell said in his news conference at the end of the NFL's annual fall meeting that Dr. Allen Sills, the league's chief medical officer, has gone through the steps that were followed and added that the union had a right to call for a review. "Obviously, there was a medical evaluation, and I think our protocols were incredibly good there," Goodell said. "The protocols were followed. Our process is to make sure that's the case, and our chief medical officer has gone through that, so we're comfortable that what we've seen in the protocols have happened." READ MORE: AP source: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts expected to miss rest of season after blood clots found in lungs and leg Sills on Tuesday offered a passionate defense of the Eagles medical staff. The NFL said officials were in touch with team doctors and trainers, as well as the Cleveland Clinic in London, where the Eagles were playing the Jaguars on Oct. 11. League executive vice president Jeff Miller said officials had a good sense of the course of events, which included Hurts being evaluated at a hospital the day before the game. Miller disputed a report that Hurts was awake for more than 30 hours before playing against Jacksonville, saying that the 28-year-old returned to the hotel and slept for roughly seven or eight hours. Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms. Goodell downplayed the role that international travel may have had in the situation. "The most important thing here is Jalen's health, ultimately, and the future of him," Goodell said. "He's a wonderful young man: not just a great player, but he's someone we all care deeply about. I'm more worried about his health, ultimately, but the protocols were followed." Sills said Tuesday the decision to allow someone with a blood clot to fly depends on several variables, including the location, a patient's history and more. "What I can tell you is expert people getting a lot of opinions," Sills said. "This isn't just one doctor saying yay or nay. You're going to poll a panel of experts both within the team and outside the team to get the best judgment and experience with a particular condition." Hurts was six games into his fifth season as Philadelphia's starting quarterback. He was Super Bowl MVP when the Eagles won it all two years ago. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A new report from the United Nations Environment Programme suggests that limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels is no longer a realistic outcome, even under the most ambitious emissions-reduction scenarios.
The report’s lowest-warming scenario, which would require steep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, would only limit peak global warming to 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
The 2015 Paris Agreement, adopted by almost every country in the world, set a goal of keeping global warming below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees. The United States has withdrawn from the agreement twice under President Donald Trump, most recently last year.
The report’s projections do not mean the world should abandon the 1.5 degree target, said Inger Andersen, UNEP’s executive director, at a press briefing.
“Every additional fraction of a degree matters, and every additional year of warming above 1.5 will increase climate impacts such as deadly floods, heatwaves, wildfires that have plagued nations this year,” Andersen said.
Robert Kopp, a climate scientist and professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey, said the report’s findings were not surprising. Even in 2015, he said, the 1.5 degree target was at the edge of what was considered feasible.
Reaching the report’s lowest warming scenario would require emissions to fall by 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. It would also require removing substantial amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, an effort that would likely involve not only reforestation, but also the rapid development of carbon-capture technologies that remain in the early stages of development.
Meanwhile, climate impacts are mounting, putting pressure on efforts to adapt to global warming. Western Europe saw thousands of heat-related deaths last spring and summer, a period which encompassed four of the region’s 10 most severe heat waves since 1950.
Still, the report highlights the expansion of renewable energy as an area of progress. Despite what Jan Minx, head of the Evidence for Climate Solutions working group at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, described as “bleak” predictions for global warming, the growth of renewable energy capacity, particularly wind and solar, has outpaced expectations. Minx co-authored a chapter in the report.
Global renewable electricity capacity expanded three times faster than was anticipated in 2015, according to the report, while solar photovoltaic capacity grew seven times faster.
Setu Pelz, a research scholar at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis who co-authored a chapter in the report, said countries must sustain that momentum to triple renewable capacity by 2030, a priority in keeping with Paris Agreement targets.
Global emissions in 2025 were comparable to those a year prior—a “welcome divergence from a growth trend of past decades,” Anne Olhoff, the director of the UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre and the report’s lead author, said at a press briefing.
But the expansion of clean energy has yet to drive down fossil fuel emissions. According to the report, emissions from the combustion of oil, gas and coal continue to rise.
“We provide some evidence that can inform the discussions about 2030, 2035 and 2040 targets in these sectors, so that we can see the same level of ambition in the fossil fuel transition as we have seen in the real renewable capacity scale-up,” said Pelz.
Released annually, UNEP’s emissions gap report is part of a growing body of research warning that current climate policies fall short of what is needed to meet international temperature targets. Under existing policies, global warming could reach 2.8 degrees by 2100—far above the Paris Agreement’s 2-degree threshold.
When asked what a world that is more than 2 degrees Celsius warmer than pre-industrial levels might look like, Andersen referenced recent extreme weather events.“Think of the heat wave … in much of Europe last year, think of the wildfires that we are seeing in Scandinavia as an example, think of droughts and harvest failures,” she said.
“Think of that happening much more frequently.”

f12c821a7e60.text: By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-political-groups-spend-nearly-277-million-in-late-midterm-blitz-on-behalf-of-gop-candidates Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's political groups spend nearly $277 million in late midterm blitz on behalf of GOP candidates Politics Oct 21, 2026 5:29 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump's political groups have spent more than one-quarter of a billion dollars to bolster Republicans in the final stretch of this year's midterm elections, an unprecedented amount for a sitting president that underscores the stakes on Nov. 3. In total, Trump's flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc., has reported spending nearly $277 million since the beginning of September, according to new federal campaign finance filings. That includes major transfers to two affiliated groups that have been spending millions on advertising: $200 million to No Going Back PAC Inc. and $25 million to Safety & Affordability PAC Inc. Please check your inbox to confirm. "It's more than any president has ever spent, by far, on the midterms," said Corry Bliss, a GOP Senate and House campaign strategist who was the executive director of the Congressional Leadership Fund, House Republicans' super PAC in the 2018 campaign. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on how Trump's unpopularity is shaping the midterms Trump had been under intense pressure to help Republican candidates as his party struggles to hold onto its slim majorities in the House and Senate. While the party in power almost always loses seats in midterm elections, Republicans are facing an especially challenging climb after Trump helped defeat several of the party's longtime incumbents and as he has been mired in low approval ratings amid deep voter frustration over persistently high costs and the unpopular war with Iran. One bright spot for Republicans has been their huge financial advantage over Democrats this election cycle, aided by billionaires such as Elon Musk. READ MORE: Elon Musk quietly becomes biggest known donor in midterm contests as he tries to save Republicans Trump-affiliated groups are now on track to spend potentially more. So far, the three that have to report their donors have spent more than $256 million on advertising, according to AdImpact, which tracks media spending and reservations. That includes tens of millions of dollars in Texas to help embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton in his race against Democrat James Talarico. Musk has also invested heavily in Texas, leading Talarico to accuse him of trying to buy the seat. WATCH: GOP's big bet on Texas Latino voters could backfire in midterms MAGA Inc. had more than $164 million cash left in the bank as of Oct. 14, meaning it still has plenty left to spend. But the Trump team's decision to wait until late in the cycle to begin advertising has diluted their spending power. The groups are paying far higher ad rates because of the shrinking availability of air time — sometimes more than five times what they would have spent if they had acted sooner. WATCH: Examining the controversial claims Trump is making at his midterm rallies In a post on his social media site Tuesday, Trump said that he planned to spend "over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day," including $300 million he said had already been spent on advertising, voter contact, rallies, tele-rallies, get-out-the-vote programs and efforts to prevent voters from cheating. MAGA Inc. began September with nearly $416 million in the bank. It has continued to raise huge sums of cash from billionaire backers including businessperson Diane Hendricks, Blackstone Group CEO Stephen A. Schwarzman and casino magnate Steve Wynn. Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 5bf6fa918566.text: Security officials are sounding the alarm over two critical vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI. Why it matters : The bugs, which researchers found partly with an OpenAI model, proves AI can uncover critical flaws humans missed for decades — raising the stakes for defenders racing to fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them at machine speed. What's happening: There are two problems hackers could easily exploit in an open-source programming language known as PHP that's used on nearly 70% of all websites . Government officials from the U.S. to Japan are warning companies to apply a patch to fix the bugs, or consider taking down their sites to avoid an attack. OpenAI touted the role its model played in discovering one of the vulnerabilities, which allowed PHP researchers to create a fix. Between the lines: Security researchers have been skeptical of AI-generated vulnerability reports, many of which have turned out to be minor bugs or false alarms. But the PHP discovery could force the cybersecurity community to reckon with the reality of AI threats. "It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post Wednesday. Threat level: If exploited, the PHP flaws would allow malicious hackers to take control of vulnerable web servers without needing a password or other credentials. Since PHP runs under a wide variety of internet applications, that access could allow hackers to take over websites, steal sensitive information and tamper with a website. Some website owners took their sites down earlier Wednesday, including certain services at Wikipedia and 4chan , until they had time to patch their systems. "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," researchers at Wiz wrote in a post. The big picture: AI-driven bug discoveries are shining a light on the fragility of the modern internet, which is heavily reliant on a slew of open-source software powered by volunteers . The two flaws in PHP existed for decades, but demonstrated that it was possible for a hacker to exploit them required "an exceptionally complex chain of steps," researchers at Wiz added. "Defenders have always relied on the gap between 'vulnerable' and 'exploitable' to buy time to patch," Michael Leland, field CTO at Island, said in an email to Axios. "That gap is rapidly closing." What to watch : Cybersecurity defenders are on guard for what could be a wave of incidents where websites and organizations are hacked using these two vulnerabilities in the next few weeks. Darline Graham as early voting begins Politics Oct 21, 2026 5:02 PM EDT PENDLETON, S.C. (AP) — President Donald Trump will visit South Carolina on Wednesday to boost U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, whose stumbles in her first campaign since replacing her late brother have Democratic voters hopeful — but not necessarily optimistic — that their candidate can break Republicans' grip on the state. Although South Carolina is not typically a midterm battleground, Trump has been deeply invested in Graham. He supported her appointment to replace Lindsey Graham after his death in July, and he backed her in a special primary when she faced several more experienced Republican opponents. But some distance emerged between the Republican president and the senator over the weekend over his decision to waive Ukraine war sanctions on Russia that were set to be imposed under a law named after Lindsey Graham. WATCH: Trump holds GOP midterm rally in battleground North Carolina Republicans want to make sure Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, doesn't pull off an upset victory. More than $34 million has flowed into the race, and Republicans have hammered Andrews as a "radical liberal" and accused her of supporting surgeries for transgender minors, which she denies. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump this week is rallying every day for candidates across the country, even in conservative areas, and imploring voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot" in hopes of averting a lackluster midterm turnout for Republicans. READ MORE: Trump's new pitch for Republican candidates? They're really good looking "Darline Graham knows that our campaign's momentum is so strong she called Donald Trump to come campaign for her in South Carolina," Andrews said in a fundraising appeal email. Darline Graham rushed to define herself — and clung close to Trump Lindsey Graham had been on a glide path to a fifth term when he died of an aortic tear. Darline Graham, former director of the state agency for the blind, received bipartisan support when she was appointed to serve out her brother's term. But her decision to run for the seat in the midterms prompted skepticism that the political neophyte was up for the job. Darline Graham had the endorsement of Trump, who campaigned for her before the runoff with U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman. A stumble over a question related to U.S. policy in Taiwan, in which Graham admitted she was "not that informed on national security," prompted questions over her readiness. Waiting for her at a weekend event in Mount Pleasant, Nanette Tumbleston said she felt strongly Graham should win, shuddering to think of what might happen if the seat fell to Democrats. "I hope that everybody's eyes will be open and we'll have a Republican win," Tumbleston said, adding that she feared progressives' influence in the Democratic Party. "I just can't see how they can see that the world's going to be a better place with those policies." Andrews pivoted from Lindsey Graham to Darline Graham Andrews launched her campaign more than a year before Lindsey Graham's death. She pivoted to criticizing Darline Graham as "Trump-endorsed and unqualified." Andrews argues that Republican policies have weakened not only the broader U.S. economy but also the financial situations of children and families, centering her message on "building a South Carolina that we can all afford," as she said last week in Columbia. As the pediatrician seemed to gain steam this fall, Republican groups infused millions of dollars into the race, characterizing the spending as an insurance policy for Graham. Trump attacked Andrews on social media, saying the Democrat doesn't represent "the Values of the Great People of South Carolina." Some Andrews supporters acknowledge that while Democrats might ultimately break through in South Carolina, it might take more time. Paul Davis, of Aiken, said "people are really angry and fed up, and they can't afford things." However, he said a Democratic victory "may be a cycle or two away." The candidates accuse each other of being unqualified At their only debate, Graham and Andrews disagreed on issues including healthcare but primarily accused each other of inexperience. "It is nothing personal, but she has shown time and time again that she is not up for the job," Andrews said, calling Graham's interim appointment "a nice gesture." Graham said serving while processing her brother's death showed "just how strong I am," adding that "I'm just as qualified as you are." At the Columbia rally, some of Andrews' supporters said they were hopeful, despite Democrats' years of Senate losses in the state. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated Democrat Jaime Harrison by 10 percentage points in a contest that turned into South Carolina's most expensive ever. "It's definitely frustrating," said Emily Glenham, a Columbia copywriter. "It's definitely been disappointing, but you can't not have hope." Sandra Martin, of West Columbia, agreed Andrews had "a good chance" but looked more toward the future. "Georgia did it," she said. "If Georgia can do it, there's no reason we can't, someday." aa4840fdf403.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/pope-leos-tests-show-he-needs-no-further-treatment-for-lung-cancer-his-doctors-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo's tests show he needs no further treatment for lung cancer, his doctors say Politics Oct 21, 2026 4:44 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localized, the Vatican said in a statement Wednesday. Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery and well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated. READ MORE: Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery The pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the pope's surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread. Please check your inbox to confirm. "A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the doctors said. The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all the cancer was removed. READ MORE: What is adenocarcinoma? Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer Additional treatment is offered in such cases if follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread or has certain other signs that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumors are caught very early, such as when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot long before it's large or causing symptoms. The pope appears to have had one of those "incidental findings," a nodule in his lung spotted during another exam. In an interview with Vatican News, Margoritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome's Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations. The pope carried on business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Putin, and has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St. Peter's Square and Wednesday's longer audience, when he greeted the faithful from all over the world. READ MORE: Doctors say Pope Leo's lung has recovered well from surgery and say his post-operative tests normal His next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Margaritora was quoted by Vatican News as saying that there was "no clinical reason" to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high altitude stops. The pope revealed that a nodule had been found and would be surgically removed during the traditional Sunday blessing on Oct. 11, in an unusually transparent disclosure. A new, purpose-built laboratory will serve as a base for scientists, universities and students to investigate Cumbria's upland landscapes, and how they respond to nature recovery.
It is hoped the research facility at RSPB Wild Haweswater, in Penrith, will become a hub for upland science, bringing researchers and conservationists together to carry out fieldwork, share expertise, and develop new collaborations.
The lab was funded by the estate of the late ornithologist Denis Summers-Smith.
"We want to build on Denis's commitment to field ecology and conservation research, creating a lasting legacy that will benefit both science and nature recovery in Cumbria and beyond," said RSPB's Will Peach.
The new lab will support current research through Cumbria Connect, whose work and scientific monitoring spans Wild Haweswater, the Lowther estate and the Lowther Valley.
Dr Mo Verhoeven, conservation scientist at Cumbria Connect, explained how the region's landscape is made up of a number of distinctive environments, including peatlands and rainforest, which play a key role in storing carbon and managing water.
"Cumbria's uplands are incredibly important for nature recovery," he said.
"We hope this laboratory will give researchers, students and conservationists a place to work together and build the evidence needed to guide restoration, both here in Cumbria and in upland landscapes further afield.
"It's about making Cumbria a much stronger base for upland science."
"Just as importantly, it will help train the next generation of environmental scientists," he said.
Cumbria Connect is part of a scheme paid for by the Arcadia Fund which was co-founded by one of the heirs to the Tetra Pak fortune.

ea978abd05bc.text: Senate Republicans are weighing three last-ditch spending moves that would have been unimaginable six months ago: a cash infusion for Mississippi and even more money for South Carolina and Kansas. Why it matters: It's been 94 years since Kansas elected a Democratic senator, 44 years for Mississippi and 28 for South Carolina. But panic is spreading through the Republican Party. "The wall has broken. The enemy is inside the fort," one national Republican political operative told Axios. "We are now fighting hand to hand." The Senate map, which once looked impregnable for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is now full of vulnerabilities. Democratic challengers are polling within the margin of error in more than half a dozen deep-red states, according to internal GOP polls. The other side: "We're nervous about Alaska. We're nervous about Michigan. We're still going to hold the Senate at the end," said another operative. Zoom in: Two weeks ago, when Senate Leadership Fund decided to take out a $5 million "insurance policy" in South Carolina, operatives took a hard look at Idaho, South Dakota and Mississippi. At the time, they concluded they didn't need to spend any money in those states, according to a person familiar with the matter. But Senate Republicans are now reviewing the Mississippi race and may need to spend there to protect Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith from a surprisingly competitive bid by Democratic district attorney Scott Colom . Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, announced a $1.2 million investment in the race on Tuesday. Zoom out: In early June, SLF started to reinforce a Midwestern red wall to protect the GOP majority, reserving $28 million in TV advertising in Ohio and $11 million in Iowa . Those investments have ballooned to $93 million in Ohio and $53 million in Iowa. After an initial $5 million buy in South Carolina, SLF's spending has increased to $8.5 million, according to AdImpact. And a super PAC linked to Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) is spending another $500,000 in South Carolina. SLF, which is linked to Senate GOP leadership, has earmarked $14 million for Kansas, and has spent nearly $12 million there so far. "No Republican seat is safe this cycle," another operative told Axios. What we're hearing: Some GOP Senate candidates do, in fact, appear safe this cycle. Republicans aren't overly concerned about Sens. Ashley Moody in Florida or Mike Rounds in South Dakota. The intrigue: The National Republican Senatorial Committee raised $31.4 million last month, but its coffers appear to be drained. It took out a $20 million loan as it spends aggressively on its coordinated campaign strategy. SLF ended September with $155 million in cash on hand, according to its FEC filing. The group has spent or reserved $169 million worth of video ads since Oct. 1, according to AdImpact. Even President Trump promised to unload another $100 million before Election Day in a Tuesday post on Truth Social, bringing the total from his super PACs to $400 million. The bottom line: Republicans can still maintain their Senate majority, but none of the polling is giving them a great deal of confidence that they will do so.

Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation.
CÃ©sar JÃ¡uregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year.
The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers.
Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said JÃ¡uregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. JÃ¡uregui has denied the allegations.
The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday.
A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports.
JÃ¡uregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country.
She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached.
The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine.
Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said.
At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, JÃ¡uregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities".

Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.
Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican.
"A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.
The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.
It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.
The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.
The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".
Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.
On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".
The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.
Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
All rather vague.
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
"Of course!"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there.
A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes.
Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee.
Reports of the new policy circulated this week, along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores.
Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy.
"Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit,"
"There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented.
Starbucks stores around the world have been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers.
Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying.
In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores, after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow.
In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers.
Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products.
Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks.
In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain.
Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (Â£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital.
In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours".

For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in technology underpinning much of the internet.
It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.
The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world scrambled to contain the fallout of this discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.
Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.
OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
What is the flaw?
Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.
PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress â the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.
AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.
It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.
What websites have been affected?
The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.
That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.
Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.
A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.
Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.
More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.
What happened after the flaws were exposed?
Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.
"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.
Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.
The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.
"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".
Its counterparts in the EU and Australia have also issued similar alerts.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X.
"If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.
How is AI finding weak spots?
The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.
The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can.
"Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said.
"The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.
Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.
The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.
The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.
"Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.
What can people do to safeguard themselves?
Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.
The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors.
"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.
The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.
He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms.
The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".
Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during second Trump administration.
The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".
It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.
For example, it says that when Industry Minister MÃ©lanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support".
Asked on Wednesday about the allegations, Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada.
"We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.
He said his government's response has been "in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy".
Carney, who was announcing a nearly C$9bn ($6.2bn) aid package in response to US tariffs, was accompanied by both Joly and Ford.
Ford said that he has "no interest at all" in interfering in US elections.
"I'll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability," Ford said, adding that he will focus on Ontario and Canada.
"The people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms," he said.
Last week, Minister Joly denied Canadian interference and said that Canadians "never accept that also being done to us in Canada", according to CBC.
She said that her recent visits to the US were "to attract investments" from American companies, which she plans to continue.
Washington and Ottawa have argued for months over tariffs and trade, which once flowed freely across their borders, and the effects of Canada's counter measures.
Earlier this month, US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned that US officials are "closely watching" Canada's politicians for signs of election interference.
Trump administration officials have also been accused of making inappropriate remarks about the separation referendum in the province of Alberta this week.
A petition calling for Hoekstra's removal from his post for "undermining the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations" has received more than 280,000 signatures.

The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.
The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.
An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives.
The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump.
Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s.
Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states.
The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed.
The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population.
At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union.
So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it?
No country for young men?
Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November.
Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters.
When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream.
The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans.
Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates.
Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (Â£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website.
Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says.
The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56.
In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington
But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively.
The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39.
There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too.
So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her.
Age versus issues
Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too.
The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later, it had risen to 30%.
Pew adds that voters under 30 were underrepresented in 2024. Voters in that age category made up 20% of the voting-eligible population, though accounted for only 15% of all the votes that were actually cast.

For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.
But that may end soon.
Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.
New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.
The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (Â£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.
Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.
A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.
A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.
"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.
Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".
While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.
Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.
But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.
Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).
Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.
Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.
