Rising food prices. Supply chain disruptions. Wars. More extreme weather.
The confluence of these factors in 2026 has prompted researchers, advocacy groups and farmers around the world to more forcefully question the architecture of an increasingly stressed global food system—and the money, both public and private, that supports it.
Coinciding with harvest season in much of the world this month, critics and activists are using a handful of agriculture- and food-focused events to home in on the structural problems of a system they say disadvantages developing countries, fattens rich ones and fails to “feed the world” as it claims to.
“It does produce food,” said Jeff Conant, a deputy director with the advocacy group Friends of the Earth. “It also undeniably produces something on the order of a third of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions. It produces illness. It produces dispossession of land-based peoples. It produces obesity and it produces wealth for the corporate elites at the expense of the rest of us.”
This month, Friends of the Earth and more than a dozen advocacy groups published a report tracking the profits of the world’s largest food companies. “It is not, in fact, a food system,” Conant said. “It’s an agribusiness financial complex.”
On Friday—the United Nations’ “World Food Day”— hundreds of farmers from around the world protested against the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, accusing the institutions of undercutting public support for agriculture and worsening hunger.
The protest, organized by La Via Campesina, a grassroots movement of small-scale farmers, came as the institutions concluded their weeklong annual gathering in Bangkok.
Earlier this month, farmers and advocacy groups convened, also in Bangkok, under the movement’s newly coined slogan, “Feed the People, Not the Debts!” The issue, they say, is that low-income countries spend so much money on debt payments they can’t feed their own citizens or invest in agricultural improvements to make food production more resilient.
“We owe 12.23 trillion Kenyan shillings,” said Kenyan farmer Susan Owiti, who traveled to Bangkok to join the protest. “This is a crisis. So what we are saying is we don’t need more debts. What we want is a trade framework that is based on food sovereignty.”
As climate-fueled weather events batter the world’s farms, the ongoing war in Ukraine cuts grain exports and fertilizer shipments remain stalled in the Strait of Hormuz, food prices have soared, making the situation especially fraught.
“Farmers are increasingly integrated into a global supply chain that controls fuel, fertilizer and grain. Every time a disruption happens—COVID, Ukraine, the war in West Asia and others—it leads to a major increase in input prices, pushing us further into debt,” said Zainal Arifin Fuat, a farmer from Indonesia and member of La Via Campesina, at the Bangkok conference. “Then the World Bank and IMF approach us with more loans, which come with even stricter conditions.”
The World Bank did not answer questions from Inside Climate News.
According to a 2023 report from the United Nations, about 3.3 billion people—more than half the world’s population—live in countries, mostly in the Global South, that spend more on interest payments than health or education. This “crushing debt crisis,” as U.N. Secretary General Antonio Guterres has called it, prompted Guterres and many economists to urge overhauls of IMF and World Bank lending policies, which they argued have favored developed countries.
The debt makes it harder for countries to feed themselves while coping with repeated climate-driven droughts, heatwaves and flooding.
In a workshop on food prices held for journalists last week, Raj Patel, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin and food systems expert, explained that the indebtedness of countries in the Global South locks them into a food-impoverishing pattern. In order to pay back loans in U.S. dollars, he said, countries are forced to grow crops for export rather than using their land to grow food for their own consumption. When selling into the international market, farmers get hammered by exchange rates, which ultimately means the countries have to cut spending on healthcare and education.
“Debt repayment is actively siphoning off the fiscal space countries need to fund the very transition required to survive climate change,” Patel explained to Inside Climate News. “The protesters are calling out the architecture that demands austerity in the Global South to maintain liquidity in the North.”
The beneficiaries of this northern liquidity are the world’s largest agricultural and food companies.
In the new report, “Food, Land and Money,” Friends of the Earth and fellow advocacy groups take a broad swipe at the corporate agribusinesses that have dominated the global food economy, from the 1950s, when the term “agribusiness” was coined by Harvard economists, to the present.
A handful of businesses control the global food system, the report says, using huge swaths of the planet and its resources to grow commodities that don’t actually provide sustenance but instead have become financial instruments.
The report identifies the 100 food and agriculture companies with the largest revenues and then points to the global financial institutions that underpin them.
The top-earning “agrifood” businesses made $4.5 trillion in revenue in 2022, the report found—with the top 10, including Walmart, Cargill and Costco, making up nearly one-third of the total. The report goes on to note that only a handful of financial institutions effectively own the food system, with giant asset managers Vanguard, BlackRock and State Street owning more than one-fifth of the shares in the top 100 companies. The Trump administration is at odds over an executive order targeting housing affordability, people familiar with the talks told Semafor. The White House has grappled with how to address the cost of living ahead of the midterms, which are less than two weeks away.
A six-section draft viewed by Semafor would make it easier for some homeowners to âproactivelyâ cancel their mortgage insurance; create an interagency task force on manufactured housing; allow more homeowners to refinance without title insurance; and direct the Agriculture and VA departments to lower interest rates for single-family home loans.
Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte is pushing for Trump to sign it as soon as this week, some of the people said, while others in the administration are pumping the brakes. Housing groups have expressed concern over some proposed changes, the people said, which they warn could wind up boosting prices.
The White House and Pulte did not comment.
âItâs definitely on everyoneâs radar, and I think people are really just hoping that itâs not something thatâs done for theatrics; that if it is done, itâs more real and has substance to it,â one industry representative said of the executive order. âI mean, people arenât against stabilizing housing costs, right? But they just want it done in a cautious and safe way.â
Scotsman Guide earlier reported on the talks.

SIOUX CITY, Iowa â President Donald Trump will touch down on Thursday in Iowa, the site of perhaps the tightest Senate race in the country. Strangely enough, both candidates are welcoming him.
Only one, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, will be at his rally on Thursday, but Democrats are banking that Trumpâs presence helps them due to his unpopularity.
âItâs good. â¦ He needs to see what the policies, like the tariffs and the war in Iran, cuts to healthcare, have done to a state like Iowa,â Democratic candidate Josh Turek said in an interview.
A couple hours away in Greenfield, Hinson denied any tension between her and Trump, despite her recent calls for him to end the Iran war and stop cutting deals with Russiaâs Vladimir Putin.
âPresident Trump knows where I stand,â she told Semafor. âI nag him a lot to get priorities for us all the time.â
At an event on Tuesday in Des Moines, she disclosed that Trump recently called her right after she dropped off her kids.
âAshley, itâs your favorite president. Howâs it looking, how are you feeling about the polls?â Hinson recalled Trump asking her. She said she asked how a deal to export more soybeans was coming together.
Know More
The Senate race is absolutely everywhere in Iowa, which is also home to three competitive House races and a governorâs race (Democrat Rob Sand is now favored to defeat Republican Zach Lahn). The Senate race appears to be the one Republicans are most worried about. Trump will swing through Iowa twice in October, a sign that Republicans need him to juice turnout in a state he flipped that hasnât flipped back to Democrats.
The radio ads are inescapable, the TV spots are relentless, and Trumpâs visit puts an exclamation point on a race where the National Republican Senatorial Committee and the RNC are both spending millions in coordinated advertising on behalf of Hinson. The top Senate GOP super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, is also spending money to counteract Turekâs competitiveness.
âYou know what that means. They wouldnât be coming unless they knew that this race was winnable for us,â Turek said.
Democratic groups are spending a lot on Turek as well, identifying his race as a top pickup opportunity in a cycle where Democrats need to net four Senate seats to retake the majority. Hinson said Trumpâs visit will help remind Iowans why they voted so strongly for him in 2024, the third straight cycle the state backed him.
âLook back to where things were two years ago, before we had President Trump securing our border,â she said. âIowans found the choice that they have in this election: somebody who wants to again go back to those policies of two years ago or move our country forward and continue working.â

Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian â have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Swiss national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Austrian Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.
Niger and the broader Sahel region have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.
The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.
Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."
Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.
If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.
A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.
Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.
"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."
Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.
There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.
Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".
To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.
At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.
I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.
"In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."
Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.
These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.
While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.
For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.
"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.
"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

Time is running out to meet key targets within Stormont's energy strategy by 2030, a committee has said.
The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) report followed an inquiry into the Department for the Economy's (DfE) delivery of the net zero strategy.
The PAC heard that Northern Ireland could lose out on significant economic opportunities if action was not speeded up.
Committee chair Daniel McCrossan said the government had a "responsibility to create the conditions needed for investment to proceed, otherwise there is a real risk it will go elsewhere".
During its inquiry, the PAC heard from business and energy sector representatives that uncertainty around future policies and delivery timescales was affecting investment decisions.
It heard investment could be diverted to Great Britain, Ireland and other European markets where existing factors were seen as more certain.
PAC members said it was unacceptable that delays were affecting projects which could support economic growth, create jobs and strengthen energy security.
Published in 2021, the NI energy strategy included a plan to fully decarbonise by 2050 and ensure that at least 80% of electricity consumption comes from renewable sources.
McCrossan, said that despite the strategy presenting a major economic opportunity for Northern Ireland, the evidence heard "pointed to growing frustration among businesses and investors over delays, policy uncertainty and a lack of clarity around delivery".
The PAC chair added: "Our message is clear - there can be no further delays. We want to see barriers removed so that delivery can be accelerated.
"Almost Â£124m of public money has been spent on energy-related programmes, since 2020. We need assurances that Northern Ireland is on track."
Report makes 18 recommendations
He said that despite the DfE "consulting widely" during the development of the strategy, the PAC found "that significant weaknesses had undermined its implementation".
PAC deputy chair Tom Buchanan said: "The next four years are critical. We need to see decisive action, stronger oversight and a clear focus on results.
"Our report makes 11 recommendations, including the publication and regular updating of the department's Energy Policy Statement. Funded plans must also be brought forward to address grid, infrastructure and energy storage constraints."
While the committee noted the department's confidence in achieving the strategy's ambition of a Â£2bn green economy, members said the challenge was turning ambition into results so that Northern Ireland could realise the investment, jobs and wider benefits promised by the transition to net zero.

Vincent van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” may have been based on one specific night sky: July 22, 1889, just before dawn over France.
If that’s true, it means the famous painting was based on real observations, not just van Gogh’s imagination, astronomer Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim and colleagues report October 22 in Scientific Reports.
“How could an invented sky fit the sky of a particular date this closely?” the team writes. “Observation and imagination have commonly been treated as an either/or, yet ‘The Starry Night’ shows the two coexisting on one canvas.”
Art historians typically date “The Starry Night” to mid-June 1889, based on one of van Gogh’s letters to his brother Theo.
“At last I have a landscape with olive trees, and also a new study of a starry sky,” van Gogh wrote on or about June 18. About a month earlier, van Gogh had entered a hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France. “The Starry Night” is thought to represent the view through the window of his room. A short time later, van Gogh experienced an illness during which he didn’t paint for about six weeks, so most historians think “The Starry Night” must have been painted before then.
That letter is taken as strong evidence, says astronomer Donald Olson of Texas State University in San Marcos, who has written about how astronomy shows up in art history. Historians favor the June date because “van Gogh himself said so,” he says.
That assumption has led to some confusion, though. In the 1980s, two astronomers tried to match the painting’s stars to real skies in Saint-Rémy in mid-June. One proposed that the sky was from June 19, 1889, and the collection of swirly stars is the constellation Aries.
But the other concluded it couldn’t have been painted on June 19, based on cloudy weather reports in Aix-en-Provence, France, about 70 kilometers away. That study claimed the painting was “a celestial composite, constructed to make an image of the morning sky.”
Kim, who founded a telescope-building company called SLABB INC in Seoul, South Korea, didn’t know about the June date when he became interested in “The Starry Night.” “Unlike previous astronomical studies, we could start freely,” he says.
Given his job, Kim had an intuition for which stars would be visible when. “People like me, who guide a telescope through its first alignment with the sky, naturally memorize where the stars are,” he says.
He was skeptical of the Aries theory. The stars in that constellation are faint enough that they wouldn’t be all that visible in the predawn sky, “hardly enough to inspire a painter,” he says.
Instead, Kim saw the stars as the Hyades star cluster, which forms a sideways V shape in the constellation Taurus. To test that theory, he and his colleagues applied a statistical technique called Procrustes shape analysis to put a number to how well the stars in the painting matched any particular constellation.
Celestial alignment?
Researchers compared the V-shaped collection of stars in “The Starry Night” (first image) with those in the Hyades star cluster (middle image). The resulting graph (last image) maps the real stars (blue) and the painting’s stars (orange) against each other. They don’t overlap perfectly, but they’re suspiciously close, researchers say. The label Sn stands for “The Starry Night.” while the constellation’s Greek letters represent typical astronomy notation.
The team tested the method on another van Gogh skyscape, “Starry Night Over the Rhône,” which clearly depicts the Big Dipper. “Apart from the Big Dipper, there is no star pattern we can say for certain that Vincent painted,” Kim says. The degree of matching between the art and the sky for both paintings turned out to be similar, a major clue.
Kim also used the position and phase of the moon (a waxing gibbous on June 19, in contrast to the sharp waning crescent in the painting) and Venus to further constrain the painting’s date. He used computer simulations that weren’t available in the ‘80s to calculate the positions of celestial objects on certain dates in 1889 down to the second. He even traveled to France in June and July 2019 to try to find the field of view van Gogh would have seen from his window. Ultimately, July 22, 1889, was the best fit for the team’s data.
“I still cannot forget the moment we finally found the spot, overlaid the drawing on the view and saw it fit perfectly,” Kim says. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier. And the thrill I felt when I confirmed that the moon, the Hyades and Venus of July 22, 1889, fit exactly within the drawing’s field of view is still with me.”
Not to douse Kim’s enthusiasm, but that field of view may not be exactly what van Gogh saw, Olson says.
“The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass ‘The Starry Night’s’ round hills and cliffs,” he says. That casts doubt on the paper’s conclusions.
Olson proposes an experiment: Tell an amateur astronomer that “The Starry Night” depicts the Hyades and ask them to point out the star Aldebaran, which is at the bottom left of the V. In real life, this is the brightest star in the Hyades. But the painting has other much more prominent stars.
“If [the authors’] theory is correct, then this should be easy,” Olson says. Kim and colleagues identify Aldebaran as one of the two stars to the left of the cypress tree in “The Starry Night.” But Olson thinks others will see it differently. “A decent guess is that an experienced amateur astronomer, even when prompted to see the Hyades, will not identify Aldebaran as either of the two stars to the left of the cypress tree.”

Strong winds of up to 75mph could cause disruption across parts of Northern Ireland this weekend as Storm Boelo moves in.
A Met Office weather warning has been issued from 18:00 BST on Saturday until 15:00 GMT on Sunday.
Strong westerly winds are expected to become widespread on Saturday evening, with very windy conditions continuing overnight and through much of Sunday.
Gusts up to 60mph (96kph) are forecast widely, while coastal and exposed areas could have gusts reaching up to 75mph (120kph).
The strong winds will come with heavy, blustery showers at times.
Conditions are expected to gradually improve from the southwest during Sunday afternoon as the strongest winds begin to ease.
In light of the warning, Causeway Coast and Glens Borough Council has cancelled its fireworks display at Ballymoney on Saturday.
In statement, the council said: "We understand how disappointing this will be, but the decision has been taken with the safety of visitors, staff and event personnel as the priority."
Risk of power cuts and travel disruption
The Met Office has warned that strong winds could cause disruption to transport networks and essential services.
Power cuts are possible, which could also affect mobile phone coverage and other services.
There is a small risk of damage to buildings, including roof tiles being blown off, while flying debris could pose a danger to the public.
Road, rail, air and ferry passengers could face longer journey times or cancellations, with some roads and bridges potentially closing.
Coastal areas could be particularly vulnerable, with large waves and beach material potentially being thrown onto seafronts, coastal roads and nearby properties.
Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen
The arrival of Storm Boelo comes just a day after Storm Austen is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Ireland.
Storm Austen is forecast to track towards the south coast of Ireland on Thursday evening and into Friday morning, bringing the risk of flooding and travel disruption.
Irish weather service Met Ãireann has issued an orange rain warning - the second highest level - for six counties in the Republic of Ireland, including Cork, Dublin, Kerry, Waterford, Wexford and Wicklow.
The Irish weather service has warned of possible flooding, public transport disruption and very difficult driving conditions.
A nationwide yellow warning for rain and wind is also in place from 19:00 on Thursday until 10:00 on Friday.
Although no weather warnings have been issued for Northern Ireland in connection with Storm Austen, widespread rain is expected on Thursday night before clearing eastwards on Friday morning.

Employers might be overestimating the downsides of offering paid parental leave and underestimating the costs of losing employees by foregoing it, argues economist Emily Oster in a new report based on research she conducted with the advocacy group Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America.
A survey of employers in four states without public-sponsored leave programs â Arkansas, Illinois, Mississippi, and Nebraska â found that 55% of employers reported no additional costs from offering it. In 77% of cases, employers said existing staff absorbed the work of the new parent.
Overall, respondents with experience offering parental leave were twice as likely to say the benefits outweighed costs (47% vs. 23%). Some employers cited worker retention as a reason they offered it. âThis data suggests it is far more manageable for employers than many people fear,â said Oster, also the CEO of ParentData, a data-driven parenting and pregnancy advice platform.
Still, 17% of employers who offered leave said it created âsignificant financial strain.â The study did not specify the length of the paid leave or examine if there were adverse retention effects on other employees within the company.
Oster suggested states should consider tax credits to entice employers to offer parental leave, and should try to increase public awareness of her surveyâs results, especially among small businesses.
Healthy Moms, Healthy Babiesâ push for paid leave research comes as part of a campaign to spend $100 million over five years to advance research and policies to push down the US maternal mortality rate by half, according to Robin Reck, the groupâs executive director.

An RJ Reynolds subsidiary is promoting fruit-flavored vaping pods with colorful scented mailers that critics say are similar to the âscratch and sniffâ ads the tobacco giant agreed to suspend 20 years ago, as part of a settlement with 39 states that had accused the company of violating an agreement to refrain from marketing its flavored cigarettes to kids.
âIt appears they havenât learned their lesson, and theyâre now using that same playbook for a different type of tobacco product, which also coincidentally remains the most commonly used tobacco product among US youth,â said Brian King, a former top FDA tobacco regulator who now works as the executive vice president for US programs at the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids. His organization flagged the materials to state and federal authorities.
The company said the advertising for Vuse Pro berry, fresh mint, peach, and watermelon pods was only sent to existing adult nicotine consumers whose ages had been verified, and who had opted in to Vuse-related communications. âOur products are for adult tobacco and nicotine consumers only,â a spokesperson said.
âWe do not want youth accessing or using them, and that principle is fundamental to how we market responsibly and in compliance with applicable laws and regulations.â
Flavored vape policy came to a head earlier this year when President Donald Trump pressured then-FDA Commissioner Marty Makary to authorize fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adults despite the agency chiefâs concerns about the potential impact on children. Shortly after, the FDA adopted a policy that effectively allowed for the sale of many flavored e-cigarettes that were still under agency review.
âItâs critical that the US government and state attorneys general take notice and take action,â King said. âWe should not be sitting idly by as companies flagrantly flout the laws using tactics we know drive youth appeal of tobacco products.â

Rallies have been taking place across Serbia on Thursday, the final day of campaigning ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.
After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar VuÄiÄ's 12 years in power.
The main threat to VuÄiÄ's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.
Why is this student movement so important?
They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija SrdanoviÄ said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."
It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.
The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.
What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.
The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by VuÄiÄ, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.
At the last election in 2023, VuÄiÄ's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties.
Who is VuÄiÄ and how popular is he?
VuÄiÄ has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities.
VuÄiÄ has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko MladiÄ, prompting EU anger at his "glorification".
Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is VuÄiÄ's biggest challenge since he came to power.
"He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President VuÄiÄ isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade.
How do Serbia's elections work?
Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation.
Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday.
There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for.
Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote.
Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List.
Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for?
Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists.
They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija SrdanoviÄ is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir StaniÄ and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Å oÅ¡kiÄ.
Under an 11-point programme, external, the student movement wants to:
- eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it
- purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime
- reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control
- stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises
VuÄiÄ and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
How fair will the vote be?
European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere".
Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence, external, and opposition activists subjected to surveillance.
In a report ahead of the vote, it said instead of ensuring equal conditions for candidates, "a range of institutions, from ministries to local governments, became involved in electoral engineering".
Serbian media has seen almost three-quarters of TV coverage devoted to government representatives, the watchdog complained, and alleged that ministries and local governments had become caught up in "electoral engineering".
Some 160 attacks have been recorded on media and journalists in Serbia this year

The virus was detected in a severely immunocompromised patient who was being treated for a serious illness in Lyon and died in early October. Please check your inbox to confirm. France's health ministry said that based on current knowledge of the virus, no public health risk to the general population has been identified to date. Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered incapable of infecting humans. "This is therefore an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient," according to the ministry. Shamonda virus is transmitted to animals by biting midges. Some readers may find this article distressing.
A 54-year-old teacher who survived a mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school said she pretended to be dead so the gunman would not shoot her again.
Becky Drury, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, said in a statement shared with US media that as she tried to shut her classroom door, the gunman shot her and she fell to the floor.
"I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again," Drury said.
The attacker - who has been identified as a 16-year-old former student at the school - killed three students and a teacher before a parent from the school fatally shot him.
In her first remarks since the 15 October shooting in Bend, Oregon, Drury said that she went to see what was happening outside the special-education classroom, and after spotting the shooter, she tried to shut the door.
The attacker still managed to shoot her, so she could not help any of the children in the classroom.
"Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she said. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else."
Drury suffered serious but not life-threatening harm from the shooting, which killed five-year-old Rhoam Summer, an eight and eleven-year-old, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.
Police have said another teacher - who has not been named - attempted to disarm the gunman by throwing her mobile phone. She was not injured.
A father of two other children who had followed the suspect into the school then shot and killed the attacker, who officials named as Griffin J John II.
Reports had emerged that another teacher threw herself on top of a student to protect the child during the shooting, but Drury said she wanted to clear the record about what happened on 15 October.
"I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she said in her statement.
Police have not yet shared a motive for the suspect, who officials say was a special-education needs student at Silver Rail.
Drury said what happened in the classroom was "unimaginable".
"[L]ike so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy," she said.

A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors.
V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu.
His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities.
In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria.
Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media".
BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denier wrongdoing in a post on X.
The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice.
Account was taken down
Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following.
Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals".
He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver.
The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.
The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019.
But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios.
A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down, external following complaints from social media users and others.
A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them.
According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported, external.
The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers.
Police complaint
Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai.
Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints.
This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life.
"We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states.
A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case".
"[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says.
Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest.
In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life".
He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish.
"I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity.
"I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote.
If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website, external or globally via Befrienders Worldwide, external. In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org, external.

1f111ffdbec1.text: By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-rallies-in-iowa-with-gop-senate-candidate-ashley-hinson Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump rallies in Iowa with GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson Politics Oct 22, 2026 10:02 AM EDT DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — After Ashley Hinson dropped off her boys at school earlier this month, she saw the initials "DJT" flash on her phone. President Donald Trump is expected to speak at a rally in Sioux City, Iowa, at 6:30 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. "'Ashley, it's your favorite president,'" Iowa's Republican nominee for U.S. Senate recently recounted to an audience of her supporters. "That's how he introduced himself." READ MORE: In final Michigan Senate debate, El-Sayed and Rogers question each other's loyalties She had had a more forceful message about communicating with President Donald Trump on the debate stage with her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, as she tried to win over undecided voters. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "I'll be President Trump's ally when it is important for Iowa, but I will push back on him," promised Hinson, who currently serves in the U.S. House. "He knows this." Although many Republicans are walking a political tightrope in this year's midterm elections, Hinson's balancing act is more challenging than most. Iowans have been hamstrung by manufacturing job losses, health care clinic closures and shrunken farm profits since Trump returned to the White House, but Hinson also is relying on the president's loyalists to show up for her. On Thursday, Hinson will join Trump for a rally in Sioux City, which is in Iowa's conservative northwest corner. The visit to safe territory is geared toward boosting turnout even as it ties her more tightly to an unpopular president. "I will be there at the rally to welcome him to Iowa because I think this is a contrast election," Hinson said on Fox News last week. "There was never a good time to elect a tax-and-spend liberal to the United States Senate but now would be the worst time." Trump is expected to visit the state again Nov. 1. He is "anxious for Iowans to hear his message before they vote," Iowa Republican Party Chair Jeff Kaufmann said in announcing the president's schedule. Turek, a state lawmaker, was in Sioux City for a campaign event Tuesday and told reporters he was happy for Trump to visit to see how his tariffs and the Iran war have "hurt Iowa more than any other state." Although Turek says he's willing to work with Trump on issues like immigration, he called Hinson a rubber stamp for the president's bad policies. There are more examples of Hinson bucking the president When Hinson kicked off her campaign last year, she touted Trump's endorsement and said she was running to be Trump's "top ally" in the Senate. Almost a year later, Hinson instead says she wants to be "Iowa's best bipartisan fighter." The message has crystallized since the summer, with more examples of Hinson vocalizing positions at odds with the president. Recent polling from late September and early October suggests it could work as she carves out about 1 in 10 voters who disapprove of the president even as she continues to secure overwhelming support from those who approve of Trump. In August, she said Trump's plan to increase beef imports from foreign countries in an attempt to lower prices was "a bad idea" that would hurt Iowa farmers. Last month, two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House broke with the White House and voted against Trump's ability to continue the war with Iran without congressional approval. Hinson didn't, but she said later the war has gotten too costly for Americans and called for Trump to bring the conflict to a "successful and immediate end." More recently, Hinson criticized Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for diesel fuel. She said Tuesday that the U.S. needs to make sure "dictators aren't allowed to win wars." "I think the president and I share the goal of lowering costs for working families and for people who are using diesel," she told reporters after a campaign event. "I, again, just don't think we need to be making any deals with Russia." Hinson said she hadn't talked with the president about the issue. "Maybe I'll have a chance to come have a conversation with him at the rally," she added. Turek says he'll work with Trump on immigration Hinson isn't the only one pitching bipartisanship. So is Turek. In fact, he's the only Iowa candidate seeking federal office who explicitly mentions Trump in general election television advertisements, according to an Associated Press analysis of AdImpact data. In one, Turek is behind the wheel speaking directly to a camera about Interstate 35, which "connects Iowa to the southern border and the broken immigration system that both parties have failed to fix." He says: "In the U.S. Senate, I'll work with anyone to fix it, including President Trump, to secure the border, stop the flow of drugs into Iowa." Turek has pushed back on the president's policies, including tariffs and the war in Iran, as the catalysts of high costs that are hurting Iowans, but his message on working with the president on immigration and other select issues stands out from other Democrats. Republicans say he's just pretending to be a moderate to get elected. Mazie Stilwell, executive director of the progressive organization Progress Iowa, said Turek's message on immigration targets a bloc of voters on an issue that's particularly important to them but doesn't overshadow his otherwise disciplined focus on the high costs facing Iowans. Trump's visit to the state Thursday, she added,

b4a2c2ab00ee.text: By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/in-final-michigan-senate-debate-el-sayed-and-rogers-question-each-others-loyalties Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter In final Michigan Senate debate, El-Sayed and Rogers question each other's loyalties Politics Oct 22, 2026 9:54 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers clashed in their final Senate debate Wednesday, with El-Sayed trying to tie his opponent to President Donald Trump and Rogers saying his rival's progressive policies would be too extreme for Michigan. The first known human case of the Shamonda virus (Shav) has been detected in a patient who died in early October, French authorities have said.
Health officials said it was an "exceptional case in a severely immunocompromised patient" and there was currently no risk to the public.
Shav is a disease that primarily affects cattle and can be spread by infected midges. Cases have also occurred in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses, but infections in people were previously unheard of.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said they were monitoring the situation, with French officials still investigating how the virus had spread to a human.
It is currently thought the patient contracted Shav through a midge bite in eastern France, the country's health and agriculture ministries said on Thursday, where cases were first identified in animals in the spring.
They said the patient was being treated for a serious illness in a Lyon hospital and experienced neurological complications thought to have been "very likely linked" to the virus, based on initial findings.
The statement stressed that their immune system was weakened, leaving them more vulnerable to getting ill.
"Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans," it noted, having only been identified in animals "despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia".
Dairy herds that catch Shav from bites can experience fever, diarrhoea and poor milk production.
The WHO confirmed this was the first documented human case of the disease.
It said it had not yet made its own formal risk assessment, but advised that current information and knowledge of similar diseases suggested the case was isolated and "unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time".
"Transmissibility of midge-borne viruses also generally declines during the cooler months of the year," it added in a statement.
The ECDC said it was working with French and European partners to investigate the "potential public health implications" of the infection.
The first cases of the virus in Europe were identified in late July, the agency said. It has since been detected in farm animals in several countries, including Ireland, Germany, Italy and Spain, as well as in Jersey.

Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid.
"With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MSN NOW, external.
In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation.
The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".
The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.
More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.
Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out."
Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed.
"We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".
The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".
Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one.
She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.
The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.
Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating.
Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".
Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".
Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.
He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".
At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it".
"You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

Campaigners who have been trying to stop the development of a town's green space have celebrated it being given "village green status" by a council.
Harding's Pits, seven acres of land beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, had previously been earmarked for a housing development and a supermarket before the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk applied to Norfolk County Council for the status.
The Harding's Pits Community Association Group has campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as a leisure space.
Rick Morrish, 64, the director of the group, said it was a "really great decision... we've struggled to get the village green status for 30 years".
The application was considered by Norfolk County Council's Planning (Regulatory) Committee on Tuesday.
Morrish told Chris Goreham on BBC Radio Norfolk that "this year's administration got right behind" the cause and it would "give more legal status to protect the site... we're safeguarding it as a public open space".
Alexandra Kemp, an Independent councillor at the borough council, said she has held nine public events in favour of keeping Harding's Pits as a space for nature.
"After the long campaign that we fought since 2017 with residents to stop the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk putting traffic on Harding's Way, the borough council's support is very important and now protects all of Harding's Pits west of Harding's Way," she said.
Kemp also campaigned with residents in July against a new car park that the borough council sought to build next to Harding's Pits.
Morrish said the Harding's Pits Association Group was formed in 2004, adding that the green space was originally a clay pit in the 19th Century, before being used as a landfill site.
"There is actually rubbish underneath the site," he added.
Harding's Pits was then turned into a public space in the early 1960s.
The site is currently used for dog walking, accessing King's Lynn town centre, picking fruit such as blackberries and for bird and wildlife spotting, Morrish said.
He told the BBC that "a hundred species of birds" had been recorded there and it was home to "three or four regular reptile residents, including a lot of lizards" who had enjoyed the warm temperatures this year.
"Within the town, this is quite a rare asset to have and that's why we think it's so important," he added.
He said the site has grown over the years, with a new community orchid and a national art project, where artists have planted a circle of oak trees.
Michael de Whalley, the cabinet member for climate change and biodiversity on Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk, said: "This is very welcome news for South Lynn and an important final step in a journey that the community has been pursuing for at least 30 years."
He added that local people valued and enjoyed places such as Harding's Pits and surrounding green spaces, where habitats could flourish.

Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend.
Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.
Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said law enforcement would be 20% higher than it was last weekend, after the government had promised a "massive" police deployment.
At least 2,500 people have been arrested across France since the disorder broke out and Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations.
"In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the RhÃ´ne prefecture said in a statement.
Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 thousand people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy".
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la RÃ©publique was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent NuÃ±ez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron.
The ÃlysÃ©e Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice.
NuÃ±ez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

Two months before the treatment that would change Lynn Montgomery-Haga’s life, she could barely walk down a hallway.
In a test at the University of Colorado Anschutz, Montgomery-Haga struggled to walk 25 feet, often reaching out to the walls for support. Usually, the 49-year-old relied on her walker or wheelchair. “She had a very stiff, hesitant gait,” says Montgomery-Haga’s neurologist, Amanda Piquet.
For about a decade, Montgomery-Haga had lived with a debilitating autoimmune disease known as stiff person syndrome. The progressive condition can lock up the body’s muscles without warning, leading to falls, broken bones, excruciating pain and difficulty moving. Singer Celine Dion, who returned to the stage in September after years of battling the disease, has said it can feel “like somebody’s strangling you.”
Montgomery-Haga’s own days were marked by dizziness, fatigue and pain. And sudden muscle spasms would send her sprawling. It was like the fainting goat videos popular on the internet, she says. “They get surprised and they fall over, and there’s nothing they can do about it.”
But stiff person syndrome is no joke. It stripped Montgomery-Haga of her accounting job and her ability to drive. She couldn’t sit up in bed unless she had a safety bar to pull on. If she dropped the soap in the shower, it’d take her 10 minutes to pick it up.
Now, Montgomery-Haga hopes those struggles are finally coming to an end. That’s because a clinical trial with an experimental therapy has helped restore mobility for her — and others like her. She can stride through her living room again. She can landscape her front yard. She doesn’t have to brace herself when her dogs jump on her. And she hasn’t fallen once since the treatment. The change has been drastic, she says. “I’m just really excited about the future.”
The treatment, a type of CAR T cell therapy, extracts immune cells from a person’s body and engineers them to attack the very cells causing the disease. First used to fight cancer, CAR T is now also targeting a variety of autoimmune diseases. If given the green light by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Montgomery-Haga’s treatment would be the first such therapy approved for an autoimmune condition — and it would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.
Stiff person syndrome may be just the beginning, says Carl June, the University of Pennsylvania immunologist and oncologist who spearheaded CAR T cell therapy for cancer decades ago. The “living drug” could herald a new era of therapeutics for autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and even multiple sclerosis. “It’s revolutionary to think how far things have gone,” June says.
But he warns that it’s far too early to know if scientists have definitively cured stiff person syndrome. And there haven’t been enough people treated to get a good handle on all the possible side effects. “There could be long-term complications in autoimmune patients that don’t happen in our cancer patients,” he says. Other researchers urge caution. “It’s very important not to oversell it,” says Marc Scherlinger, a rheumatologist at Strasbourg University Hospital in France.
For Piquet, one crucial question is how long the treatment will last. In Montgomery-Haga’s case, the answer seems to be at least two years. Montgomery-Haga still considers herself disabled, or “disabled-ish,” as she calls it. But when rating how she used to feel on a scale of one to 10, she’d put herself at a zero before treatment, she says. These days, she’s more like a seven.
What’s more, Montgomery-Haga says, “I think I’m still improving.”
No approved therapies
There’s no single symptom that clued Montgomery-Haga in to her disease. In 2014, she started having difficulty picking things up off the floor. Then her boss asked her why she was limping — Montgomery-Haga hadn’t noticed. Her balance was off and her head felt weird, like “I was walking around in a fishbowl,” she says. It got to the point where Montgomery-Haga had difficulty crossing thresholds between rooms.
Montgomery-Haga would startle easily, prompting her body to stiffen up like a board. One time when cooking, she burned her finger, spasmed and collapsed, cracking the back of her head on the cabinets. She lay on the floor crying, but finally managed to right herself. “As soon as you hit the floor,” she says, “your muscles are like, ‘Fine,’ and you can get up again.”
Those unpredictable symptoms capture a slice of what life is like with stiff person syndrome, or SPS. The disease, which affects roughly 2 in 100,000 people in the United States, typically develops in a person’s 30s or 40s. It is about twice as common in women as in men.
Scientists don’t know what sets off the disease. But they think a person’s own antibodies start attacking a neurological network that helps muscles throughout the body relax. And when those tensed muscles are in opposition, like the biceps and triceps, they start fighting one another, Piquet says. That’s when people can end up in a stuck position, leading to stiffness. But because everyone’s immune system is different, patients’ experiences with the disease can vary greatly.
For Tara Zier, a former dentist based in Maryland, SPS started with extreme neck pain, blood pressure spikes, shortness of breath and feelings of impending doom. While some people struggle with mobility, Zier’s difficulties include standing and extreme fatigue. When she holds herself upright, her muscles clamp down on her spine like it’s in a vise. “Have you ever had a charley horse in your calf?” she asks. “Imagine one in your whole body that stops you in your tracks.”
Zier and Montgomery-Haga went years before learning what was behind their symptoms. Their cases mystified doctors — Zier saw 13 specialists and visited the emergency room nine times before getting a diagnosis. When she finally found out she had SPS three years after her first symptoms, Zier says she felt validated, like medicine was confirming

Some of the arguments against data centers sound familiar.
Opponents say the projects will change the look and feel of a place, harm the air and water and reduce property values.
This rationale is familiar because residents have raised the same concerns in campaigns against wind and solar. Whether these objections to very different types of development are accurate or not, they seem to stem from the same feelings of lack of control and fear of change, especially in rural places.
Jeffrey Jacquet, a rural sociology professor at Ohio State University, agrees that the pushback against data centers and renewables shares some common traits, but he is cautious about drawing broader conclusions. His research focuses on the social effects of developing renewables and fossil fuels.
“People have their reasons for opposing stuff, and it’s sort of hard to second-guess those or to play like some sort of logical consistency game,” Jacquet said in an interview.
I wrote this month about some of the people behind Ohio’s resistance to data centers, and, in a separate story, how the issue is playing out in the state’s U.S. Senate race.
Resistance to data centers reminds me of campaigns I covered in many Ohio communities to limit or ban wind and solar, such as in Pickaway County, just south of Columbus. Sure enough, Pickaway County is now a hot spot for data center opposition, but not in the same villages or townships that were against a big solar project in 2022.
And yet, almost every time I ask a data center critic whether they see a similarity between their arguments and those against wind and solar, they disagree with the premise. They are bemused by my grand theory of resisting everything.
Jacquet finds it helpful to think about opposition to data centers and renewables in terms of “construal-level theory,” which is a social science concept that says a person’s views on a topic become more precise with first-hand experience and more abstract without it.
If someone hasn’t lived next to a data center, wind farm or solar farm, they are likely to form opinions about what it’s like based on social media, friends or other sources.
“The best they can do is just try to make decisions on the information they have, which comes from all sorts of different places and it gets mediated through different factors like the political party they belong to,” Jacquet said.
Later on, as people get actual experience with these projects, their attitudes tend to soften, he said. The opponents become less hostile.
So let’s step back and ask why a rural resident may recoil at the idea of a data center (or a wind or solar farm) even if they don’t yet know what the project will be like as a neighbor.
In my view, a big factor is suspicion of large companies, especially tech companies. A resident may have no experience living near a data center, but they are predisposed to question the intentions of Amazon, Meta, xAI and others.
Energy companies also face challenges with trust, but no wind or solar developer is as well known as major data center developers.
To accept a project, a community will want benefits significant enough to make the disruption worthwhile. That’s a challenge for data centers, wind and solar because they don’t offer many long-term jobs.
The final factor I’ll list is the public’s tendency to generalize from extreme examples. This means an especially contentious project becomes the lens through which people view a similar development proposed in their own neighborhood. In the case of data centers, the xAI projects in the Memphis area are notorious for noise and emissions, and they sometimes serve as a stand-in for the broader industry.

It’s difficult to find wind and solar projects that can compete with the worst data centers in terms of disregard for the aesthetics of a place. But if you’re curious, look at Facebook groups opposing renewables to see photos of extreme examples of barren landscapes, poor drainage and general blight.
There is a lesson here for wind and solar developers: Don’t behave like data center developers. Realize it’s normal for residents to feel distrust and try to counter it by prioritizing trust and transparency. Avoid non-disclosure agreements and secrecy. Make sure a community learns about your project from you, not through rumors that send them to social media to form initial impressions.
I asked John Smillie, the Indiana renewable energy advocate I recently wrote about, about the common ground between opponents of data centers and opponents of wind and solar.
“The anti-data center bubble is very big,” he said. “So if you’re going to draw a Venn diagram, the opposition’s up to like 70 percent of the public, and you’re going to find different groups overlapping with that big bubble. And people have gotten mad at me for pointing out that, hey, a lot of the people in the anti-data center bubble are anti-renewable people.”
Polling data supports his view. In a March report, Gallup found that seven in 10 Americans oppose data centers. In a different poll about energy sources published in April, Gallup found declining support for wind and solar over the last decade, but approval remains high: 66 percent said solar should be emphasized more than it is now, and 55 percent said the same about wind. The share saying those resources should be emphasized less was 16 percent for solar and 24 percent for wind, both increases from prior years.
If polling focused on the rural Midwest, I suspect opposition to wind and solar would be higher, though still lower than for data centers, with many people who dislike “all of the above.”
But this overlap doesn’t imply that the groups’ arguments have equal merit.
