If you listen to the candidates running for the U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, some of the biggest issues in the race revolve around the state’s fisheries, its oil and gas development and soaring prices for fuel and other staples.
Left largely unsaid, however, is that climate change is playing a role in at least two of these issues. Warming waters are affecting the state’s fish, including declining salmon runs. Concerns for climate change are a chief cause of opposition to expanded oil and gas development in the Alaskan Arctic, where rapid warming is melting permafrost, damaging infrastructure and altering animal migrations that many Alaska Natives rely on for subsistence.
Yet the candidates have hardly mentioned climate change. And that might be one of the few ways the race is similar to others around the country.
But first, what’s different. Take fish.
Mary Peltola, the Democrat who represented Alaska in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2022 until January 2025, has adopted a slogan of “Fish, family, freedom.”
“Potentially that was strange to have fish as one of your top three words for folks in D.C.,” said Chantal de Alcuaz, co-executive director of The Alaska Center, an environmental advocacy group, “but it’s not strange at all for Alaskans.”
Despite stretching across an area nearly one-fifth the size of the contiguous 48 states, Alaska has fewer than 740,000 people. And many of those people consider fishing, and fish, central to their lives. For Alaska Natives, salmon are not only food—cultures revolve around the harvest and processing of the fish. Across the state, many non-Indigenous Alaskans fill their freezers each year with fish they catch, too. In recent years that’s all been getting harder.
Runs of some salmon species have declined sharply. State and federal authorities have issued repeated closures of subsistence and sport fishing along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers, which cut across the state.
During a debate last month, Peltola and her main opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, agreed that climate change is one of numerous factors affecting Alaska’s fisheries, including salmon runs. Scientists say the causes of the decline in some salmon species are complex and multifaceted, but include warming waters.
Yet the candidates have focused their attention on trawling, a commercial fishing practice that targets other species but is allowed to kill a certain number of salmon and other fish as bycatch. Peltola has proposed banning “factory trawling,” which she characterizes as large, out-of-state boats distinct from smaller, local operations.
At the debate, Peltola said climate change was “not as easy to get our arms around” as trawling. “This is the one place where Congress, Alaskans, has an opportunity to say no,” Peltola said of the fishing practice. “This is a man-made impact.”
Peltola has stressed her history of fishing on the Kuskokwim River with family. Sullivan has worked hard to establish his own credentials on the topic, and has introduced legislation to limit bycatch from trawling.
Alaska’s Senate race is unusual when it comes to oil and gas, too. Unlike the national parties, there is little daylight between the candidates when it comes to drilling.
Alaska relies on oil and gas revenue to fund the state budget, and residents receive an annual dividend from a sovereign wealth fund that was built with petroleum royalties. Many Alaska Native communities in the Arctic North Slope have also generated substantial income from fossil fuels. But production is on a decades-long decline.
The Trump administration has pushed through a series of changes to allow drilling on new lands, including areas some Alaska Natives consider critical to their subsistence hunting of caribou. Recent proposals would strip environmental reviews and opportunities for public comment on drilling in the Western Arctic. Sullivan has said he pressed the administration to take these steps. He also sponsored a bill signed into law last year that repealed protections in the Western Arctic enacted by the Biden administration.
Peltola has stressed that she, too, supports oil and gas. At a September forum of the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, she claimed credit for pressing the Biden administration to approve the Willow project, a large Arctic oil development, and criticized Sullivan for voting in 2021 to confirm Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, who had been critical of oil and gas drilling before taking office.
A Peltola spokesperson declined to answer questions about whether she supports the Trump administration’s moves on oil and gas development, instead issuing a statement saying, “Mary will aggressively advocate for every solution on the table to bring costs down—including increased oil and gas production, as well as restoring tax credits for solar, wind, and hydropower projects that were cut by Dan Sullivan. Alaskans expect their Senator to do both, and as an independent voice for Alaska, Mary will stand up to anyone to deliver.”
Sullivan says he supports an “all of the above” energy policy but voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which repealed renewable energy credits. His office did not respond to requests for comment.
Yet while the candidates’ attention to fish and their similarities on oil and gas might be unusual, their reluctance to discuss climate change is not. Across the country, many Democrats have decided it is safer to discuss energy prices.
“I think some of it is just advertising savvy,” said Amy Lauren Lovecraft, a professor of political science at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. Peltola knows she has support from people who care about the issue, she said, “because Sullivan doesn’t care about climate change. His record is pretty clear.”
Enei Begaye, executive director of Native Movement, an Indigenous advocacy group in Alaska, said many Alaskans care about warming, “led by Alaska Native people who are feeling the impacts, the deadly impacts of climate change right

The Trump administration is steadily ratcheting up pressure on Iran with sanctions, but experts and former officials say the penalties thus far are having a limited effect on the Islamic Republicâs willingness to negotiate.
Nate Swanson, who served as a State Department representative on the second Trump administrationâs Iran negotiating team, said the pressure has failed to change Iranâs strategic calculations.
âThink about everything Iranâs been through in the last eight months. Theyâve endured incredible setbacks to their physical infrastructure, military, and physical livelihood,â Swanson said. âWeâve not seen any kind of capitulation or even willingness to compromise, but a more rigorous hard ine taking form. Theyâre not more willing to negotiate, theyâre actually less flexible. They would rather have more war than compromise. So I donât see it leading to a positive strategic end game for the US at this point.â
Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said that the blockade has been more difficult for Iranian authorities to manage than sanctions alone, as it has cut off much of Iranâs trade.
âThe blockade is whatâs different from sanctions. It will have an additional cost and impose a pain on an economy that was already in a very bad place,â Vatanka said. Yet âthere is no sign â as far as I can tell â of an imminent collapse of the Iranian economy.â
A further limitation on the Trump administrationâs strategy on sanctions is Iranâs ability to maintain trade ties with China, a country that has little incentive to enforce US restrictions.
âChina views our sanctions as unilateral and illegal, so they have no interest in abiding by them,â said Philip Luck, director of the Center for Strategic and International Studiesâ economics program. âAs long as Chinaâs not going to concur with our sanctions, Iranâs going to be able to get what it needs, and itâs going to be able to get some amount of revenue from its sales of oil.â
Luck added that Chinese manufacturers can supply many of the industrial goods and components Iran needs to rebuild damaged military components and infrastructure.
The failure of sanctions and the blockade to bring Iran to the negotiating table on Washingtonâs terms is likely why the US is reportedly considering renewed military strikes as another way to force concessions. But experts caution that escalating pressure does not necessarily mean Tehran will back down.
âThe regime will try to bend, but not break,â Tom Warrick, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, said.
âThe problem here is both sides are intent on wanting the other side to be seen to be defeated,â he continued, adding conflicts are harder to resolve when âyour only way out to end the war is the strategic humiliation of your opponent.â Such conflicts, he warned, âtend to go on longer than they otherwise would have.â
The administration insists its strategy of inflicting economic pain is working.
âOperation Economic Outcast is isolating the Iranian regime into desperation,â a Treasury spokesperson told Semafor. âIran has loaded zero oil onto vessels since August 25, the day after Economic D-Day. The value of the rial continues to reach new lows. Inflation is through the roof as the regime scrambles to print more money. Iranâs access to foreign currency is severely diminished. We have seen flights grounded, Iranian bank branches shuttered, and trade halted. The regime is out of options, and the clock is ticking.â
Warrick also cautioned against dismissing sanctions as a tool for diplomacy, pointing to past diplomatic deals with Iran following sanctions, including the 1981 Algiers Accords; an agreement at the end of the Iran-Iraq War in 1988, and one alongside the Obama-era nuclear deal, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action.

Could the Tesla-SpaceX merger that Elon Musk floated this week pose antitrust problems?
One former Justice Department official told Semafor that the risks are real.
Antitrust regulators view such âverticalâ mergers as pro-competition, the official said â because they can make supply chains more efficient â but could try to stop the merger if Tesla-SpaceX gets deemed a possible âvertical foreclosure.â
A foreclosure situation arises when a firm uses its position to restrict competitors operating at another level of its supply chain, the official explained; in this case, other driverless or electric car companies could stand to lose out if, in the future, only Tesla cars got access to SpaceX technology like Starlink.
Of course, that depends on the terms of the still-hypothetical deal. It also depends on how much Trump-aligned US antitrust enforcers want to clash with Musk, a major Republican donor.
Even so, should Democrats take back the House next month, Musk would face congressional investigations â and lawmakers would closely scrutinize any attempts to merge his companies.
âIf Elon Musk moves forward with the merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the deal would carry real risks that âantitrust enforcers across the world would scrutinize,â Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., told Reuters. âWhen one person controls the infrastructure that governments and militaries depend on, his business decisions become national security decisions, too.â
Reuters reported that Teslaâs work in China could also complicate things, as Starlink technology is used in foreign conflicts and the company has a relationship with the Pentagon.
Any Tesla-SpaceX merger could also get examined by global antitrust enforcers for its impacts on overseas auto, AI, and aerospace industries.

ALLENTOWN, Pa.—In all her 38 years living in South Whitehall Township in the Lehigh Valley, Laurie Gilley had never attended a municipal meeting, much less gotten involved in the politics of her community. But then she learned that a data center was being planned for 400 acres of land across from her home and the local high school.
Now, Gilley, who helped form the South Whitehall Township Civic Alliance to fight the center, is at the vanguard of an informal political movement experts say could impact the midterm congressional elections, especially in tight races like the one in her district, where incumbent U.S. Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican narrowly elected in 2024, is now facing Democrat Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter.
Gilley said she has been energized by the unified resistance to data centers. “Both sides of the aisle seem to come together on this,” said Gilley, 61, who runs Madeline’s Fairgrounds Marketplace at the popular farmers market here, where the chatter these days in her baked goods and sandwich shop often turns to data centers and politics. “Everywhere I go, we’re talking about it.”
Opposition to data centers—especially in places where they are proposed near residential neighborhoods or close to environmentally sensitive land or water—has been intense in Pennsylvania. Residents worry about property values, rising utility bills, the impact on the water and power supply, the loss of the state’s rural character and environment and even whether artificial intelligence is a good idea at all. And the voices are coming from both parties.
With the looming midterm elections, the question is whether all that talk will translate into votes—and which candidates might benefit.
“It doesn’t take much to tip elections” in Pennsylvania, said Christopher Borick, a political science professor and director of the Lehigh University Opinion Observatory. He said it’s still hard to predict the impact of the opposition that has spread “almost like a wildfire” across Pennsylvania.
But “it is front and center,” he said, in the Mackenzie-Brooks race and three other congressional races that are expected to be decided by thin margins.
Borick said President Donald Trump’s declining approval rating could hurt Republican incumbents in all four of those districts. “That’s a big weight and anchor on Republicans” in tight races, he said, adding that the “straw that breaks the camel’s back” may well be how the data center issue resonates with voters. And there may be far-reaching implications up and down the ballot, he said. “It’s in all the races,” said Borick.
Trump won the state in 2016 and in 2024, and helped two Republicans eke out narrow wins in Pennsylvania in 2024 for their first terms in the U.S. House of Representatives: Mackenzie, who is now facing Brooks in the 7th Congressional District in the Lehigh Valley; and Rep. Rob Bresnahan, who is facing Democrat Paige Cognetti, the mayor of Scranton, in the 8th Congressional District in northeastern Pennsylvania.
Two longtime incumbents also won new terms in 2024—U.S. Rep. Scott Perry, a Republican who is now facing Democrat Janelle Stelson, a former TV anchor, in the 10th Congressional District in the Harrisburg area, and U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican who is facing Democrat Bob Harvie, a county commissioner, in the 1st Congressional District in Bucks County.
All eight candidates essentially agree that developers should pay for infrastructure and power needs and not leave residents with higher utility costs. Harvie is the only candidate so far to say he supports a moratorium. Perry, meanwhile, has adopted Trump’s strong overall support for data centers, saying they are essential to helping the United States stay ahead globally on artificial intelligence.
“The last thing we need are data centers raising our energy costs while big corporations get rich,” Brooks said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “My job is to make sure the people of the Lehigh Valley have the final say over what gets built in their backyard.”
Bresnahan, a Republican, struck a similar note in the 8th District race: “I am not going to allow data centers to be forced on northeastern Pennsylvania without the approval of the people,” he said in a campaign ad, adding that “families know what is best for our communities. We should decide if data centers get built here.”
Ginny Marcille-Kerslake, a senior organizer for the environmental advocacy group Food & Water Watch who is involved in the fight against data centers in Pennsylvania, said she doesn’t know how the issue will play out in the elections, but candidates clearly recognize “that support for these projects makes them vulnerable” in this election.
“I have never seen anything like this in terms of public engagement,” said Kerslake, with opposition coming from “across the political spectrum. We don’t see that these days.”
A Quinnipiac University poll of registered voters in Pennsylvania, published in July, found that 74 percent would oppose a new data center being built in their community. That’s up from 68 percent when the same question was asked of voters in February.
With lots of open space, water and energy resources, Pennsylvania is attractive to data center developers, who are looking for large chunks of land that are near adequate power sources or in places that will allow them to build their own power source, as well as near water, which is needed to cool the massive computer systems housed in these centers.
So far, about 70 data centers have been proposed, are under construction or have some kind of preliminary activity in Pennsylvania, according to the Data Center Proposal Tracker, a citizen-run database that tracks projects across multiple states. They are scattered in and around each of the four competitive districts, with a heavy concentration in the northeastern Pennsylvania region that includes the 8th District.

11ed2dbc6620.text: Democrats in a pair of deep-red states are testing the religious right's dominance by putting their Christian faith at the center of their campaigns — potentially creating a template for the party to compete in similarly forbidding terrain. Why it matters: Upsets by Texas' James Talarico and Kansas' Adam Hamilton would all but ensure that Democrats take the Senate. A recent poll from Pew shows both an opening and an obstacle: White evangelicals still strongly favor Republicans, while many other Christian groups lean Democratic or are more narrowly split. The big picture: Talarico , a Presbyterian seminary student, and Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, are challenging conservatives' claim to speak for faith. Their bids come after Democrat Raphael Warnock, senior pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, was elected to the Senate in 2021. President Trump won both Texas and Kansas by double digits in 2024. Neither state has sent a Democrat to the Senate in the 21st century — the last time Kansas did was in 1932. Both races this year are considered toss-ups . Zoom in: Talarico's "religiosity is a way to soften his liberalism" and potentially win over Christians turned off by his scandal-plagued opponent , says Brandon Rottinghaus, who co-hosts Houston Public Media's "Party Politics." Talarico has also made several visits to Black Baptist churches . Trump made inroads with minority communities in Texas, and Talarico looks to do the same after besting Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), who is Black, in a brutal primary. He's harnessed scripture in his pitch against Christian nationalism and for protecting the vulnerable, invoking the biblical campaign slogan, "It's time to start flipping tables." "We're in a populist political moment, and many of the teachings of the social gospel give him an opportunity to link the politics and his faith together," Rottinghaus adds. By the numbers: A September Marist survey of 1,139 Texas registered voters showed Paxton with a 75% to 22% lead over Talarico among white evangelical Christians. In Kansas, the race will hinge less on whether Hamilton can win large numbers of religious Republicans and more on whether he can replicate Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly's coalition, says Alexandra Middlewood, the political science department chair at Wichita State University. Hamilton has presented himself as a bridge-builder, drawing on his experience leading the largest United Methodist church in the nation. His well-known religious background could appeal to less engaged, moderate Christians and center-right voters, Middlewood says. Yes, but: While Kansas has elected blue governors and voted to keep abortion legal in the state, Republicans have a massive registration advantage that's made a Democratic Senate win "near impossible," notes Bob Beatty, Washburn University's political science chair. Establishment Democrats have long been viewed with suspicion, especially in western Kansas, he said. But Hamilton being a pastor "gives him an open doorway to approach those voters in western Kansas that I would argue previous Democrats have not had." Zoom out: Black clergy — including Warnock — have a history of political action. But white clergy are stepping up to run as Democrats in substantial numbers. In Iowa, Sarah Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister, and Lindsay James, a Presbyterian pastor, are running in tight House races. Pastor Doug Pagitt, executive director of progressive Christian group Vote Common Good, says the religious left's surge is driven by candidates' personal convictions and years-long efforts from groups like his that have trained politicians on how to connect with faith voters. But Trump, who Pagitt says has repeatedly offended Christians , is also a motivator: "There is no single person who could be more helpful to Democrats reaching out to religious people right now than Donald Trump. He is the greatest recruiting tool." Yes, but: Trump has repeatedly defied predictions that the religious right wouldn't vote for him. The other side: Ralph Reed, chair of the conservative Faith and Freedom Coalition, tells Axios he's doubtful the Democrats' effort to lean into religion will attract voters of faith. "Voters will not vote for a candidate who professes to hold to their faith, but doesn't share their values," he says. One GOP opponent labeled clergy running for office as Democrats "PINOs" — Pastors in Name Only. But while Reed says he's confident Republicans will turn out after Trump's battleground blitz, he acknowledges their economic struggles. "Evangelicals and other conservative voters of faith, they live in the real world too," he says. Whether evangelicals are motivated to show up will be a major story of the midterms, says Ryan Burge of the John C. Danforth Center on Religion and Politics. The other will be how Catholics shift: "If the Adam Hamiltons, the James Talaricos of the world can win over people, it's going to be ... marginally attached Catholics," Burge predicts. The bottom line: There's a clear movement on the religious left — but the question remains whether voters will join it. Go deeper: "Shocking" number of white clergy run as Democrats in 2026

Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.
Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.
Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El NiÃ±o heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .
After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,
However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.
Taiwan's $5tn (Â£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.
This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.
The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El NiÃ±o - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

The Signal Interview
âWhen I came to Silicon Valley, we thought we were all making the world a better place,â Brian Chesky recalls, 19 years after he co-founded Airbnb. Now, he tells The CEO Signal, âSilicon Valleyâs in a bubble, and society feels like AI is happening to them, not for them.â
Chesky is an unusual figure in Californiaâs tech heartland. An industrial designer surrounded by mathematicians and engineers, he describes Silicon Valley as a nightclub he somehow snuck into as a 26-year-old when the bouncer wasnât looking.
âI wasnât supposed to be here,â he says. But he has grown close to CEOs like OpenAIâs Sam Altman, and he thinks he can help the AI industryâs leaders understand what people who stay in Airbnbs really think of them.
The aesthetic Chesky honed at the Rhode Island School of Design permeates his San Francisco headquarters, a former Eveready battery factory whose meeting rooms look like Airbnb rentals from around the world. But he implies that other pioneers around him have lost sight of who theyâre designing their products for. Tech executives love talking in lofty terms about âhumanity,â he says, but his fellow founders should be talking about people â like school teachers and mill workers â and listening to them, too.
âI talked to one famous person â I wonât mention who â and I said, âDo you talk to a regular person?â He goes, âYes, such and such.â Iâm like, âWell, thatâs your nanny,ââ Chesky says. âWe should talk to normal people we donât pay, people who are willing to tell us to F off and tell us why they donât like us.â
A $250 million pitch to get on âthe right sideâ of the housing issue
Chesky has had plenty of blunt feedback as Airbnb has grown, with cities from New York to Barcelona blaming his company for making housing less affordable. Despite years of engaging with local politicians, Airbnb has failed to stop some of them from implementing caps or outright bans on short-term rentals.
Asked whether he has any responsibility for the housing affordability crisis, Chesky replies: âI think we have a responsibility. I think thereâs a difference between having responsibility and being the primary cause.â
Listings on Airbnb typically comprise just 0.5% of the housing stock in cities where it operates, he says, and many of those properties are primary or second homes someone is already living in, rather than units that have been removed from the long-term rental market. Bans on short-term rentals havenât reversed housing inflation in cities like New York, he notes.
The bigger issue, Chesky argues, is a shortage of new construction. Last month, Airbnb positioned itself as a partner in solving that problem by announcing a $250 million fund to provide âlast-dollarâ financing for housing projects with funding shortfalls. Itâs a small sum for a company with a $100 billion-plus market capitalization, but he says it should unlock an additional $5 billion of new housing.
âItâs not philanthropy,â he says. Airbnb will make a return â albeit a smaller one than some real estate investors would expect â âbut weâre also going to be on the right side of this issue.â
Even so, he says, concerns about housing affordability are only going to get âmuch worseâ as more people want to move to cities. The two biggest issues in the 2028 US presidential election, he predicts, will be affordability and AI.
Cheskyâs advice for AIâs âPromethean momentâ
Chesky says he does not believe that AI will destroy humanity any time soon, but he thinks society is unprepared for the technological power that has been unleashed in this âPromethean moment.â Technology used to feel like a train that people just had to jump on to âride into the promised land of progress,â he says. âAnd now people feel like theyâre [on] the train tracks, and the train called AI is coming for them.âÂ
Silicon Valley cannot credibly police AI, he believes, warning his peers that if the technology is left unregulated, âbad sh*t is going to happen, and thereâs going to be overcorrection, and then thereâs going to be a hammer coming down.â
Nor does he believe that Washington can regulate AI successfully, because policymakers donât understand the technology well enough. âBridge-buildersâ between Silicon Valley, Washington, and ordinary people are needed â and he is putting himself forward as one of them.
One of his recommendations, he says, is that AI founders should stop talking about impossible-sounding goals like âsaving humanity.â Instead, they should take on one issue at a time, starting with the most immediate problem AI has exacerbated â cybersecurity. In the meantime, Silicon Valley is âlosing people because weâre not talking about people,â he warns. âWe just need to put design principles and humanity into AI.â
A new mission in matchmaking
Even as Chesky critiques Silicon Valleyâs blind spots, he is using them to define a new ambition for Airbnb.
Innovations like e-commerce and online banking mean that people are spending more time on their devices and less time bumping into friends and strangers in shopping malls, banks, and âthe real world,â he observes. Even our on-screen lives are more isolating than they were, he adds, since tech companies have rejected the form of social networking that was filled with updates from our friends for more advertiser-friendly social media. AIâs potential to fuel isolation is far greater, Chesky believes, saying that this may be âthe loneliest time in human history.â
His hope is that Airbnb can âuse a device to get you off a device.â And heâs not just talking about customers using its app to book a room in a strangerâs house, or sign up for one of the add-on experiences that Airbnb has been encouraging hosts to offer, like cooking lessons or sightseeing tours.

Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda's main airport earlier this month.
Both travelled through Entebbe airport on 3 October and investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday.
Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established.
Nigeria is battling its first Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including one death.
The Nigerian patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja, is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
She is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Nigeria, Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed. Her husband, who accompanied her on a trip to Uganda, is also in isolation but has not developed symptoms.
The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, travelling through Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, where she had a two-hour stopover.
She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.
Health officials are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient.
The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death ever.
Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.
"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.
The WHO said it was too early to determine where the patient in Nigeria became infected.
"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.
He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.
Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.
"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.
Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.
However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.
Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.
Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.
"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.
"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.
Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.
In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.
Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.
He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.
The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.
Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.
The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.
Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.
The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.
Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media.
The centre of the quake hit BaqÃªn County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.
Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries.
The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas.
Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.
The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km.
Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes.
Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape.
Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu told Tibet Daily that she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, her "legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home.
Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us".
Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet.
Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks had been registered since the quake occurred.
China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media.
Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude, around 4,800m (15,750ft), and prone to aftershocks.
The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations.
Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (Â£5.6m; $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet.
Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark. These have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly.
In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet.
The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

A farmer hit by England's first outbreak of avian flu this season has said the loss of 32,000 egg-laying birds is likely to cost her business more than Â£100,000.
Catherine Armstrong, who has a free-range farm near Belford, Northumberland, told the BBC of the "shock" of her worst fears coming true when she found "a carpet of dead birds" in her barns this week.
The outbreak's source is not yet known but the virus is thought to have been brought onto the site, which has strict biosecurity measures, by wild birds. The farm's remaining poultry were culled.
The Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) has put control measures in place to contain the outbreak, external but warned cases were likely to rise.
So far, there has been one other case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in the UK, external, on the Isle of Lewis, Scotland.
Armstrong said her birds, which normally produce 28,500 eggs a day, which are then supplied to a range of UK supermarkets, began to die a week ago.
"At this age of the flock, you would tend to see the odd death but on the Friday my lady who works in the shed messaged me at night to say that 39 had died," she explained.
During the weekend, the virus spread rapidly, with more than 1,000 birds dead by Sunday night.
The APHA was contacted and a vet came out to carry out tests but Armstrong said she knew it would be bird flu: "In my heart of hearts, when you are shovelling dead birds out of a shed, you feel... well, I didn't need the results. I knew what the results would be."
By Tuesday, the virus had been confirmed, with thousands of birds dead. Within two days, all the remaining birds had been culled to control the virus' spread.
"All your worst fears, I suppose, are realised then. It is an emotional roller coaster. I mean, for instance, on the Sunday, I just felt numb. On the Monday, just a bit like 'Why me?'. Angry, cross, upset.
"On the Tuesday, it's a bit matter of fact. It's like, 'Right, we've got to do this. I've got to do that'. And on Wednesday, I was just desperately sad.
"Normally, you'd open up a hen shed door and there'd be 16,000 birds looking at you but to see them all lying dead, just a carpet of dead birds, is quite shocking.
"As a poultry keeper, it's a horrible shock."
'Dreadful disease'
Armstrong praised the APHA staff for their work and the wider industry for its support.
She said despite the high cost of the outbreak - which she estimated would be more than Â£100,000 - she was "not going to sit back and let it beat us".
Gary Ford, of the British Free Range Egg Producers' Association (Bfrepa), said the farm had high standards of biosecurity but "sadly, as was the case here, that does not always prevent infection as free-range hens come into regular contact with wild birds, which spread this dreadful disease".
He added the association would be calling on the government to bring in a regional housing order to protect "those poultry farms close to coastal areas and known flight paths of migratory wild birds".
Meanwhile, farmers are still waiting for the results of a recent government trial of a bird flu vaccine in turkeys.
A spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said that, while the trial concluded in August, results would not be available until the end of the year and vaccination would not be an option for this bird flu season.
Meanwhile, an APHA spokesperson said it expected colder temperatures and the arrival of migratory birds "to see a rise in infection cases, which is why it is so important that bird keepers have robust biosecurity measures in place to limit the spread of this devastating disease".
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the risk to the general public's health posed by avian influenza remained very low while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said it posed a very low food safety risk, with properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, safe to eat.

On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.
Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.
Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.
Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.
The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.
Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.
The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.
During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.
Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?
Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.
D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.
In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.
Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.
Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.
But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.
"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."
That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.
Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.
Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.
Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."
The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.
In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, whil

US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.
The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October, though Ukraine and Russia have so far not commented.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added.
Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.
The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".
The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.
Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.
They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.
Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.
The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.
The city was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".
Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.
In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.
Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.
According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace.
"I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year.
"And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home'."

Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said.
Another 28 people were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing, in what government spokesperson Dr al-Momani Mohammad described as a "heinous attack".
Jordan's King Abdullah II said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties."
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.
Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.
A news briefing by interior ministry officials is expected shortly, and al-Momani has said the country's prime minister will chair a meeting of the Security Council to be attended by all ministers.
In his post on X, King Abdullah II offered his condolences to the families of the victims, writing: "Whoever imagines that the bullets of treachery can divide the ranks of Jordanians will fail in his endeavour before our steadfastness and unity."
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in Jordan, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the country in the past.

85f692654a79.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/rescuers-search-for-survivors-after-deadly-earthquake-in-chinas-tibet-region Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in China's Tibet region World Oct 23, 2026 10:25 AM EDT BEIJING (AP) — Rescuers combed through a remote area in the Chinese region of Tibet on Friday after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes, according to Chinese state media. The disaster struck Nagqu, a city north of Tibet's capital Lhasa that's some 4,800 meters (5,249 yards) above sea level, on Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, and officials told journalists they were concerned about further building collapses from aftershocks, as well as casualties from rockslides. WATCH: Wall of mud and debris floods communities in Nepal and Tibet Search and rescue efforts are complicated by the geography and low temperatures, officials said. As of Friday afternoon, rescuers had done three rounds of searches, going through each household, and each village, said Dunzhu, the acting mayor of Nagqu city, said in a press conference. More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 2,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,400 tents and 2,000 folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region. The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu. It put the earthquake's depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles). The U.S. agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles), according to its website. China's official news agency Xinhua said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities have taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region. The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua. Intermittent snows are expected in the earthquake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. Chinese President Xi Jinping called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work, issuing instructions Friday morning. Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon has been pushed back 24 hours to Monday as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.
The fixture at the Parc des Princes in Paris had been scheduled to kick off at 19:45 GMT on Sunday but will instead take place at 20:30 on Monday.
The Ligue de Football Professionnel (LFP) announced the postponement in a statement, external on Friday after French police prohibited the fixture from taking place on its original date.
French authorities are preparing a major security operation for demonstrations planned for Saturday.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations last Saturday to protest rising fuel prices, education standards and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.
Marches took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions and student groups, and were marred by some incidents of violence, looting and destruction.
The security challenge is further complicated by Sunday's NFL match between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France, an event expected to require a significant police deployment.
The game will be played in Saint-Denis, about 10km from Place de la Bastille, where the protests are expected to begin.
The disruptions have already affected France's domestic football schedule with Toulouse's Ligue 1 home game against Troyes moved from Saturday to Sunday at the request of authorities.
Reigning French and European champions PSG are second in the standings after seven matches, while Lyon lead the table on 14 points, ahead of the holders on goal difference.
The match will also now be played on the same day as the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London.
Injured PSG pair Ousmane Dembele, the 2025 winner, and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are among the contenders for the award.

One person has been killed and five others wounded - three seriously - in a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which authorities are investigating as "terrorism".
Several drive-by shootings took place on Friday - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La VerriÃ¨re. The rampage lasted almost 15 minutes, said Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez. A12-year-old girl is among the wounded.
The suspected attacker has been arrested. The motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".
NuÃ±ez told reporters in Trappes: "It's clearly a terrorist crime, that's what [the prosecutor] has said."
The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.
The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.
The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La VerriÃ¨re.
A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La VerriÃ¨re on the main N10 road that runs through the town.
Asked what the motive for the shootings may have been, the mayor of Trappes said that the victim who had died was of African origin and one of those in a critical condition was of North African descent.
The attack had a "racist, probably Islamophobic overtone", he said.
In its own statement, the anti-terror prosecutor called for caution regarding the identity of the victims.
However, among the alleged offences covered by the investigation, the prosecutor listed "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise" with the aggravated circumstance of acts committed because of "real or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnicity, nation or religion".
The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window.
A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two.
Rabeh said the shooter had hit a health centre, a petrol station and several vehicles during the spree.
The suspected attacker was then arrested at the nearby town of CoigniÃ¨res, local media report.
The interior minister said the motive of the attacker remained unclear.
The suspect, a 39-year-old, was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.
PNAT said their investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts.
The anti-terrorist office also said its investigation is looking into "conspiracy with a terrorist group for the purpose of preparing crimes against persons".

The life of a woman who filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped at a Cornell University fraternity house has been completely upended, her lawyer has said.
Speaking to the BBC ahead of a hearing in the civil case on Friday in New York, her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said: "She feels under fire."
The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former school and the fraternity over the alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.
When the case went viral, a series of "I am Jane Doe" solidarity posts appeared, but there was a separate campaign aimed at unmasking her and defending the men, who have all denied any wrongdoing.
The men, who are also being sued by the woman, have not been charged with any crimes.
With initial proceedings now under way in the civil case, Giuffra told the BBC that these last few weeks have been "a very hard time" for his client, who isn't doing a lot beyond "surviving".
Her decision to sue was rooted in a desire for closure and to take power back, he said.
Giufrra visited Jane Doe this week and found that she hadn't been sleeping well â relying on medication to get rest.
Now in trauma therapy, he says she doesn't feel safe in her own home following malicious threats that were directed at her and her family.
After her address was published online without her consent, someone called in a fake emergency that led to police in full tactical gear drawing assault rifles on her father, her friend and her brother at their family home.
"It's just constant fear," he said.
He added that despite this her resolve hadn't been shaken and she remains determined to overhaul the university system at Cornell, and across the country, to protect survivors.
Cornell University, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of Jane Doe's case.
After facing intense pressure, the college's president announced that fraternity parties would be suspended until the end of the academic year to allow for a thorough review to determine whether and how they can safely continue.
The school also said it would add sexual assault investigators to its police force.
Giuffra, however, says he is surprised that Cornell has not reached out to him and believes they have been focused solely on "damage control".
He says any agreement with Cornell to resolve the civil lawsuit will need to include "steps to ensure there are no more Jane Does" and if there are, that they are going to be supported.
The BBC contacted Cornell for comment who directed us to the university's previous statements and comments on its internal investigation in 2024.
New York's governor Kathy Hochul appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.
Giuffra expects it will take a long time to do a proper investigation but is concerned that they will be going after evidence that is now "stale".
"A lot of the communication was on Snapchat, Snapchat goes away," he told the BBC.
"The best time to get evidence is around the time of the crime and that just didn't happen."
However, Giuffra believes he can win the civil case against the university, the men and others, where the burden of proof is lower than a criminal case.
Civil cases require a preponderance of the evidence, that it's more likely than not it happened, while criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Recent high profile cases have shown the way juries evaluate consent can be unpredictable.
"I wouldn't have taken the case if I didn't think it was a strong case that I could win and get her some closure."

Do you have three days' worth of food and water in your home?
That is what the government has told all of us to have on hand to get through a national emergency, as well as some other basic items.
Its "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.
On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
As one expert warns the UK is "light years" behind our neighbours when it comes to preparing for major disruption, we've drilled down into what you need and why.
What is on the 'Be Ready' checklist?
The government recommends having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended - you can scroll through below to see the full list.
Disaster planning expert Professor Lucy Easthope said the goal of asking household to prepare is to make it easier for emergency service to cope in the event of a national emergency.
For example, the government says people who need medication should have an extra supply just in case. Prof Easthope says: "If people have got their heart pills for an extra for an extra 48 hours, it stops [response crews] from having to immediately find an emergency pharmacist."
While the latest government campaign only launched on Thursday, some people are well ahead of the game.
Speaking to Radio 5 Live, Bridgette Clamp, who lives in near Penzance in Cornwall, said she has stocked up on "lots of tinned goods" as well as "flour, yeast and everything to bake bread".
"We're rocking and rolling," she says.
One woman, who spoke to 5 Live anonymously, said she bought "loads and loads" of emergency food - but ended up eating it before it was strictly necessary.
Like others, she wondered if the government was "scaremongering", adding: "I don't know but I've certainly bought into it."
Rob, who lives off-grid in north Wales, told the programme he has stocked up on so many supplies he "wouldn't even notice" if a disaster struck.
But he said he still felt there was "a bit of scaremongering" going on and wondered if he would ever need it all.
Why is the government telling people to stockpile now?
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally.
The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".
Prof Easthope said she has been lobbying the government to launch this sort of campaign for "about 16 years".
She said successive governments have been hesitant of "putting out information that might cause tension" - and speculated that this advice may have been "rushed" out ahead of Storm Austen hitting the UK.
While many of us will already have a stash of tinned food in the cupboards, fewer homes are likely to have a store of bottled water.
Paul from Torquay, Devon, said to Radio 5 Live: "Who on earth carries three day supply of water?"
He added: "I think they've made it our responsibility, rather than their responsibility."
Do other countries have similar emergency advice?
Prof Easthope described the UK as "light years" behind neighbouring countries when it comes to preparedness.
"Countries like Scandinavia, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, they've been good at this for years," she said.
France advises people to store 72-hours' worth of food, while the German government says homes should have enough supplies to last for a 10-day period.
"This is one area where I'm very comfortable saying we are playing massive catch-up," added Easthope.
Awareness campaigns such as "think 72 hours" make a big difference in the US, Australia and "all around Europe", she said.
However, in the UK, she said disaster messaging often gets parodied, or governments are accused of "panic-mongering".
"We have seen the pendulum shift" in recent years, she adds, saying that "we are now seeing people recognise this" as an issue that needs tackling.

The Welsh government has announced plans to ban the use of traditional steel pylons to support electricity lines over which it has control.
Plaid Cymru ministers favour burying cables underground instead.
Plans for a network of pylons in the Towy Valley have faced a fierce local backlash with local Plaid politicians speaking out against the proposals.
The company behind the plans, Green Gen Cymru, said it welcomed the consultation and that it supported using "the right infrastructure in the right place".
Prohibiting the use of large steel lattice pylons for new lines up to 132 kilovolts was a Plaid Cymru manifesto pledge before May's Senedd election.
Launching a consultation on its policy on Friday, the Welsh government said undergrounding electricity circuits could "reduce the visual impact of electricity infrastructure, helping to protect landscapes and local amenity".
It also said that burying cables could make them less vulnerable to severe weather and could reduce the potential impact on birds and other wildlife.
However, the consultation document also acknowledges that undergrounding was "generally considered more expensive to install and maintain and could create construction impacts during installation".
The government's policy would allow for wooden poles or "equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure" to be used to support overhead cables where undergrounding isn't feasible.
Green Gen has plans to build three major power line routes connecting onshore wind farms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network.
It has previously said it would invest nearly Â£1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire.
But it has faced considerable opposition in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners taking the company to court in 2025.
In a bid to address concerns, Green Gen recently unveiled a "slim and compact" 22 metre (72ft) pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind".
The company has consistently said that undergrounding its cables would cost on average 4.5 times more, external than running them overhead.
That would mean an extra cost of Â£500m for the Towy Usk project between Carmarthenshire and Powys, according to Green Gen.
Welsh Energy Minister Adam Price said: "We know the necessary changes in the way energy is generated and used in Wales will require new grid infrastructure, however, we also know that new infrastructure can impact on the communities and the environment that hosts it.
"We want to see infrastructure that is sensitively designed to minimise impacts on the environment and the communities that host them, while offering the maximum benefits for Wales."
Andrew Hardcastle, executive director at Green Gen Cymru, said: "We welcome the Welsh government's consultation and its recognition of the importance of delivering the electricity infrastructure Wales needs in a way that is sensitive to our landscapes, environment and communities.
"Like all grid companies across the UK, we believe there is no one-size-fits-all solution to developing new electricity networks.
"Our approach is to use the right infrastructure in the right place, drawing on a range of technologies including underground cables, wooden poles and our recently announced lower-profile monopoles."
The company said it was "pleased that the consultation recognises the potential role of less visually intrusive overhead infrastructure, including monopoles, and invites evidence on their use".
Reform's Senedd spokesperson for rural affairs, Laura Anne Jones, said: "As part of our energy policy, we will continue to push for new power lines to be placed underground wherever possible, protecting our landscapes and rural communities.
"Reform will always stand up for our countryside and fight against its industrialisation."
The Welsh Conservatives welcomed the policy consultation.
The party's environment spokesperson, Andrew RT Davies said: "We recognise that Wales needs a modern electricity network to support economic growth, but communities should not have to accept eyesores across our beautiful natural landscapes, which must be conserved."
The consultation, external will run until 15 January 2027.
