For people with asthma, switching from a gas stove to an electric one might be a breath of fresh air. The combustion that creates the flame of a gas stove or oven releases pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, which can trigger asthma symptoms. After a research-backed electric stove replacement, people reported more symptom relief than is often achieved with asthma medications.
“We were really surprised at how large the benefit was,” says Ashwini Sehgal, a clinician who studies community health at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. With funding from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration, Sehgal and colleagues spearheaded a project to install electric stoves in Cleveland households that had at least one person with asthma.
Eighty-five participants who had poorly controlled asthma were given a questionnaire a few months after the switch. They reported symptom improvement that was roughly two to three times as large as what’s typical with medication. Those with the worst symptoms saw the biggest improvement. Participants also reported fewer emergency room or hospital visits and said they missed work or school less often.
One 38-year-old woman told Sehgal’s team that whenever she cooked on her gas stove, she felt like her throat was closing. But the sensation disappeared after she switched to electric. Another participant, a 36-year-old man, found it difficult to walk uphill and play with his kids. With the stove swap, “he described how much better he felt as ‘magical,’ ” Sehgal says.
While heating, steaming or frying on a gas stovetop, nearby NO2 levels can skyrocket, reaching hundreds of parts per billion. That’s much higher than the EPA’s one-hour outdoor air quality standard of 100 parts per billion. NO2 exposure is linked to increased asthma symptoms. For example, research in children has found the pollutant can boost wheezing, coughing and asthma attacks.
The project was initially funded to follow 1,200 households for 12 months. But the Trump administration terminated the EPA’s Community Change Grants early, which drastically reduced the number of study participants. Yet even with this small group, the symptom improvement was significant.
The decision to replace a gas stove “depends on how much you are struggling with your own illness,” says environmental epidemiologist Carrie Breton of WashU Bursky School of Public Health in St. Louis. As a trial run, Sehgal suggests using an electric hot plate and a toaster oven to see if keeping the gas stove off helps improve symptoms.
If a stove swap isn’t in the budget, reducing NO2 exposure is still worthwhile, says pulmonologist Laura Paulin of Dartmouth Health. She recommends using kitchen ventilation, either via an exhaust hood that vents to the outside or an open window. A HEPA filter with a carbon insert can trap NO2 to decrease airborne concentrations. And try to keep children with asthma out of the kitchen when the stove is on, Paulin says. “It is a daunting task to replace a stove, but it doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing thing.”
For researchers, the next step would be to measure lung function before and after a stove switch, Breton says. It would also be helpful to account for more factors, such as seasonal effects. “Many things can trigger people’s asthma,” Paulin says. Researchers could do a randomized trial in which some people get the electric stove right away while others wait for six months, Sehgal says, to allow time for comparison.
If electric stoves continue to be linked with fewer trips to the emergency room, fewer hospitalizations and better symptom control than medication can provide, “health insurance companies should consider paying for or subsidizing” stove swaps, Sehgal says. “If it truly works this well,” Breton says, “it’s got a bigger bang for your buck.”

Gulf economies as a whole are expected to shrink 4.8% this year, almost matching the COVID-19 shock, with non-oil output receding in four countries. âThis conflict has disrupted energy production, shipping, tourism, trade, and confidence,â Jihad Azour, director of the IMFâs Middle East and Central Asia Department, told reporters in Dubai.
Non-oil activity, a key metric watched by businesses in the region, is expected to rebound to 4.5% growth in 2027 if the conflict is resolved. Financial buffers are also weakening, with the regionâs current-account surplus expected to narrow to 1.3% of GDP, from 5% last year, while the combined fiscal deficit is expected to widen to 2.3%, from 0.8%, according to the IMF.
Oman is the outlier, having implemented economic reforms before the war and remaining relatively unscathed by the conflict. Worst-hit has been Bahrain, the smallest Gulf oil exporter, which has long relied on its neighbors to prop up its economy. With debt levels now at more than 150% of GDP and foreign reserves down 50% since March, the kingdom is reportedly in talks for a cash infusion led by the UAE, according to Asharq Bloomberg.

October's full Moon, nicknamed the Hunter's Moon, is set to light up the night sky this weekend.
It will be visible in the UK from Sunday 25 October into the morning of Monday 26 October.
Marking the 11th full Moon of 13 in 2026, it is the final one before a run of four consecutive supermoons, external.
If you want to catch a glimpse, keep an eye on the forecast to see if the weather will allow a clear view.
When is the best time to view the Hunter's Moon?
The Moon will rise in the east at just after 16:00 GMT on Sunday and set towards the west between 07:00 and 08:00 GMT on Monday - times vary across the UK.
The Moon will be officially full at 04:11 GMT on Monday. This is the moment of "syzygy" when the Sun and Moon will be aligned either side of the Earth.
However, the Moon will appear full on both Sunday and Monday nights, giving skygazers two chances to spot it.
During a full Moon, the whole of the Earth-facing side of the Moon is illuminated by the Sun.
You may notice an orange or reddish hue to the Moon when it is low in the sky due to the scattering of short wavelength blue light as it passes through a large depth of the atmosphere.
The longer wavelength red and orange colours are not scattered as readily so pass through to our eyes.
The Moon may also appear larger in the sky near moonrise and moonset - something called the "Moon Illusion".
This is when our brain makes us think the Moon looks bigger because it is viewed alongside objects on the horizon such as buildings and trees.
As well as looking out for the full Moon, there is also a chance to spot some shooting stars, with the Orionid meteor shower just past its peak.
The extra lunar light, however, may obscure some of the meteors, so be patient and leave time for your eyes to adjust.
Why is it called the Hunter's Moon?
Full Moons throughout the year have traditionally been given names that reflect what is going on in nature.
Different cultures use different names for the 12 or 13 full Moons across the lunar calendar, but many of the common ones we use today originate from Native American cultures.
In October, the term Hunter's Moon comes from the time of year hunters would have been most active, preparing for the colder and darker winter months ahead.
The Hunter's Moon is known to sit in the sky for a particularly long time - similar to the preceding Harvest Moon - giving hunters extra light in the skies.
Will the weather be clear enough to see the Moon?
Storm Boelo will continue to bring rain and very strong winds to northern Scotland early on Sunday night, but prospects of seeing the Moon increases as the night wears on.
There will be plenty of blustery showers in west Scotland and north-west England - any gaps between these could give a brief chance to view.
For the rest of the UK prospects are better, especially early in the night with clearer skies, before cloud tends to spread in from the south-west later.
If the weather fails to cooperate where you live, the next chance to see a full Moon will be on 24 November as the Beaver Supermoon.
This will be followed by a Christmas Eve Cold Supermoon on 24 December.
The succession of supermoons will then continue into 2027, with January and February's full Moons both set to be supermoons too.

Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.
Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice.
Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare.
"A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said.
The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them.
However, the current coalition government, elected in June, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday.
Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare".
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.
However, its production has slipped behind that of other countries, such as Poland and China, in recent years.
The industry faced a crisis during the coronavirus pandemic, when the government ordered a mass cull of mink after a mutated strain of Covid-19 was found in the animals. Approximately 15 million were killed.
At the time, the country had huge export markets to China and Hong Kong. The government later admitted it had no legal basis for the culling.
There are now approximately 15,000 mink left in Denmark.
No costs have yet been determined for closing Denmark's seven remaining mink farms, but an animal welfare spokesperson for one of the governing coalition parties previously estimated it would be around 14m Danish krone (Â£1.56m), local media report, but the final amount could be higher.
The wearing of fur is a controversial subject within fashion circles, with publications and fashion brands choosing not to use or promote it several years ago.
But it re-entered the spotlight last year, with celebrities and fashionistas wearing both vintage and so-called faux fur.

5fb8a1db7381.text: On a recent evening near a secure U.S. facility, three federal agents saw a flying object they couldn't identify: a large "matte black triangle" that moved as fast as a fighter jet, made no sound and then disappeared, according to FBI and Defense Department reports. Why it matters: The 15-foot flying triangle is classified as a UFO-like "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" because the U.S. doesn't have the technology to make such a craft — and neither do its adversaries. The reports of the drone-like aircraft is of growing interest and concern to intelligence and military officials. Driving the news: The two reports about the mysterious triangle were included in a batch of 10 documents released Friday by U.S. officials under President Trump's order this year to disclose UAP records from all government sources as soon as possible. Friday's disclosure marks the seventh release of a tranche of documents under the order. Some of the documents found in the National Archives are from the 1940s. Zoom in: The flying triangle reports are the most intriguing because the incident — from this year — is so recent. The month and day are redacted. The FBI document is labeled an "Unidentified Aerial Object Observation Report" and the Defense Department 's report on it is classified as a "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena" report. The observers were federal agents, including two with "extensive operational experience" and familiarity with drones. One had a "thermal monocular" for infrared tracking and yet couldn't detect "discrete heat sources associated with propulsion" from an engine on the mysterious craft. The agents reported seeing the drone-like triangle, with a wingspan of about 15 feet, rise vertically for as many as 300 feet above a mountain ridgeline without tilting or swaying. It stopped, hovered for about 20 seconds, and then flew horizontally as fast as a fighter jet for about 1.5 miles in three seconds without making a sound before it vanished. The intrigue: One of the documents released Friday doesn't concern a flying object. It's a declassified 2010 report about the Utah property known as the "Skinwalker Ranch," named after supernatural shapeshifting witches in Navajo culture. "Witnesses have reported unidentified balls of light at close range, daytime sightings of "dog-like" creatures running on two legs, unnatural animalistic howling/screaming, 'little people,' prehistoric-like birds and a maggot which measured about 8 feet long and 2- to 3-feet in diameter," the report said. The report's authors present no final conclusions or hard evidence, such as photographs, of the supernatural. DNA tests from one clump of hair from a suspected "Skinwalker" showed it came from a raccoon. The ranch is now the subject of a Netflix show . Other items in the tranche include: A 1954 report from a Swedish Transair pilot who said he and his crew witnessed flying saucers: "Previously I have been extremely skeptical about all the stories of mysterious objects — called flying saucers — that have been seen at diverse points," the captain said. "Now I don't know exactly what to think; but it did seem to me that we had seen a robot of some kind." A 1957 report from a B-52 pilot over Saudi Arabia who said he witnessed an unidentified aircraft. 1949 and a 1952 UFO reports from California's Catalina Island, site of some of the nation's first "flying saucer" sightings. A 1963 interagency coordination memo and 1960s records concerning how NASA and the Defense Department would handle and publicly discuss the collection of "fragments or suspected fragments of space vehicles of all types." Yes, but: The records released by the administration do not express any conclusions as to whether the government believes the UAPs represent the existence of alien life. They also don't indicate any conclusions as to whether UAPs represent a national security threat to the U.S.

7f22a8f4658e.text:
Matthewâs view
Just four years ago, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was at the peak of his powers. He was feted by the Chinese president and snubbed the US president, all while sitting atop a gusher of oil wealth that allowed him to pour money into trying to turn his wildest ideas into reality.
Those days seem a long time ago.
This year was always going to be tough for MBS, as Prince Mohammed is widely known. Even before the Iran war, Saudi Arabiaâs budget deficit was widening, signature investment projects were being scaled back, and the sugar rush from the sweeping economic and social reforms was wearing off.
US President Donald Trumpâs war with Iran, which MBS warned against, has made matters worse. MBS now faces crises on multiple fronts: a global energy shock, a regional security emergency, and a deteriorating domestic economic outlook. Together, they form a perfect storm and expose the limits of his ability to shape events in the region.
Looking through the prism of oil, the attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb boosted prices enough to offset lower export volumes. But the short-term gains mask a longer-term risk. Despite heroic efforts to keep crude moving, the Gulfâs reputation as a reliable energy provider has been damaged. The longer the disruption lasts, the more key energy importers will prepare for life without Saudi oil. Consumers will seek alternative sources of hydrocarbons and accelerate investments in renewables. The result could spur a global scramble to pump more oil as quickly as possible, leaving the kingdom fighting to win back market share when the conflict ends amid a glut and lower prices.
But that is the future, and the war may be showing signs of escalation, making MBSâs vision of Saudi Arabia as the center of a prosperous Middle East â a place for international firms to invest, holidaymakers to visit, and the wealthy to buy homes â a much tougher sell. To be sure, as the recent Kuwait oil pipelines deal showed, attracting global capital into some critical infrastructure will still go ahead. But sustained uncertainty will make the kingdomâs diversification push harder to pull off.
The Houthis in Yemen, whom the kingdom has been battling on and off since 2009, have demonstrated an alarming ability to strike deep inside Saudi Arabia, from airports to the Aramco head office, with no regard for civilian lives. Residents and potential visitors are unnerved. If the war with Iran intensifies again, foreign executives will be reluctant to even visit Saudi Arabia, let alone invest in it.
Lastly, efforts to diversify the domestic economy away from oil and build new industries are losing steam. After allocating about 8% of GDP to NEOM, once contract cancellations are included, the government has admitted a costly defeat. Plans for the 2034 menâs soccer World Cup are being scaled back, as are other giant projects. Yet the security crisis and higher fuel costs are pushing expenditure up faster than oil revenues. Government debt is still low by global standards, but is climbing. Higher defense spending will be vital, but wonât do much for economic diversification.
MBS sits in an uncomfortable position, facing the limits of his power. Efforts to get close to Trump by promising investments into the US and putting money into Trump family business interests havenât translated to leverage in Washington. Despite Riyadhâs $1 trillion US investment pledge, Trump remarked in March that MBS never imagined heâd be âkissing my ass,â a crude display of how roles have been reversed since the prince snubbed Trumpâs predecessor, Joe Biden. China, which brokered a rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023, is either unwilling or unable to help. And despite huge military spending, Saudi forces have struggled to deter their enemies.
The crown prince revealed a bold ambition to transform the kingdom, and the region, by 2030. The vision has never felt further away.

Nurdles found along the Danish coast are likely to originate from the spill in north-east England, according to the country's environment agency.
Masses of plastic pellets were found along the western coast of Denmark in September.
The Danish Environment Protection Agency has now confirmed tests carried out on the microplastics suggest they originated from the River Tyne spill in July.
It said the nurdles had the same characteristics as the one billion which had been spilled in north-east England and their arrival in Denmark in late September and early October - about 390 miles (630km) away - was consistent with "current patterns and circulation in the North Sea".
Signe Simonsen, the head of startup Race for Oceans Technology, first spotted the nurdles on the island of MandÃ¸ in Denmark on 26 September.
"There were just so many milk white plastic pellets," she said. "So many that I've never seen before in this area."
Simonsen said the discovery of the nurdles had made her "really sad" considering the "pristine" nature of the Wadden Sea.
Simonsen then said she drove along the coast of several nearby islands which are roughly on the same latitude as Newcastle.
She said there were nurdles "all over" where the tide had washed up.
Simonsen said she had collected nurdles from 10 different spots along the Danish coast and Sylt in Germany.
Simonsen, whose firm aims to detect microplastic pollution from drone images, then passed on some of her samples to the Danish Environment Protection Agency.
The agency, which tested the pellets alongside Aarhus University, said another factor which suggested the Danish nurdles were the same as those spilled in the River Tyne was the fact there were no other recorded spills in the area that could explain their presence.
Nurdles from the spill have washed up along the coast of north-east England including Teesside and Durham.
As of September, about 28% of the nurdles are believed to have been recovered.

The News
South Africa has proposed a new fiscal law in an attempt to shield its public finances from future populist governments as the treasuryâs current projections show debt is set to decline for the first time in nearly two decades. Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana framed it as protecting âhard-won gainsâ at a time when his party, the African National Congress, dominant since Nelson Mandela led it to victory in 1994, can no longer assume it will remain in charge after it was forced into building a coalition following the 2024 election.
Under the draft measure released alongside Wednesdayâs budget update, future governments could set their own targets such as debt-to-GDP ratio â a key measure watched by rating agencies â but an independent parliamentary oversight body would check if they were being adhered to. If it was decided that the government had deviated elected officials would have to explain their reasoning. Unlike laws in many other countries, South Africaâs prospective fiscal rules have no prescribed numerical ceiling on debt or spending; rather they would enshrine the principle that governments should keep to their announced plans.
In his statement to parliament, Godongwana said that government debt stabilized at around $366 billion, or 78% of GDP, after rising from around 24% in 2009. He told lawmakers that the budget deficit would start to decline as a proportion of GDP over the next three years. He also announced a last-minute decision to offer a second fuel-price relief package costing $600 million â further help for struggling motorists.
Economists say the numbers are good enough to warrant a credit rating upgrade. Gina Schoeman of Citi says the US bank sees a shift as âprobableâ but more likely to come in the first six months of next year rather than in the next few weeks.
Know More
South Africa first floated the idea of this fiscal anchor in March 2025, when the treasury published a discussion paper that presented two options: The establishment of a numerical target, which is more conventional, or an approach that weds governments to their own announced goals.
Godongwanaâs approach puts him at odds with the IMF, which argued earlier this year that a âfiscal rule, anchored in a prudent debt ceilingâ would bolster South Africaâs credibility. But while the idea is becoming more popular in Africa, there is no guarantee that setting a specific target works. Both Ghana and Kenya have missed fiscal targets with the former hit by pre-election slippages in 2024, and the latter suffering under revenue shortfalls, punishing interest payments, and repeated budget overruns.
Tiisetsoâs view
The treasuryâs effort to lock in the progress in reining in spending rests on an optimistic premise that letting politicians explain themselves will keep them in line. The flaw in the proposed anchor is that South Africaâs fiscal problems have never been short of explanations.
Since the 2009 financial crisis, Africaâs biggest economy went on a spending frenzy, running deficits, racking up debt and offering a rich menu of excuses â ranging from global crises, sluggish growth, state capture and COVID-19. That is not to say these explanations were not valid. But debt rose anyway, from 24% of GDP in 2009 to nearly 80% last year.
The draft law asks future governments to disclose, assess, and explain. Worse still, it requires each administrationâs fiscal plan to be âconsistent with the electoral mandate.â Thatâs disappointing. For one thing, imagine an election campaign fought on populist policies such as raising welfare grants and public sector hiring sprees. An incoming government would simply write those ambitions into its fiscal plan in keeping with the proposed measure. A cascade of ratings downgrades will follow, bond market investors would demand higher risk premiums and the economy would take a hit after spending commitments were already made.
Granted, governments bend or break hard numerical laws when politics demand it, as is the case in Ghana and Kenya. In fact, a 90-country study by the Bureau for Economic Research, a South African think tank, shows half of the countries broke their own debt-ceiling rules. If politicians can toss out hard and visible targets, why would anyone expect them to feel constrained by a law that only asks them to explain?
Room for Disagreement
Godongwana argued that the disadvantage with setting specific targets is that they lack flexibility and require well-defined escape clauses if economic circumstances change and his proposal takes that into account.
âMost importantly, it helps to ensure that developmental priorities and constitutional obligations are pursued at a pace that public finances can sustain,â he told lawmakers.
Michael Grobler, fixed-income strategist at Ashburton Investments, echoed this sentiment, writing in Business Day that âits appeal is flexibility. Shocks are inevitable, and a rigid annual target can force damaging cuts in a downturn or encourage decisions designed only to hit a number.â

Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties.
The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips.
"Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said.
Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum.
Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera.
He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020.
His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa.
On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges.
He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs.
"The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge."
He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency.
The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs.
Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private."
He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration.
"That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added.
On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe.
Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment.
Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information.
Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well.
Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration.

A Â£2m fund has been launched to help businesses switch their vehicles to greener vehicles, Bradford Council has announced.
Reform UK council leader Stephen Place said it would help businesses counter the rising cost of petrol and diesel as well as modernise their fleets.
The funding is part of Bradford Council's Clean Air programme, which will allow businesses to apply for up to Â£16,000 in support.
Announcing the fund at the Scale Up Bradford event on Tuesday, Place said it would help businesses invest in cleaner, more efficient technology to "future proof their operations for years to come".
Earlier this month, Place said he was committed to scrapping Clean Air Zone (CAZ) charges as it had a negative impact on businesses.
He accepted the move would have "quite a lot of legalities surrounding it" but said the council would "work to run it out naturally".
Funded by the Labour government, the Zero Emission Grant Programme will be targeted at small businesses, charities and organisations, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Businesses will be able to apply for up to Â£16,000 to improve heavy-duty vehicles and Â£4,500 for light-duty vehicles.
Bradford Council said the fund would provide practical support to help businesses remain competitive while adapting to new vehicle technologies.
"We want to help organisations to upgrade their fleets and position themselves for future success," said Place.
"I hope that this will appeal to tradies, they are the people out there every day keeping the nation moving."
Petrol and diesel prices have risen significantly since the US-Israel war with Iran.
Currently the average price of petrol in the UK is 173.2p per litre, while diesel costs 199.9p per litre.
Mark Casci, of West Yorkshire Chamber of Commerce, welcomed the plans and said a lot of businesses were looking to "decarbonise" their vehicles.
"Every large business with a fleet is looking at this issue very carefully, it is very much on their agenda," said Casci.
"It is the right thing to do and what customers want. It is driven by customer demand as well as moral responsibility."

Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).
A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.
Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".
The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.
The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (Â£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.
The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.
A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.
When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."
He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."
Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.
Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over â¬25m in unpaid VAT.
Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.
So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?
The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions â or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.
Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.
It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.
The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.
With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.
And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.
The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now.
Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties.
The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic.
"Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital.
"This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai."
The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works.
But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip.
Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms".
Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website.
It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets.
During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani.
The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products.
Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil.
"They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters.
Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East.
Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer.
Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil.
India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude.
In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties.
India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority.
Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
In that context, experts say Rubio's Jamnagar visit is aligned to three goals that the US appears to be pursuing: reducing India's dependence on Russian crude, encouraging greater imports of Venezuelan and American oil, and advancing a trade deal in which energy cooperation could become a key area of agreement.

Experts are testing out a new method that could see a way to tackle blue-green algae blooms.
The toxic algae is actually cyanobacteria rather than a true algae and can increase dramatically in heat, making people and animals sick when ingested.
Dr Sanjay Nagarajan, from the Institute for Sustainability and Climate Change at the University of Bath, took his child to the Warminster Pleasure Grounds in Wiltshire when he saw the lake there closed because of the bloom.
He and colleagues have since created a machine to help eliminate it from the water which he hopes he can make bigger and loan to councils.
More from Wiltshire
From January to October this year alone there have been more than 168,000 visits to the park in Warminster.
People would usually be able to take boats out onto the lake and an active model boat club is in the area.
However, while it tends to die off in wintry weather, the algae has been causing problems over summers and this year it has been closed to activities for several months, with warning signs up round it.
"Every year it gets worse and worse with climate change," said Kevin Whitehorn, the estates manager for Warminster Town Council.
"Water levels in the lake have gone down which meant the blue-green algae has grown even more than it has done in the previous years," he added.
Nagarajan, a chemical engineer, visited the park with his child and emailed the council saying he wanted to test something.
His colleague, Dr Madhubalaji Chegu Krishnamurthi, has been studying algae for a decade and said "there many good algae as well as bad algae".
"Whenever the bad algae grows more, because of the nutrients in the lakes, it will release the various toxins that are very harmful for humans."
Nagarajan, with colleagues and a PhD student, have put together a machine with a reactor that uses bubbles to get rid of the algae. The type of reactor is not new, but its use like this is.
As with many new inventions, in order to get the water in and out of the reactor, they have had to improvise. This devices uses a generator and equipment usually used for home beer brewing.
A small box at the side does a lot of the work - Nagarajan explained that it is the reactor.
"If you take a small drinks can, fill it up with some water, heat it up and then invert it into an ice bath, it gets crushed. That's exactly what happens inside the reactor and we call it cavitation.
"Whenever we are able to manipulate the conditions to produce these cavitation bubbles, these bubbles will actually be crushed or imploding.
"Once the implosion happens those effects will help in destroying the bloom."
Nagarajan said they have had positive results: "We've seen up to 20% degradation in terms of toxins and we've also seen a lot of the algal cells being destroyed because of the effect of cavitation."
The next stage is to get their results published and apply for funding to create a bigger machine they can loan out to councils.

1e54b71e448f.text: By — Hannah Schoenbaum, Associated Press Hannah Schoenbaum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/trump-administration-stopped-sharing-evidence-in-good-and-pretti-killings-minnesota-officials-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration stopped sharing evidence in Good and Pretti killings, Minnesota officials say Nation Oct 23, 2026 2:56 PM EDT The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers, state officials said in recent court filings. Minnesota officials sued President Donald Trump's administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings during Trump's immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don't have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don't trust the federal government to investigate itself. READ MORE: Renee Good's family sues U.S. government and immigration officials over her killing The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews. State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at the time that the state expected to receive "all the evidence." But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the U.S. Attorney's Office for Minnesota told her on Sept. 10 that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely "in light of challenges with D.C.," according to the documents. State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they "have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations." In a reply filed Tuesday, attorneys for the Justice Department argued it's within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities. They cited the department's rules for responding to record requests, known as the Touhy regulations, which apply only when formal legal proceedings are underway. The attorneys said there was no active court case when Minnesota made its requests. READ MORE: Minnesota prosecutors obtain long withheld evidence in probe into fatal shootings of Good, Pretti Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good's clothing, the cell phone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view. An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, while she was leaving a Minneapolis protest on Jan. 7. Bystander video shows Good in the driver's seat of an SUV, repeatedly honking the horn, when masked immigration officers order her to step out of the vehicle. She starts to pull forward, and an officer standing in front of the car fires at her windshield. The officer, now standing about an arm's length from the open window on the driver's side, fires twice more, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others. Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense. Good's death and that of Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who was killed weeks later by a federal officer in Minneapolis, ignited nationwide protests against the Republican president's immigration enforcement efforts. No criminal charges have been filed in connection with the fatal shootings. Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings, and a gun taken from Pretti before he was shot. The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.
In a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday, the justice department said the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.
Polls suggest the race between Sen Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.
The government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Sen Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan.
"I'm the one that said do it," President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.
Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it.
Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.
For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan".
The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year.
In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator.
"Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J. Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.
Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign.
In a separate interview with Courthouse News, he said that it is his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".
In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot.
Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit.
The Senate race in Alaska - which President Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections.
The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

More than 15,000 homes are without power as Storm Austen continues to batter southern England and Wales, with more bad weather expected this weekend.
The first named storm of the season brought gusts of up to 84mph (135km/h) to Jersey, while in southern England the wild weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.
In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.
On Saturday, Storm Boelo is forecast to bring more strong winds and heavy rain. The Met Office has put in place an amber warning for wind on Saturday and Sunday to cover parts of Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland.
Austen made landfall in the south-west overnight and tracked eastwards throughout the day. All schools on Jersey and Guernsey closed for the day and some in Cornwall were closed or started later than normal.
Ahead of the worst of the storm on Thursday afternoon, families were evacuated from a holiday park in Perranporth, Cornwall. Among them was Hannah Dawson-Turk, who told the BBC "the night before last, it sounded like our caravan was going to be ripped apart".
"The storm is very loud outside now, and the waves look huge from our windows," she said from a nearby hotel.
The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began.
Some ferry services between the UK and France were cancelled, while National Rail advised many routes were travelling at slower speeds.
In Brighton, onlookers filmed as a section of the West Pier fell into the sea as it was pummeled by large waves.
Stephen Royle, who lives opposite, said the waves rolling in were "enormous" and he is "shocked" by how much of the pier ended up in the sea.
The pier closed to the public in 1975 and fell into disrepair, but the ruined structure became a symbol of Brighton for some.
On the Channel Islands, fresh food shortages are expected in the coming days due to a lack of ferry services, according to the boss of the Co-op there.
"It's rare we get this level of disruption to storms backing up so quickly and probably a little bit more heavier than what we've had to deal with in the past," Mark Cox said.
Paul Aked, head of Jersey Met, said there were gusts in Guernsey up to 76mph (122km/h), equivalent to a severe gale, force nine. Residents told BBC Radio Guernsey that they could hear the wind rattling through their homes.
Jersey Airport said flights won't be running "until at least 17:00" while Cornwall Airport Newquay is warning passengers to check with their airline before travel.
Departure boards at Exeter airport were showing multiple cancellations.
Train operators across the country have warned that services are likely to be disrupted over the weekend.
The UK will continue to be battered by strong winds and heavy rain over the weekend as Storm Boelo follows on the heels of Storm Austen.
The Met Office has issued an amber weather warning for wind for much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England.
Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph.
The Central Lowlands could also experience disruption as strong winds funnel through the region.
Damage caused by strong winds could lead to further power cuts, while travel disruption is also predicted.
Yellow wind warnings also cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England.
Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph.
Alongside the strong winds, heavy and persistent rain is forecast across the UK on Saturday.
Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding.
The Met Office has advised the public to drive cautiously in strong wind, and to secure loose items outside their homes such as bins and trampolines.
People living or working in coastal areas were advised to take extra care during windy or stormy weather, including staying indoors as much as possible.
The storm came as the government released general advice for households to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.
The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "It's not about panic buying... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
Last month, the National Audit Office warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.
It said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.
Additional reporting by Joshua Askew and James Kelly

Mississippi authorities have released body camera footage showing how a toddler was fatally shot by a police officer responding to a report of shoplifting in a Walmart car park.
Kohen Wiley, aged one, was on his mother's lap in a moving car when officers surrounded the vehicle in the city of Senatobia on 14 June.
The state's attorney general found the policeman was justified in using force, and the officer's lawyer argued in a statement to the BBC that the driver was attempting to kill law enforcement.
The child's family disputes that the shooting was justified. Their lawyer, Ben Crump, has called the police response "excessive from the very start".
Crump said an allegation of shoplifting "does not warrant the death" of a child.
Kohen Wiley was riding in the vehicle with his mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and another woman at the time of the incident.
Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed to the BBC's US partner CBS that Hunter Foster, the officer who opened fire, had resigned.
The Senatobia Police Department did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for confirmation.
The footage released by Mississippi authorities on Thursday shows a first-person perspective of the officer who opened fire.
After being told by a staff member that suspected shoplifters were getting away, five law enforcement officers run towards the car with guns drawn.
The vehicle reverses, crashing into a parked car, before pulling forwards.
The officer wearing the body camera raises his gun and aims it at the moving vehicle as he runs closer, shouting: "Stop!"
As the car closely passes the officer, he fires his gun, shattering the passenger-side window.
Four gunshots can be heard, as police command the driver to stop. The car continues to drive off slowly through the car park.
CCTV video from the storefront appears to show that at the moment the policeman opens fire, another officer is standing near the front of the moving vehicle.
"The driver of the vehicle was attempting to kill those 5 officers," Martin Zummach, an attorney representing the officer, said in a statement to the BBC, adding that his client "had no choice but to discharge his weapon".
"We are very sad for the loss of life," Zummach said. "But the outcome of the investigation was not only expected, but it was overdue."
The child's mother, Wiley, has denied she and her friend stole nappies from the store. No charges have been filed against them.
The boy's death has sparked protests and vigils in Mississippi.
At a news conference, relatives demanded accountability.
"After what I've seen today, I'm having a difficult time understanding the word, 'justified,' said LaSandra Williams, Kohen Wiley's grandmother.

7167973faba2.text: The Trump administration sued Alaska on Thursday to delay certification of election results if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. Why it matters: The race between incumbent Sullivan, Democrat Mary Peltola , and retired teacher Dan Sullivan has been marked by controversy, with Republicans accusing Democrats of trying to confuse voters by planting a candidate with the same name. Alaska's use of ranked-choice voting, which eliminates candidates in rounds if no one gets 50% of the initial vote, complicates matters. "An election result may be impacted by voter confusion if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election," the lawsuit , filed in Alaska District Court, states. Zoom in: Because of a previous Alaska Supreme Court decision and Sullivan's name already being on the ballot, the administration contended in the lawsuit that the only means to ensure that the winner of the race is voters' choice "is to ensure that the certification is not impacted" by his candidacy. The lawsuit requests a delay in certification until after an investigation determines "whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan." What they're saying: "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. "Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters." The White House referred Axios to the DOJ. Catch up quick: The retired teacher Sullivan will appear on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. after the state's Supreme Court ordered the state's Division of Elections to include him in the race in June. Senator Sullivan will appear as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent," per the state's sample ballots. Sullivan has argued his candidacy is not a sham, and Peltola's campaign has denied any involvement with his run. The intrigue: The race is among those being closely watched as Democrats appear to be making inroads in red territory . The administration acknowledged the tight race in its lawsuit, saying "there is a realistic chance" that the non-incumbent Sullivan's presence on the ballot could tip the scales for Peltola. Flashback: In the primary, Senator Sullivan collected around 41% of the vote, versus Sullivan's 2.5%. Peltola earned 49.5% Cook Political Report currently rates the race as a toss-up. Reality check: Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller tells AP that the Alaska suit won't survive long, since the statute "simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification." By 2075, the vast majority of the world’s shallow coral reefs could cease to function as both critical habitat for marine life and a lifeline for hundreds of millions of people who rely on them.
According to a new assessment by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, 96 percent of the planet’s 127 major warm-water reefs are now classified as critically endangered, primarily due to heat stress induced by climate change. These ecosystems—which people depend on for food, livelihoods and protection from storms and flooding—include the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System in the Caribbean and the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific Ocean.
“They are at extremely high risk of collapse in the next 50 years,” said Mishal Gudka, the
For coral reefs, collapse means losing most, if not all, of their living hard corals that build and maintain their defining three-dimensional structure. As vibrant coral communities disappear, so do the fish and other marine life that live amidst them. Eventually, the reef becomes rubble covered in algae. “It’s effectively degraded into a different type of ecosystem,” Gudka said.
This is the first time the International Union for Conservation of Nature has produced a global assessment of coral reefs as part of its Red List of Ecosystems initiative, designed to guide and encourage conservation efforts before irreparable loss occurs. And its findings are “alarming,” said Susanne Pedersen, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s director of the Centre for Science and Knowledge.
“It must serve as a renewed call to action on climate change and other drivers of biodiversity loss to save the world’s coral reef ecosystems,” she said during a news conference Thursday at the United Nations biodiversity summit known as COP17.
The two-week conference is being held in Yerevan, Armenia, where representatives from nearly 200 countries are taking stock of their progress toward achieving a set of 23 targets outlined in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The landmark international agreement, adopted in 2022, is aimed at halting and reversing biodiversity loss through commitments such as conserving 30 percent of the world’s land, inland waters and marine areas by 2030, restoring degraded ecosystems and reducing pollution.
But several recent reports indicate countries are falling behind on their commitments, especially when it comes to conserving marine ecosystems. More than 90 percent of ecosystem restoration efforts are occurring on land in comparison to just 2 percent in coastal and marine areas, according to a joint report, released Friday, by the Society for Ecological Restoration and the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity.
Changing the trajectory for coral reefs outlined in the latest Red List assessment is vital. At least a quarter of all marine species, including thousands of species of fish, live and feed on coral reefs.
“The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people,” Gudka said at the press conference in Yerevan.
As global temperatures rise, the intervals between marine heat waves are shrinking, leaving reefs less time to recover in between. Even under a moderate warming scenario, the new global Red List assessment for coral ecosystems projects that within the next 50 years, these events will occur too frequently for most reefs to withstand.
When corals become too hot, they expel the algae living within their tissue that provides them with much of their food and color. The invertebrates then turn white in a process called bleaching. If water temperatures cool down fast enough, corals can recover. But if not, they eventually die. Already, that trend is accelerating and taking a toll.
From January 2023 to September 2025, during the world’s fourth global bleaching event, more than 80 percent of the world’s coral reefs in at least 83 countries and territories were impacted.
In Florida, a record-breaking marine heat wave in 2023 wiped out most colonies of two important reef-building species: staghorn and elkhorn corals. Both have since been deemed functionally extinct there, meaning there are too few left in the wild to reproduce naturally and they can no longer help build or sustain reef ecosystems.
In many places, including the Caribbean, climate change and other local pressures exacerbate one another.
“Rising sea temperatures are adding to the damage caused by overfishing, pollution and poorly planned coastal development, making it harder for reefs to recover after each disturbance,” said Tadzio Bervoets, from Sint Maarten, who was not involved in the assessment. He is a Caribbean coral researcher for the Coral Restoration Consortium and the executive director of a marine conservation organization in Jamaica, the Alligator Head Foundation.

She has condemned Ramaswamy for the ad. "I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I'm complaining about," she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio. A message seeking comment was sent Friday to her campaign. The ad has stirred significant reaction, including from President Donald Trump, who said it was like "hitting pay dirt." At a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump told the crowd Ramaswamy called him to ask for advice. "You've got to ride with it," Trump recalled telling Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate. Trump expressed jealousy that he didn't have such a strong ad to run during his own campaigns. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on the deeply personal attack ad in Ohio Other Republicans have been critical. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine criticized Ramaswamy and said the ad should be taken down. "It's wrong to run this ad," DeWine said Thursday. According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. Viruses may be minuscule, but one could have influenced major differences between human and chimpanzee brains.
Millions of years ago, a virus left DNA behind in an African ape’s genome, and the genetic material stuck around in modern day chimps. Those ghosts of infections past appear to influence genes involved in neuron development, which may help explain how human and chimp brains ended up so different, researchers report October 23 in Science Advances.
Compared with the brains of their chimpanzee kin, human brains are three times larger and more cognitively powerful. Yet “most of their protein-making genes are very similar,” says Johan Jakobsson, a neuroscientist at Lund University in Sweden. In the absence of large differences in the genetic code, Jakobsson and his colleagues decided to look at the parts of the human and chimp genome that control when and where genes are turned on or off.
Changes in gene regulation can come from viruses. Some viruses called retroviruses insert their own DNA into their hosts’ genomes to command host cells to build more viruses. But those parasitic bits of DNA can linger long after an infection. If this happens in reproductive cells, the viral DNA gets passed down with the host’s DNA.
These leftover bits, called endogenous retroviruses, no longer code for the production of infectious viruses, but they can have a big impact on the host’s biology — especially if they make copies of themselves across the genome. And they have. Such viral remnants make up at least 8 percent of the genomes of humans and chimps alike. More generally, these DNA leftovers have been linked with some major evolutionary events, such as the evolution of the mammalian placenta.
Jakobsson and his colleagues focused on a particular viral vestige in chimps. The holdover came from an infection in an ancestral African ape somewhere between 5 million and 7 million years ago. In chimpanzees, the viral DNA had stuck itself into the genome at 158 different locations. However, it is curiously absent in humans. It’s still unknown why.
The researchers wanted to know how that exact pathogen footprint might affect chimpanzees’ brains compared with those of humans. Working with chimpanzee stem cells, they removed the viral DNA using CRISPR, a gene editing technology that allows for precise, targeted cuts in DNA. Once the viral DNA was gone, a nearby gene called LINC00662 — normally silenced in chimpanzees — turned on, making RNA the team could detect. This matches the normal condition in human brain cells, in which LINC00662 is active. The team also used CRISPR to shut off LINC00662 in the human cells, matching the silenced condition seen in chimpanzees.
When LINC00662 was active in chimp or human cells, the researchers noticed activity boosts to other genes that may be important to brain development — such as genes involved in the development and maturation of neurons and in making new neural connections. It’s not yet clear exactly how the viral DNA’s shutdown of this brain gene network affected the biology of chimpanzee brains. However, this genetic difference may have contributed to a divergence in how human and chimpanzee brains evolved, Jakobsson says. “Our findings show one way an ancient viral [DNA] insertion could create a lasting difference in how a gene is regulated in humans and chimpanzees,” Jakobsson says. Other genetic and environmental changes could be involved in the puzzle as well, he says.
Researchers have previously looked to single letter swaps in DNA to help explain how humans and chimp brains drifted apart in their evolution. But the new study highlights that creatures can rack up genome changes in other ways, says Giorgia Modenini, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Padua in Italy who was not involved with this research.
The researchers do a convincing job of showing that these particular viral leftovers influence developmental differences between human and chimp neurons, says Ravinder Kanda, an evolutionary geneticist at Oxford Brookes University in Oxford, England. “They’ve proved that absolutely. How far that goes, I don’t think we can quite say yet.”
It could be that other controls on genes’ activity are also involved or that this particular ancient lever-puller may represent just a sliver of the viral holdovers that have shaped brain development, Kanda says. “I think there are many, many more retroviruses to be discovered, and at the moment we’ve only touched the tip of the iceberg.”

The News
Casino operators and sports betting companies have spent record amounts on campaign donations and on lobbying in Washington thus far this year, hoping it will help win back millions of bettors and gambling dollars that prediction markets have lured away.
Sportsbook operators, including FanDuel and DraftKings, have funneled more than $80 million into state senate and congressional races, via Win for America, a PAC launched in November 2025. The casino industryâs primary lobbying group, the American Gaming Association, has spent a record $2.06 million through September â the biggest lobbying spend by the group since 2013, when online gambling was reinstated after being banned in 2006.
Prediction markets and some of their executives have also been spending on local elections and on lobbying â primarily spending on the campaigns of politicians who oversee and shape their regulatory body, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Kalshi executives, including co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, have contributed more than $1.6 million directly to campaigns and to PACs supporting both political parties â nearly as much as the $1.79 million, including $1.28 million to outside firms, the company has spent on lobbying thus far this year. Polymarket has spent $270,000 via outside lobbying firms this year, and has made a $1 million donation to a Democratic nonprofit, according to a private remittance document seen by Reuters. And a new PAC, Coalition for Prediction Markets, backed by Kalshi, along with prediction market operators Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com, and Underdog have spent an additional $200,000.
âKalshiâs political giving reflects our strong relationships with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle,â John Bivona, Kalshiâs head of federal government relations, said in a statement, adding that their giving reflects the companyâs belief that keeping prediction markets safe âisnât a partisan issue.â
Lobbying efforts are to âsupport the responsible development of federally regulated markets,â a Coalition for Prediction Markets spokesperson said. Polymarket declined to comment, and FanDuel, DraftKings, and Win for America didnât respond to requests for comment.
Know More
Prediction market companies are fighting against several state attorneys general, who argue that the sites operate as illegal online gambling operations and should be shut down, limited to non-sports betting or regulated on a state-by-state basis instead of by the federal agency.
Sports betting companies are hoping to retain their footholds in more than 30 states amid new scrutiny of the industry. Some recent studies have highlighted addiction problems, and some organizations have raised alarm bells that the rise in youth gambling is a public health crisis, which has motivated policymakers to propose legislation to regulate sports betting.
Four major sportsbooks â FanDuel, DraftKings, Bet365 and Fanatics â are also donating money to state races via Win for America â a super PAC that disperses money to the states via subsidiary partisan PACs, American Future and American Conservative Fund. Their aim is to fight tax hikes on gaming, and to expand the number of states that allow âiGamingâ products. Sportsbooks are also lobbying against legislation to regulate sports wagering on a federal level, such as the SAFE Bet Act, which would establish a minimum national standard for regulating mobile and sports gambling if it passed.
âItâs spooked a lot of legislators,â Brianne Doura-Schawohl, the director of Campaign for Fairer Gambling, told Semafor about state-level political giving efforts by sports betting companies. âTheyâre worried about their seats and their ability to continue to legislate, and if they pick a fight with [them], I believe so to speak, it could become an issue.â
The casino industryâs spending efforts are aimed at supporting or swaying policymakers to restrict prediction marketsâ operations, which they argue is eating into their businesses illegally.
There are âso-called âprediction marketsâ that state attorneys general across the country have declared to be illegal gambling operations,â the American Gaming Association said in a statement, adding that the gaming industry creates jobs and helps grow the economy. Prediction markets, it says, âare mocking congressional intent on sports betting, thumbing their nose at state and tribal law, allowing teenagers to sports gamble, and robbing the states of revenue.â
The traditional casino operators and the sports betting companies are also lobbying in Washington for tax relief. They want to be able to deduct 100% of their gambling losses from their taxes, a shift currently written in the FAIR BET Act, that recently passed through the Ways and Means Committee. At least six cosponsors of the bill have received political contributions from sportsbooks. Casino operators have also donated to individuals on the Ways and Means Committee.
Eleanor Mueller contributed reporting.

Silicon Valley has decided to build a better dog.
Warhound, a new defense technology company, has launched with $200 million in seed funding from investors including Sequoia Capital to create dogs genetically engineered for military use.
The company is a collab between Anduril and Colossal Biosciences, the biotech startup looking to bring back the woolly mammoth, and aims to use Colossalâs genetics platform and Andurilâs defense tech to genetically modify and clone military working dogs. The homegrown super-dogs would replace foreign-bred combat and security dogs, primarily Belgian Malinois and German shepherds. The US Department of Defense maintains about 1,600 military working dogs today. If they can pull it off, itâll be a rare reshoring win for the Trump administration.

Rodriguez, Associated Press By — Claudia Lauer, Associated Press Claudia Lauer, Associated Press By — Amy Taxin, Associated Press Amy Taxin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/immigrants-seeking-u-s-citizenship-targeted-in-trump-administrations-illegal-voting-crackdown Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown Politics Oct 23, 2026 1:15 PM EDT SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Most of the immigrants targeted by federal authorities in California this week for alleged voter fraud had applied for U.S. citizenship and now face charges related to lying on forms or during interviews. Those charges could lead to years in prison and thwart their efforts to naturalize. One of them is José Antonio Bañuelos-Díaz, 42, who applied for citizenship in October 2025 after living in the country for 40 years and spending his entire adult life as a legal permanent resident. The federal government has alleged in charging documents that he improperly claimed to be a citizen in 2007 when registering to vote, then later lied about it on his immigration paperwork. The government hasn't accused him of casting a ballot. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
