Bañuelos-Díaz told The Associated Press he had no idea he had registered to vote until he was arrested Monday outside his Los Angeles home, though he recalls getting a driver's license around 2007. In California, people are prompted to register to vote when applying for a driver's license. "I have never voted because I know I can't vote," he said. "If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later." READ MORE: Justice Department charges more than 2 dozen foreign nationals in California sweep targeting noncitizen voters He was released from custody after his arrest but faces up to five years in prison if convicted. Federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents in California in a crackdown on people accused of illegally voting or registering to do so. As of Thursday morning, the government had filed charging documents in 10 of the 28 cases, offering additional details about how authorities relied on voter registration data to pursue broader criminal charges around immigration status. Most of the immigrants charged in California have lived in the country for at least five years, and some of them for decades. They registered as Republicans, Democrats and independents, according to voter data, and they could face deportation if they lied on their citizenship application. Lying on immigration forms carries a heavier sentence than illegal voting Immigrants convicted of illegally voting in the United States face up to a year in prison. Those convicted of lying on applications to become American citizens face up to a decade. The Justice Department said in a statement that six people would be charged with voting as a noncitizen, a misdemeanor. The 22 others were facing a combination of felony charges including lying on their naturalization application during interviews or on voter registration forms. In one case, Homeland Security agents arrested Pamele Arbues Line immediately following her Oct. 15 naturalization interview in San Diego. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say In charging documents, the federal government said Line had allegedly registered to vote five times and had submitted ballots in several elections but said in her paperwork and in the interview that she had never voted or claimed to be a U.S. citizen. She later admitted to registering to vote while getting her driver's license renewed last year and said she voted once, according to the charging documents. Line, who is from the Philippines, told authorities she thought she was a U.S. citizen because her mother had become naturalized after they moved to the United States more than four decades ago. But Line, now 56, was 19 at the time and not covered by her mother's citizenship, according to the government. She learned she was not a citizen in June when she went to get a renewed Social Security card, and she told agents she applied for naturalization the same day, according to the documents. She faces at least 10 years in prison if convicted of two charges. Trump tackles alleged noncitizen voting as midterms near The cases are part of a Trump administration effort to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. The Department of Justice has sued California for not complying with a request to verify the citizenship of roughly 20,000 registered voters it says may be noncitizens. California, which has more than 23 million registered voters, has argued the state complies with federal law and that the Trump administration's numbers are likely significantly inflated. In June 2013, torrential rain spurred one of the worst flooding events in Canada’s history. Sadie Vipond, who grew up in Calgary along the Bow River, was just a young child at the time when she and her family had to flee their home. “That was pretty scary with the evacuation,” she recalled.
Her family was among thousands forced to evacuate as the city declared a local emergency. The disaster was the costliest Calgary had ever experienced, with $1.7 billion in insurable damage, and many residents—including Vipond—still carry that trauma to this day.
Vipond is now a 20-year-old university student studying environmental science at the University of British Columbia. Next week, she will be sitting inside a courtroom in Vancouver telling her story of how extreme weather and climate change have affected her health and quality of life.
She will not be alone. More than a dozen other young Canadians will also be in court testifying in a historic climate change trial against their federal government. It will be the first time in Canada, and one of the first times anywhere in the world, that a national government faces a full evidentiary trial over the adequacy of its climate policies in a case brought by youth activists.
The trial, which starts Monday, is happening against a backdrop of warnings that the climate crisis is accelerating and that in just a few short years warming will exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit that countries agreed to strive to avoid surpassing. Current climate policies are off track to achieve the Paris Agreement objectives, and some countries like Canada and the United States are doubling down on fossil fuel production while at the same time rolling back measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and advance green technologies.
Activists around the world have turned to the courts in recent years in pursuit of accountability. Last year the International Court of Justice delivered a landmark advisory opinion affirming that governments have legal obligations under existing laws to do their utmost to act on climate change in accordance with the best available science.
Now that guidance, and the strategy of pursuing climate accountability through the courts, faces a critical test in a case putting one of the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitters and oil and gas producers on trial.
The case, La Rose v. His Majesty the King, challenges Canada’s climate policies, specifically the Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and its 2030 climate plan. The 2021 Net-Zero act establishes a legislative framework for Canada to emit no greenhouse gases by 2050 beyond the amount removed from the atmosphere, requiring the government to set interim emissions reduction targets and develop plans to implement them.
The lawsuit argues that this legislation, as well as Canada’s 2030 reduction plan, enable a “trajectory that is inconsistent with a safe climate system.” Youth plaintiffs say this violates their constitutional rights, namely the rights to life, liberty and security of the person under section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They seek not only a court declaration that their rights have been violated, but also an order for the government to develop and implement a science-based plan for rapid decarbonization.
The young activists filed their case in 2019, launching it during a Fridays for Future climate rally in Vancouver attended by an estimated 10,000 people, including environmental activist Greta Thunberg. The suit had originally targeted a wide range of government conduct, inspired by a similar youth-led case in the U.S. that ultimately never made it to trial.
After a federal court initially tossed out the Canadian case, an appeals court allowed the plaintiffs to amend their complaint by honing in on a specific action or piece of policy. The revised case was greenlit for trial, which is about to begin nearly seven years to the day since the suit was first filed.
Defendants include Canada’s federal government and attorney general. Government representatives did not respond to a request for comment on the case or the trial.
Plaintiffs are 15 young Canadians, including several indigenous youths. Like Vipond, they have all personally experienced extreme weather and health impacts linked to climate change, from extreme heat and floods to increasingly severe wildfires and toxic wildfire smoke.
“Every summer is now defined by how bad the wildfires are, by the extreme heat, by either drought or extreme precipitation and flooding,” plaintiff Lauren Wright said during a recent webinar. Wright enjoys farming and working outside, but climate change is making that at times uncomfortable and harmful to her health.
“When I’m out in the field, I can’t exactly take days off when the smoke is so bad that my lungs are burning and my eyes are blurring,” she said. “It’s a struggle to work in 30-plus degree [Celsius] temperatures outdoors in the sun without any availability to avoid the harms.”
“Carney Climate Carnage”
According to a scientific climate assessment report released by the Canadian government in early September, Canada has warmed twice as fast as the global average since 1970. Under current global climate policies, the country is expected to experience an average temperature increase of 5 degrees Celsius toward the end of the century.
Climatic changes already occurring today—extreme heat, catastrophic fire seasons, melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, more severe droughts, flash floods—will continue to intensify.

NORWAY, Maine â Susan Collins and Joe Manchin arrived right on time â Maineâs Republican senator and West Virginiaâs last Democratic senator, in matching red fleece, making a cheerful Wednesday stop a New Balance factory.

Manchin celebrated Collins. âShe is the soul of the senate,â said Manchin.
One day later, Troy Jackson, the Democrat challenging Collins, brought his own guest to Maine: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.. The future of agentic commerce hinges on the ability to know whether itâs a human or an AI agent thatâs making a purchase, and the tools to do that are arriving fast.
Proof-of-human technology, which can let a person vouch for the AI agents acting on their behalf, could keep bad bots off of websites without forcing platforms to block all of them. But it also opens up new possibilities for how business gets done online.
World, the startup co-founded by Sam Altman that scans peopleâs irises to verify theyâre human, this week announced new tools that let people link their proof of humanity to an AI agent.
The companyâs product chief Tiago Sada told me that could eventually lead to online sellers offering perks to verified agents, such as discounts and free trials. âIf you know that an agent is coming from a human, you can actually be much more generous,â Sada said.
E-commerce may get comfortable with agent transactions before other industries. Several large US banks are restricting interaction with third-party agents, in part because they canât tell which ones a customer actually authorized, Axios reported.

Reedâs view
The world finally suffered the kind of catastrophic security disaster that experts have been warning about.
OpenAI models helped discover a set of bugs that make the majority of the internet vulnerable to a powerful exploit. Then, a botched disclosure process gave hackers a head start on taking advantage of it before the world had a chance to react.
AI didnât create this problem. Human complacency did.
The bugs have existed for more than a decade, and PHP, the programming language that contained them, is 30 years old. A security researcher named Stefan Esser discovered the class of bug that roiled the internet this week back in 2004. And during a 2024 security audit by the PHP Foundation, this weekâs discovery was theorized, but the group didnât do anything about it; it deemed other issues more pressing, according to the foundation, the organization that maintains the software.
There are so many flaws in the aging, crumbling infrastructure of the internet. Only the ones deemed most critical have been fixed, but AI makes it possible to see all cracks more clearly and connect them together to catastrophic effect. But AI canât force people to devote resources to fixing whatâs wrong.
With some luck, the PHP bugs will create more inconvenience than economic and human damage. Thereâs still time for bold efforts to proactively overhaul the foundation of our software-dominated world. But it could also go very badly.
The same can be said for other effects of AI: In parts of society or in businesses, AI could exacerbate existing weaknesses, like extreme income inequality and the loneliness epidemic. But if policymakers work on solving those vulnerabilities, the technologyâs negative impacts might not be felt.
Technology always gets better and no policy or regulation will change that. What we can do is face the things weâve long neglected and make them stronger.
Notable
- âWeâre going to have a couple years where every single week itâs going to feel like the sky is falling,â Matthew Prince, CEO of cybersecurity firm Cloudflare, told Reuters as AI uncovers new software vulnerabilities.

When PFAS concentrations in drinking water fall below laboratory reporting limits, they are sometimes treated as “zero” in statistical analyses. But a new study published in Cell Reports Sustainability, which reanalyzed federal monitoring data, found that estimated PFAS concentrations in U.S. drinking water could be more than twice as high as calculations that treat results below laboratory reporting limits as zero suggest.
PFAS are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals used for decades in products ranging from nonstick cookware to waterproof clothing. Often called “forever chemicals,” they break down very slowly in the environment and have contaminated drinking water supplies across the United States.
“About 98 percent of the roughly 1.86 million individual PFAS test results in EPA’s January 2026 dataset were below reporting limits,” said the study’s author, Gehendra Kharel, an associate professor of environmental and sustainability sciences at Texas Christian University.
But even without an exact concentration, he said, “those records still tell us something”—that PFAS contamination of drinking water is far more prevalent than generally acknowledged.
For PFOA and PFOS, two of the most widely studied forever chemicals, the EPA sets a maximum allowable concentration of 4 parts per trillion.
By using statistical models to estimate concentrations below laboratory reporting limits, the researchers found that more sampling locations could reach or exceed the study’s comparison threshold of 4.05 parts per trillion, just above the EPA’s drinking water limit of 4 parts per trillion. Depending on the model, an additional 16 to 33 locations crossed that threshold for PFOA, and 4 to 25 for PFOS, said Kharel.
None of the newly identified sampling locations crossed the threshold for both chemicals simultaneously.
For Laurel Schaider, an environmental chemistry and engineering scientist at the Silent Spring Institute, who was not involved in the study, the findings highlight a broader problem with how scientists interpret measurements that fall below detection or reporting limits. “I think the paper raises an important point about how we think about results when we find that a chemical is not detected,” she said.
Schaider offered an analogy: Imagine you’re moving and packing all your belongings into boxes. Before shipping them, you might want to weigh each box to figure out how heavy the entire shipment will be. Some boxes might be heavy, while others might be pretty light. But assuming the lighter ones weigh nothing would underestimate the total weight of your belongings. “You don’t want to call those all zero,” she said.
Under the EPA’s Fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 5), public water systems across the U.S. are required to test their drinking water for 29 PFAS chemicals. Water suppliers collect samples and send them to EPA-approved laboratories, which use specialized equipment to measure the concentrations of these chemicals.
The EPA then receives the results, which help it assess how widespread PFAS contamination is in the nation’s drinking water. But the tests have limits. When a concentration falls below the reporting limit, the result is reported as below that threshold rather than a precise number. That does not necessarily mean the chemical is absent from the water. “Simply substituting zero is not the best way to handle a non-detect,” said Schaider.
How low a concentration a laboratory can measure reliably depends in part on its equipment and methods. “There are differences in the type of instruments. The instruments that can measure lower concentrations probably cost more,” said Schaider.
But as chemistry techniques improve, “we can be more sensitive across the board, and then we don’t have to make so many guesses anymore,” said Shelly Liu, associate professor of population health at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who was not involved in the study.
Still, finding higher concentrations in drinking water samples does not necessarily mean people are exposed to more PFAS than previously thought. While the researchers’ statistical models produced a higher estimate of combined low, under-the-limit PFAS concentrations, it did not measure individual exposure.
“That’s not the same as demonstrating underestimated exposure,” said Kharel. “We studied water entering distribution systems, not the water people actually drank,” he said.
The findings also raise questions about whether current reporting practices provide enough information about low levels of PFAS contamination, and whether more sensitive testing, where labs can reliably achieve it, could help close those gaps.
Agencies could clearly report the limits used and how often results fell below them, show estimates that account for below-limit results alongside zero-substitution averages, and explain the uncertainty of those estimates, said Kharel.
The EPA acknowledged the request for comment but did not provide a statement in time for publication.
Understanding how much PFAS is present in drinking water matters because exposure to these chemicals is already widespread. “Over 99 percent of people have PFAS in their blood,” said Schaider.

An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.
Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".
Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.
Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.
But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
Tanker hit 14 days ago
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.
Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.
Additional reporting by Charlotte Green

While a spoonful of sugar might help us gulp down a bitter-tasting antibiotic, it also may increase the damage that these drugs cause to the gut microbes.
In patients being treated for blood cancers, eating sugary items during antibiotic treatment was linked to a greater reduction in gut bacteria diversity than taking the antibiotics alone. The combination was also tied to the growth of gut bacteria associated with hard-to-treat infections, researchers report September 30 in Nature.
Cancer patients have lots of variation in their diets and take medications that can damage their microbiome. So, these patients provide a unique opportunity to study dramatic gut changes “that we believe are also relevant in the healthy context,” says Jonas Schluter, a microbiologist at NYU Langone Health.
Previous evidence separately suggested that antibiotics and sugars can disrupt the gut microbiome. But their combined effects, particularly in people at greater risk of infection, was unclear.
Researchers closely tracked more than 9,000 meals eaten by 173 people hospitalized in a treatment center to undergo blood-forming stem cell transplants. “Diet records are one of the biggest black boxes in a lot of diet microbiome studies,” since meals are often self-reported, says Tiffany Weir, a microbiologist at Colorado State University in Fort Collins, who was not involved in the research.
Standardized hospital meals allowed researchers to measure multiple days’ worth of food intake down to the gram, then compare the amounts of various nutrients eaten with bacterial diversity data obtained from stool samples.
For every additional 100 grams of sugar (the equivalent of 2.5 cans of Coke) that patients on antibiotics ate in the two days before sampling, the team found a 24 percent decrease in bacterial diversity. Consuming sweets and sugary beverages during antibiotic treatment was also associated with blooms of Enterococcus bacteria, which can be drug-resistant and are linked to difficult-to-treat infections associated with longer hospital stays and higher mortality.
“Some bacteria, sometimes, survive antibiotics, or perhaps more dangerously, they are resistant to [them],” Schluter says. By giving these bacteria the “universal resource for life, which is simple sugars, we are exacerbating their dominance. It’s almost like burning down the rainforest with a lot of fire, and then trying to extinguish the flames by putting in more petrol.”
The researchers also exposed mice on standard or sucrose-rich diets to a single dose of antibiotics. They found that the sugar exacerbated the enterococcal abundance after antibiotic exposure.
“Reducing sugar intake could be another way for patients to support their gut microbiome during antibiotic treatment,” says Sarah Berry, a nutrition scientist at King’s College London who was not involved in the study. Still, more research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to anyone on these drugs.
Schluter hopes that further studies and clinical trials can help uncover more about the exact relationship between sugar, antibiotics and the gut microbiome.
“You need to take antibiotics to fight infections, but you should also be aware that they have side effects to the microbiome,” Schluter says. “Now, we need to find strategies to mitigate this damage.”

Wyoming mechanic and amateur moonshiner Geno Stecks proudly details the modifications he's made at his two-bedroom residence to facilitate his hobby of distilling liquor in his own home.
"I turned my dining room into my shining room," boasted the bearded 66-year-old, who uses a power drill fixed to a bowl to mix some of his recipe.
Two years ago, he began tinkering with recipes for home-producing spirits. The pastime has taught him new skills and given him a signature product to share with friends and neighbors - "coffee-flavoured shine". It also happens to be illegal under US law.
"You know, keep quiet - don't make commercials or nothing," Stecks said.
But some home distillers hope they won't have to keep their hobby a secret for longer. The Supreme Court announced this week that it would reconsider the 1868 legislation forbidding the practice, and hobby distillers hope that their spirits will soon be treated like beer and wine, which are both legal to brew at home across the country.
Plaintiffs who brought the cases say Congress overstepped its powers in restricting distilling for tax purposes during the Reconstruction era. They want the highest judges in the country to agree.
But lawyers for the government argue that Congress's measure was lawful, and necessary to stop producers from avoiding taxes.
One lower court found the almost 160-year-old ban unconstitutional, but in a separate and similar case, another lower court came to the opposite conclusion. The Supreme Court will hear the case early next year and could make a ruling in the summer of 2027.
Currently, distilling alcohol in a private home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 (Â£7,460) fine or both.
"The particular law in question here is both absurd and unconstitutional," said lawyer Robert Alt, representing the plaintiffs. "It's interesting to note that this is a hobby which is as American as apple pie - and certainly a lot older."
Alt, Stecks and many proponents of the change point out that George Washington himself distilled spirits at home. Historian Daniel Pierce told the BBC that home distilling was first criminalised for revenue purposes, requiring anyone making spirits to pay a tax.
When federal agents began enforcing the law, small farmers who were distilling on the side as a way to make some extra money or to barter were left with few options.
"If you're a large distiller or something, you could afford to [pay the tax], but for most people, it was out of the question," Pierce said.
When the US implemented Prohibition - the nationwide ban on the production and sale of alcohol between 1930 and 1933 - it created a whole new market for illegal distillers, particularly moonshiners, Pierce said.
NASCAR, the racing sport, was born out of the high-speed, modified cars that bootleggers once used to transport illicit liquor and outrun the law.
Many continued their illegal distilling after Prohibition's end, often passing on family recipes in secret (or, at least, in tightly-knit circles) for generations.
Then moonshine and home distilling enjoyed a new renaissance in the early 2000s, he said, thanks to reality TV shows like Moonshiners, the internet and popular culture.
"You start to get this pretty dramatic revivalâ¦. in terms of home distilling," Pierce said.
Rick Morris, the founder and president of the Hobby Distillers Association, was one of the challengers who sued in Texas to change the law. He first entered the drinks industry working with soda machines and bottled water, then became a hobbyist home brewer of beer and wine with his wife.
They made a frustrating discovery when they tried to take the "next step" into distilling.
"It didn't make sense," he said. "I could make beer, I could make wine, both perfectly legally â¦ and it was frustrating that I couldn't take what I had already legally made and do one more step to it, to start to try to make a bourbon or a brandy."
The allure for Morris and many other hobbyists, they say, is the mechanics and innovation behind the process.
"There is a lot of science and details to get straightened out, but there is still a big vein of creativity in the art that goes into it - blending flavours and aromas and all that," said Ohio challenger John Bream, an aerospace engineer by trade.
He first took up the hobby when his wife gave him a home-brewing kit around 17 years ago. He set up his operations in their kitchen but "made too many messes and got kicked out into the garage".
"Through homebrewing, I became aware that going to the next level of distilling was illegal â¦ so I stayed away from it," he said.
But he realised he could be "part of the force for good" by joining legal challenges to the archaic law.
Not everyone is on board with the move, Courtney Armour, chief legal officer at The Distilled Spirits Council of the US, told the BBC. She worries about the challenges and dangers that come with home producing.
"The distillation process can be quite dangerous, including risk of explosion, burns, fires, and more," Armour said. "The spirits industry has a clear focus on safety and process management to mitigate these risks, but even in that careful environment there are still accidents, injuries and even fatalities."
And then there are health concerns that can arise when alcohol has not been produced properly.
"In a home-distilling setting, these dangers would not just be limited to the individuals engaging in the production but also their neighbors in the surrounding area," Armour said.
While home distilling remains federally banned, states like Missouri and New Hampshire have passed legislation allowing the production of certain amounts at home for personal consumption.
Attorney Alt pointed out that "alcohol, traditionally, has been an area of state regulation â¦ so this question of state versus federal authority is really at the very heart of this case".

Tomorrow Together, an AI-focused Democratic PAC, is moving into Senate races with $2.5 million in ads against Republican Sens. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roger Marshall in Kansas, according to an announcement shared first with Semafor.
The group, founded by Biden White House alum Rob Flaherty and former Bernie Sanders spokesman Karthik Ganapathy, is âfocused on building political support for AI regulation and ensuring voters trust Democrats on AI issues,â Ganapathy told Semafor.
The Ohio and Kansas ads paint Husted and Marshall as beholden to data center projects and âtech guysâ who want to âtake our land â¦ our water â¦ our quietâ and jobs. A second ad running in both Ohio and Kansas focuses on former Trump AI czar and venture capitalist David Sacks and his influence with the Republican incumbents.
âRepublicans gave Sacks a government job pushing AI data centers and blocking AI regulation. Sacks gets rich. His friends get rich. The only person who losesâ¦ is you,â the ad states.
Tomorrow Together previously announced $4 million in spending in House races in Wisconsin, Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Michigan.
Ashleyâs view
Concerns about AI and technology have simmered under the surface of American campaign politics for years, but have never been a fully salient everyday issue for voters until lately.
Democrats are trying to tune their messaging to ensure they are seen as more trustworthy on AI issues and paint themselves as the party that will pass AI regulation. The decision to jump into competitive Senate races just before the midterm elections shows that Democrats think they can break through to voters concerned about AI with this argument.
The real test will come if and when Democrats gain back power in Congress. The party will need to unite its different factions and bring along enough Republicans if it wants to tackle AI regulation, a highly difficult feat with a regulation-opposed Trump still in the White House.

b5d30be46f8f.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/2-ex-fbi-officials-charged-with-making-false-statements-about-hunter-bidens-laptop Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 2 ex-FBI officials charged with making false statements about Hunter Biden's laptop Politics Updated on Oct 23, 2026 2:45 PM EDT — Published on Oct 23, 2026 11:19 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Two former FBI officials were charged Friday with lying to Congress about their involvement in investigating Hunter Biden's laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election, the latest in a series of splashy and politically charged actions the Justice Department has undertaken ahead of next month's midterm contests. Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, former leaders of a since-disbanded task force set up to counter foreign election interference, appeared in federal court in Washington, where their lawyers pressed for a speedy hearing at which they could contest allegations that they lied to lawmakers by saying that they did not participate in FBI investigations of Biden. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The prosecution, a rare Department of Justice criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and peculiar saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race. It also comes amid a broader, backward-looking effort by FBI Director Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation's premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau's recent past that for years have animated President Donald Trump's conservative base. Floris' attorneys called her "a patriot" and said she has "served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years." "Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," her attorneys said in a statement. "It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election." Attorneys for Benavides accused the government of bringing "baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint." "This is another sad day for the Department of Justice," his lawyers said in an emailed statement. "But now we are in court, and the truth will come out: Brad Benavides is a true patriot who devoted his career to protecting this country and its people. These charges are a disgrace." A criminal complaint comes just before the midterms The case was filed 10 days before the Nov. 3 elections via criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have not yet presented the allegations to a grand jury for an indictment. The Justice Department has repeatedly struggled in high-profile cases to convince grand juries in the nation's capital to return indictments. READ MORE: Takeaways from Hunter Biden's deposition with Republican lawmakers During the former FBI employees' court appearance, both defense attorneys and the judge noted the unusual move to charge the case through a criminal complaint, which is more often used by prosecutors when they have an urgent need to take people into custody because, for example, they present a danger or a risk of flight. U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui remarked that it is "rare that we have charges this old coming in this nature." Faruqui set a preliminary hearing for next Tuesday over the objections of prosecutors, who pushed for more time given what the judge described as the "sword of Damocles" hanging over the defendants' head. The laptop discovery created turmoil in 2020 election The revelation of the laptop's existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump, the Republican incumbent, and Biden's father, Joe Biden, Trump's Democratic challenger, who went on to win the race. The laptop were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop about a year earlier. The criminal complaint aims to build on longstanding congressional Republican complaints about the FBI's handling of the laptop, including allegations that the bureau was not forthcoming to the public that the materials on it — including emails that showed discussions of the younger Biden's foreign business dealings — were authentic and not the product of Russian disinformation. The curious circumstances of the laptop's discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly at a time when the Trump administration's own intelligence community was Moscow that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump's behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens. Dozens of former U.S. intelligence officials signed a letter saying that the laptop bore the "classic earmarks of an Russian information operation." But Trump's then-director of national intelligence, John Ratcliffe, said in a letter to Congress that there was no proof foreign actors had anything to do with Hunter Biden's laptop. The FBI under then-Director Chris Wray subsequently backed up that assessment. Hunter Biden was charged with, and convicted of, gun and tax offenses during his father's administration. Joe Biden pardoned him in his final weeks in office. The case shines a light on an FBI task force on foreign intelligence The complaint alleges that in their capacity as leaders of the Foreign Influence Task Force, Floris and Benavides were deeply engaged in the investigations into Hunter Biden, and that Biden was a recurring subject

546f184245ee.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-files-lawsuit-to-block-possible-democratic-win-in-alaska-senate-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump says he ordered DOJ lawsuit over Alaska Senate race Politics Updated on Oct 23, 2026 2:27 PM EDT — Published on Oct 23, 2026 11:14 AM EDT President Donald Trump said he told his administration to file a lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida. The lawsuit centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman. The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate. The lawsuit Thursday by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. "The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections. The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set. The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused. Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people. The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course," campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. "Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska." Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses," said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Watch the segment in the player above. In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to "mislead:" voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot. "The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the DoJ statement said. The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed. The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department. Constitution gives states the power to run elections Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. "The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Muller said. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month." d11eeddd1aea.text: By — Shlomo Mor, Associated Press Shlomo Mor, Associated Press By — Sam Mednick, Associated Press Sam Mednick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israeli-military-says-2-soldiers-were-killed-in-the-west-bank-attack-that-also-left-2-gunmen-dead Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israeli military says 2 soldiers were killed in the West Bank attack that also left 2 gunmen dead World Oct 23, 2026 11:06 AM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning that also left two suspected gunmen dead, the military said, violence that is likely to heighten political tensions and security concerns ahead of Israel's parliamentary election next week. The army said two soldiers, Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, were killed and three others were lightly wounded during an attack by Palestinian gunmen. The attack took place near the Yehuda Junction outside the West Bank city of Hebron. The army said it had prevented a "terror attack against Israeli civilians" and that the two suspects, both Palestinians from Hebron, were armed with an M16 rifle and a handgun. It said the men arrived at an Israeli military position in the morning, triggering an exchange of fire lasting approximately 20 minutes, after which the gunmen were killed by Israeli troops. The army said its forces prevented the men from advancing further where the attack could have resulted in civilian casualties. READ MORE: Photographer attacked by settlers in the West Bank feels insulted by Netanyahu Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank, starting Friday. During a visit to the site of the attack on Friday, the prime minister said Israel would retaliate with a sweeping anti-terror operation in the Hebron neighborhood where the gunmen had resided. "We will evacuate the residents, we will go house by house, we will also remove the weapons there, and all the terror infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed," Netanyahu said. Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term in office — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza. Israel's government has warned of potential attacks by the country's "enemies" in the lead-up to the election. Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting Netanyahu later met with his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies in an emergency meeting, blaming Hamas for Friday's attack. "Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination," he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed. "I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery," he added. WATCH: 'Act of terror': U.S. condemns Israeli settler siege of Palestinian homes in West Bank Earlier in the day, Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians' freedom of movement in the West Bank. He and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, another far-right member of Netanyahu's Cabinet, both called for Israel's military to wrest control of the West Bank from the Palestinian Authority, though there was no evidence Friday to suggest the governing body had any ties to the gunmen. "There is no alternative to a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect the weapons, and eliminate the terrorists, exactly as we did in Gaza and Lebanon," Smotrich wrote on social media. Dozens are arrested in West Bank security operations Following the shooting on Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups. WATCH: Violence surges in West Bank as Israeli settlers escalate attacks on Palestinians It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns. Eyal Zamir, the Israeli army's chief of staff, said a "large quantity of ammunition was found" in a vehicle used by the gunmen. "This ammunition was intended to be used in a larger-scale attack," he added. Palestinian life is 'impossible,' says U.S.mo congressional candidate Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. It was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads. Roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays. U.S. Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander, who was in the West Bank on Friday, said the Israeli army's closure following the attack was an example of Israel enforcing an apartheid system on Palestinians. WATCH: Palestinian American family recounts siege of West Bank home by Israeli settlers "It's part of the effort to take more control, to make Palestinian life impossible," Lander, who was detained by Israeli forces on Wednesday, said in an interview. Yishai Fleisher, an international spokesperson for Hebron's Jewish community and a political candidate for the far-right Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, party, said Israel had the right to defend itself from a "hostile majority." The US Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating whether Corey Lewandowski, who was a top aide to former Department â of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, personally profited from his role, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
Lewandowski worked closely with Noem as a special government employee until March, when the two were both ousted after a series of controversies, including the fatal shootings of US citizens by immigration officers.
The probe is related to contracts the agency signed under Noem's leadership, a source told CBS.
The BBC has contacted Lewandowski's attorney, who told CBS his client denies any wrongdoing.
"Mr Lewandowski has not been contacted by the justice department regarding any investigation," his attorney, Adam Trigg, said.
Asked about the investigation on Thursday, President Donald Trump told reporters he had heard about it but did not know the details, adding, "I want my people to be honest".
"And if they're not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted," he said.
Lewandowski served as a campaign manager to Trump during his first presidential run in 2016 and helped advise his 2024 campaign.
DHS officials told Reuters that Lewandowski had approved some DHS contracts despite not having the legal authority to do so as a special government employee.
He also allegedly put certain grants and contracts on hold, including some involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the officials told Reuters.
Special government employees serve as temporary advisers to federal agencies and are given strict limits on how much they can work and what they can do.
The justice department took on the investigation after receiving a referral from the DHS inspector general's office, which is made up of lawyers charged with monitoring the agency's conduct and operations.
At DHS, Lewandowski served as Noem's de facto chief of staff.
Noem also faced a contract controversy. Shortly before she left office, lawmakers pressed her about the process she had used to award a $220m (Â£164m) advertising contract to two companies with ties to her and people in her inner circle.
The Wall Street Journal has reported, external that Lewandowski also allegedly tried to use his role at DHS for financial gain by asking Middle Eastern countries to hire him on the side to help with visa and other DHS issues.

52ab4932660e.text: By — Matthew Brown, Associated Press Matthew Brown, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/defense-attorneys-in-case-over-charlie-kirks-killing-say-they-need-years-to-prepare-for-trial Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Defense attorneys in case over Charlie Kirk's killing say they need years to prepare for trial Nation Oct 23, 2026 6:03 PM EDT Defense attorneys for the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk are suggesting a 2029 trial date because they say it could take them that long to prepare their case. Attorneys for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, said Thursday that the defense's proposed schedule was "absurd" and defendant Tyler Robinson was simply trying to delay. READ MORE: Utah judge decides Tyler Robinson will stand trial over Charlie Kirk's killing Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf has scheduled a Friday hearing to set a trial date. Robinson pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in last year's killing of Kirk while the ally of President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of several thousand people at Utah Valley University. The 23-year-old defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting, and his lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk's death. He could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted. Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with "Hey Fascist! CATCH!" and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out." Trump weighed in on the trial date in a social media post prior to the hearing. He said the case should be tried "within a month" and accused the judge of "taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to." Prosecutors said in court filings they anticipated a 17-week trial and said they would be ready by October 2027. But rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed the trial begin Jan. 31, 2028. Erika Kirk's attorney, Jeffrey Neiman, said the trial should start next October, the earliest date identified by prosecutors. "Under the Defendants' proposed schedule, Mr. Kirk's two children, who were one and three at the time he was murdered, will be six and eight years old by the time the trial concludes," Neiman wrote. "They will face the uncertainty of this criminal proceeding longer than they had their father in their lives." But Robinson's attorneys said in court filings this week that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They said they'll have to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson's life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and must devote "substantial time" to issues such as jury selection. The defense lawyers said they respected the court's attempt to set a "realistic trial date." Yet because it's a complex death penalty case, trying to predict when it will be ready for trial "is an exercise that, at this time, will necessarily be infected with false precision," they wrote in a document filed Wednesday. 8c919093e43f.text: By — Meg Kinnard, Associated Press Meg Kinnard, Associated Press By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-at-gop-rally-in-florida-revives-idea-of-military-intervention-in-cuba-after-iran Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran Politics Oct 23, 2026 5:40 PM EDT FORT MYERS, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country. Watch the rally and Trump's remarks in the video player above. Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days ahead of midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the U.S. war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries. WATCH: Cuban official on Trump's threats as tensions with U.S. rise "We'll do a little stopover," Trump said. "Actually, what we're going to do with Cuba is, we're going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal." Both Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would "be next" in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of U.S. military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island's former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous U.S. presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that "it looks like I'll be the one that does it." Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba has been a national security threat for years because of its ties to U.S. adversaries and that Trump is intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wants to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the U.S. could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island's current government. WATCH: Rubio says Trump prefers Cuba diplomatic solution, but says likelihood 'is not high' Moments after Trump spoke at the rally, Rubio posted on social media that "now is the time" for action on Cuba, addressing his post "to those who seek to create positive change" and urging them "to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA." Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a Sept. 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity. "The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn't have a functional economy and it's governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that's never worked," Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation. "We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they're facing," he said. "We're never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear." Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the U.S. side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government. During his address to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio — son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba's socialist leadership — was "deep into negotiations with Cuba," saying he would "not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep." Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries "will make a deal," adding, "I don't think we'll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly." Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington's decades-long economic embargo against Havana. Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk, and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have migrated, many to the United States. Kinnard reported from Columbia, S.C. CALERA, Ala.—Fenn Church knew what he had to do.
“I’m going to stand in front of that gate and say, ‘This is my home, and I’m not letting you drive through that gate,’” Church said on Thursday morning. “And then if they want to arrest me, they can handcuff me and take me to jail or run me over. But this is where I take my stand.”
For months, Church had fought Alabama Power’s effort to use eminent domain to secure access to his property in Alabama’s lower courts, arguing that the utility could easily use alternative routes to build a transmission line that would not be as disruptive to homeowners like himself in rural Shelby County, about a 45-minute drive south of Birmingham.
In September, that legal battle resulted in a victory for Church when Circuit Court Judge Jonathan Spann issued a temporary injunction preventing Alabama Power from accessing Church’s property. In his ruling, Spann found that Alabama Power, one of the state’s most powerful companies, had failed to follow the necessary procedures for condemnation of Church’s land outlined in state law.
Church was likely to succeed on the merits of his case, and without a preliminary injunction, he would be irreparably harmed, the judge wrote.
Spann also noted that an Alabama Power employee had testified in court that the route for the planned transmission line crossing Church’s property had been finalized with “no consideration” to zoning plans or the “development potential or suitability” of properties it would cross.
That unrebutted testimony made it likely that Church would be able to prove that Alabama Power’s siting of the transmission line was illegally arbitrary and capricious, Spann ruled.
Church’s victory would be short-lived. On Wednesday, in a 5-1 ruling, the Alabama Supreme Court issued an order granting Alabama Power’s motion to stay Spann’s injunction against it. The state’s highest court did not provide reasons for its decision.
“Alabama Power understands that property is personal, and we remain committed to treating property owners fairly and respectfully,” the electric utility said in a statement after the state Supreme Court ruling. “The Alabama Supreme Court’s decision allows work on this section of the transmission line to move forward, supporting a project that is an important investment in the security and reliability of the electric grid for the customers and communities we serve.”
Desperate in the wake of the high court decision, Church called his federal lawmakers—Sens. Katie Britt and Tommy Tuberville and Rep. Barry Moore. He didn’t hear back.
John Rich, a country music star and a Trump-appointed, so-called Special Envoy for American Homeowners, had also pledged support for Church’s cause.
“We can build out our energy infrastructure and treat landowners with respect simultaneously, and that’s what I intend on doing in this case,” Rich had initially said publicly. “About 200 yards away, there’s a wide open, clear-cut path that doesn’t involve driving bulldozers and trucks and 18-wheelers for the rest of eternity through this man’s property, right through his front driveway.”
But it wasn’t long before Church said he felt that Rich was hitting a roadblock somewhere in the administration.
“Somebody must’ve got to Trump and told him to back down,” Church said.
Hours after the Supreme Court ruling against Church on Wednesday afternoon, representatives of Alabama Power notified Church’s lawyers that its crews would arrive at the property between 7 and 8 a.m. to begin the work to which he’d long objected.
With few options left, and on Rich’s advice, Church turned to social media, calling on supporters to show up the next day.
“Tree cutting crews are coming to my front gate in the morning,” he posted. “Appreciate any support that anyone can give me standing at my gate in the morning!”
Within hours, the post had been viewed more than 100,000 times on the social media platform, eliciting dozens of comments from across the country.
Rep. Phillip Ensler, a Democrat running to become the state’s lieutenant governor, showed up Thursday morning to stand alongside Church. It wasn’t the first time he’d visited Church’s property in solidarity—the only public official to do so, according to Church.
“Alabama Power thinks they can just walk over anyone and everyone,” Ensler said. “They’re just trying to flex their muscles and intimidate people, and if they can do that to him and do it here, they can do it anywhere.”
Ensler and Church talked more as the nippy morning began to slowly warm. One by one, cars and pickup trucks rolled up Church’s driveway. Whenever the hum of an engine could be heard coming down Township Road toward Church’s front gate, the group would crane their necks toward the gravel entrance.
Each time, one of the men, this time Church himself, would approach the vehicle stopped just outside the gate.
“Hey there,” Church said, a smile stretched across his face. The driver of the truck rolled down his window.
“You’re not here to cut down my trees are you?” Church asked.
The man in the truck laughed. “No. I’m here to help you stop them if I can,” the driver said.
Church waved the man through, instructing him to park wherever he’d like and make sure he grabbed himself a Hardee’s biscuit. Soon, Church and the newcomer would rejoin the growing group ready to resist Alabama Power, and the wait would continue.
The Alabama Power trucks never came.
Instead, close to 8 a.m., Church and others looked to the sky. A faint buzz overhead had drawn their attention. Just above the towering pines, a drone strafed into view, pausing briefly around a hundred feet above Church’s driveway before flying away.
“I wonder if they liked what they saw,” one man said. Church and the others laughed.
A couple hours later, cameras on the southern side of Church’s property showed crews surveying and marking trees, having accessed the property via another route.

Boeing has almost completed the demolition of five buildings at its infamous Santa Susana Field Laboratory in Southern California, even as concerns mount among nearby families about potential health harms.
The buildings at the former Rocketdyne facility—where one of the worst nuclear meltdowns in U.S. history took place in 1959—were once used for Cold War-era nuclear energy research.
Larry Yee, the former chair of the LA Regional Water Quality Control Board, on Wednesday called the site “a mini Chernobyl in our backyard.”
Despite a groundswell of concerns about the process, the SSFL demolition at the lab between Simi Valley and Los Angeles began in late September. Four of the five buildings slated for demolition, all of which have sat unused for over 15 years, according to Boeing, have been brought down so far. The fifth demolition, at a site where more than 50 structures once stood, is slated to be completed this year.
Among the already leveled structures is “Building 55,” known in its heyday as the Nuclear Materials Development Facility, which for decades was a storage, handling and processing facility for “unspent fuel rods,” explained local historian William Preston Bowling.
“So they took fuel rods from all reactors from across the nation and took them to the Santa Susanna Field Laboratory and had them de-cladded and repurposed and shipped off for disposal at other sites,” Bowling said.
California’s Department of Toxic Substances Control told community members that the state Department of Public Health and the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission previously determined that remaining structures at the site are below or near background levels of radiation—what would occur naturally—and “pose no elevated risk to the public.”
Opponents of the current work dispute that finding.
“We don’t agree on the premise that these buildings were across the board uncontaminated,” said Jeni Knack, co-director of the grassroots organization Parents Against SSFL.
Instead, Knack told Inside Climate News, the DTSC has “accepted Boeing’s claim” that the site was safe to demolish.
In 2023, the California Court of Appeal ruled in Boeing’s favor on litigation brought by the nonprofit Physicians for Social Responsibility over the responsibility for oversight of the SSFL cleanup, determining that the demolition did not have to be approved by the state and is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).
Elizabeth Leslie-Gassaway, a DTSC spokesperson, did not immediately clarify what, if any, additional radiation readings were taken prior to the recent demolitions.
DTSC deferred questions related to dust control and air monitoring to Ventura County, which permitted the work. But according to Knack, when Parents Against SSFL approached Ventura County about oversight of the demolition, the group was directed to the DTSC.
During an inspection on Sept. 28, “DTSC observed Boeing conducting dust control mitigation and confirmed that demolition activities are not disturbing slabs or surrounding soil,” a DTSC official wrote Tuesday in a letter to Parents Against SSFL.
However, advocates argue that given the site’s well documented history of processing and storing of plutonium-239, which can cause cancer if inhaled or ingested, further protections for the nearby community—including the more than 120,000 people in Simi Valley—are critical. Group leaders have shared documents outlining the site’s history with state regulators.
“Is there contamination in these buildings? Almost certainly,” Michael Ketterer, a part-time faculty member in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at Northern Arizona University, told Inside Climate News after reviewing documents outlining the SSFL site and residents’ concerns.
“Does it cause an egregious situation on the local community? I don’t know,” Ketterer said. Not enough information on the radiation readings was available to determine the risks to people, he said.
Still, Yee, the former LA Water Quality Control Board chair, and others who have followed developments at SSFL for years, are worried the demolition puts people in the area at risk.
The Ventura County Air Pollution Control District does not require specific dust control measures, district spokesperson Karin Grennan told Inside Climate News.
She deferred questions about monitoring for radiation and broader environmental effects to the DTSC and other agencies. The DTSC did not provide additional comments this week.
“Facilities must take measures sufficient to comply with Rule 55 requirements, which restrict visible dust emissions beyond the property line,” Grennan said. “But facilities can select the specific dust control measures they implement.”

Ventura County said it has received complaints about potential dust-related issues but it has not been notified of emerging or ongoing health impacts as a result of the demolition.
Boeing declined to provide the cost of the demolition or specifics on the dust-mitigation or monitoring steps the company has taken, outside of noting that it would follow the law.
“As we have done and as work continues,” Joshua Barrett, a Boeing spokesperson, said, “we will follow the sitewide Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan, apply water for dust suppression, restrict access to authorized personnel and transport debris to an authorized offsite disposal facility.”
“Removal of these buildings is a key step toward the site’s ultimate open space use,” Barrett said.
The site is eventually slated to become a public recreation area, despite fierce opposition from groups like Parents Against SSFL and the Committee to Bridge the Gap, a nonprofit focused on nuclear policy.

6e9e40f119df.text: By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/oregon-father-who-killed-school-shooter-says-he-regrets-there-were-children-he-didnt-save Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Oregon father who killed school shooter says he regrets there were children he didn't save Nation Oct 23, 2026 5:19 PM EDT The Oregon man who fatally shot a teenage gunman to end a deadly rampage at an elementary school last week says he was the children's "last line of defense" and that he regrets not arriving soon enough to save them all. Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary, where the Oct. 15 attack occurred, said he feels like he failed the families of those who died. WATCH: What makes the Oregon school shooting different – and what can be learned "I want to apologize for not saving their babies, that's probably the biggest thing for me right now," Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting in an interview published Friday. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome. But there were ones that I didn't save." Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the school in Bend, Oregon, last week when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized. Police say another teacher threw her phone at the attacker and wrestled with him before Giamanco shot and killed him after following the gunman into the building. Giamanco said he dropped off his daughters at the school that morning before driving to work. A few hours later, the 36-year-old carpenter was passing the school again as he was heading home for lunch. He said he spotted someone wearing black and carrying a long gun fire shots into a pickup truck and at a person mowing the school's lawn before the shooter climbed a fence and headed toward the school building. Giamanco said "panic fled into my brain." He grabbed a .40-caliber handgun from his truck's center console and went after the gunman as he dialed 911. He asked the dispatcher to send help before hanging up his phone. "I said 'I'm sorry I have to go in. People are going to die,'" Giamanco said in the interview. 'This is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do' As he got closer to the building, Giamanco said, he lay on his stomach and used his elbows to crawl across the ground. "That's when I started hearing children pleading for their lives," he said. "And then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster. And I told myself: 'This is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do.'" READ MORE: Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a U.S. mass shooting Giamanco said he entered the school through a window that had been shot out. Peeking into a nearby classroom, he saw a teacher grappling with the shooter. He said he faced them both in profile, giving him an open shot. "I felt like I was the last line of defense between him and the rest of the children," Giamanco said. He swung the door open, stepped into the room and fired his gun. Both the gunman and the teacher dropped to the floor. The teacher bolted from the room as the shooter reached for his shotgun. "He was scrambling for his weapon," Giamanco said. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else." 'I was supposed to be there' Police have said Giamanco was carrying his gun legally in his truck and have credited him and the unarmed teacher who confronted the gunman with saving lives. A day after the shootings, President Donald Trump said that Giamanco was a "great hero" who "took care of business." A second teacher in the classroom, Becky Drury, said in a statement Wednesday that she lay on the floor, helplessly playing dead, after being struck at close range by a shotgun blast that nearly severed her left hand. The teacher who struggled with the shooter hasn't been publicly identified. Giamanco told the public broadcaster that she's "a real true hero" whose actions gave him an opening to kill the attacker. "I can't tell you what it feels like to take a life … but I can tell you that I genuinely feel like I was supposed to be there," Giamanco said. "If I wasn't there, I just don't know what would have happened." Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
