A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped.
The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.
The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra , which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.
He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.
Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category", and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.
Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.
The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.
But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.
It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.
The Argentinian president, though, insisted: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it" in an interview with local media Todo Noticias'.
The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine if the president had acted improperly.
Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".
And, in a TV interview, he insisted that those who invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday it was working to "protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people".
The exemptions could also boost Republican candidates in the midterms elections on 3 November, as many US voters list affordability and economic pressures as top issues.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race in Maine to keep her seat in the election, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
After trade talks collapsed this summer, the US and Canada started an escalating tariff war that has affected both sides of the border.
The White House, in a statement, said that starting 30 October the US would remove certain products from the list of Canadian goods it taxes, such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes.
It added those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets, waste products, among others.
The White House said the action reflects President Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade", as well as "offsetting the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada's discriminatory treatment".
The BBC has contacted the White House, US commerce department and trade representative for further comment.
Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said that Canada is "working very hard" on a â trade âdeal with the US.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal, but is willing to wait it out.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said, according to CBC.
Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met with members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.
So far, Canada has not commented on the White House's announcement.
LeBlanc's office did not immediately respond on Friday to the BBC's request for comment.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.
The reductions could be offset by raising levies on âother Canadian goods, the Journal reported.
In a statement Collins put out before the White House announcement, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said she had "secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".
"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she posted on X.
Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.
âMaine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the month-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.

f17e2c765a17.text: By — Genesis Magpayo Genesis Magpayo Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/why-experts-are-pushing-rfk-jr-to-release-a-federal-definition-of-ultraprocessed-foods Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Why experts are pushing RFK Jr. to release a federal definition of ultraprocessed foods Health Oct 23, 2026 4:24 PM EDT Significant delays in the Trump administration's effort to tackle the health risks of ultraprocessed foods have obstructed a pillar of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" agenda and caused growing frustration inside and outside the government. More than 100 science, medical and nutrition experts signed and sent an open letter Friday to the Office of Management and Budget, urging the administration to release the first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed foods (UPF). "It is critical that special interests not hold up this process," the letter read. "Most Americans are aware of UPF and wish to avoid them, but deeper familiarity with UPF remains limited, signaling a need for guidance." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Trump administration first announced their efforts to define ultraprocessed foods back in July 2025, but according to media reports, food company CEOs intervened in the definition's release. Adding to the pressure is the resignation of Calley Means, MAHA's top ally and senior adviser to Kennedy, on Thursday. While Means didn't cite the reasons for leaving, saying he has "tremendous respect" for President Donald Trump and Kennedy, Politico reported that the stonewalled UPF definition was a "breaking point." READ MORE: RFK Jr. adviser Calley Means resigns amid growing MAHA discontent over lack of progress Since becoming the nation's top health official, Kennedy has linked Americans' overconsumption of ultraprocessed foods to childhood obesity and said the U.S. could not "reverse America's chronic disease epidemic without transforming our food system." Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. participates in a "Make America Healthy Again" summit in Washington, D.C., in September. Photo by Nathan Howard/Reuters The Department of Health and Human Services and U.S. Department of Agriculture took an incremental step toward this goal in August by submitting for final review a proposed definition of these foods, which range from sugary cereals and sodas to burgers and store-bought breads. "If industry pressure can delay even this first step toward greater transparency, what does that tell us about the challenges of making meaningful improvements to our food supply?" said Ashley Gearhardt, a professor of psychology at the University of Michigan who signed the letter. The move could lay the groundwork for consumers to make informed decisions on ultraprocessed foods, which accounts for more than 70% of the packaged food supply in the U.S., according to one study. Ultraprocessed foods are cheap, convenient and readily available, but numerous studies have linked them to negative health outcomes like cardiovascular disease, obesity and Type 2 diabetes. Experts told PBS News that establishing a clear, structured definition is key to developing effective policy that aims to reduce people's consumption of ultraprocessed foods and improve public health. Where did the term 'ultraprocessed foods' come from? The term "ultraprocessed foods" comes from the NOVA classification system. Proposed in 2009 by researchers in Brazil, the NOVA system categorizes food and drinks into four different levels based on the amount of industrial processing a product undergoes after it's removed from nature and before it's prepared for meals and consumed. Under the NOVA system, foods in the ultraprocessed category are those that have undergone "extensive industrial manipulation," said Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition epidemiologist and professor at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who also signed the letter to OMB. These foods "have been broken down and then reassembled using cosmetic additives like added colors, added flavors, emulsifiers, or things that make the texture more palatable to people," she added. Many ultraprocessed food products are "barely even food" and "not designed for nourishment," said Gearhardt. Instead, she said they are designed for consumers "to finish the whole bag before you even realize it." Watch the clip in the player above. Kennedy told lawmakers at his confirmation hearings last year that ultraprocessed foods are a threat to children's health and "making them sick." Roughly three-quarters of infant and toddler foods are considered ultraprocessed, according to a February study published in Nutrients. Ultraprocessed foods are often sugary, salty and fatty, and packaged for long shelf lives and portability, Taillie said. The other three groups in the NOVA system are: Fresh or minimally processed foods. That includes unprocessed fruit, seeds, eggs and plain meat, and minimally processed foods such as fruit that's been dried, squeezed, chilled or frozen. Culinary ingredients. Think butter, sugar, honey, among other substances that have been extracted from whole foods for cooking. Processed foods. These are products that have experienced some level of processing or preservation, including canned vegetables, cheese, salted nuts and smoked meats. What experts would like to see in a federal definition of ultraprocessed foods Watch the segment in the player above. The public comment period on the government's effort to craft a definition for ultraprocessed foods ended Friday. Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.
He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.
"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.
"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

74be22ee5d96.text: By — Liz Landers Liz Landers By — Joshua Barajas Joshua Barajas Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/doj-has-monitored-elections-for-decades-heres-why-some-state-officials-are-concerned-this-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DOJ has monitored elections for decades. Here's why some state officials are concerned this year Politics Oct 23, 2026 4:16 PM EDT The Department of Justice is preparing for a large-scale effort to monitor the upcoming November midterm elections, with the goal of dispatching 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states on Election Day. The agency regularly monitors polling places. But this year's effort on Nov. 3 will more than double the number of federal monitors deployed during the 2022 midterms, when the DOJ under President Joe Biden sent out 388 people to polling places, confirmed by a DOJ official to PBS News. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. A senior DOJ official who spoke on background with reporters during a briefing last week said these efforts on Nov. 3 will be guided by federal statutes. The monitors, who include DOJ lawyers, will not be deployed to early voting sites. Traditionally, election monitoring is a way for the DOJ to ensure that voting rights laws are being followed. The job of a DOJ election monitor has been historically "pretty passive," said Stacey Young, executive director of Justice Connection, a support and legal network of former DOJ alumni. "They're there to just do as their name suggests, which is to observe," she said. In the past, the agency had been "very careful" to make sure monitors were not perceived as interfering with elections and didn't intimidate voters, she added. Still, state officials and voting rights groups have aired growing concerns over election meddling from the federal government. President Donald Trump continues to falsely claim that the 2020 election was rigged, while also casting doubt on the security of voting by mail. His administration has also made rooting out election fraud a priority this election cycle, repeating unfounded claims that a large number of noncitizens cast votes or are on voter rolls. Noncitizen voting is vanishingly rare. When asked by PBS News if the president had been briefed on these election monitoring programs, the official declined to say, adding, "I'm not going to get into conversations with the president about our election monitoring." Watch the segment in the player above. David Becker, a former voting section attorney in the DOJ's Civil Rights Division from 1998 to 2005, said the scale of this year's monitoring efforts are "not normal, but I'm not particularly concerned," adding that the agency does not have "blanket authority to be everywhere" and monitors must follow local and state laws about whether they are allowed inside a polling location. Here's what to know about election monitoring and what experts say is different this election cycle. What's new this election cycle? States have started to receive notifications from the DOJ about where the federal monitors will be sent. The department plans to focus on "high-population areas because that's where the most voters are," the senior official said. They are also identifying jurisdictions based on past problems with language access, disability access, among other considerations. Jurisdictions with competitive races could be "hot spots for potential voter intimidation" and thus could be a spot for their monitors, they added. DOJ monitors rarely get involved with election operations, said Young, who's been deployed three times as a civil litigator to monitor elections. They will sometimes interview people and observe them casting their ballots to make sure nobody is excluded or intimidated from voting. If there's active litigation, they will make sure court orders are followed or they may try to gather information for ongoing or potential litigation. When asked by PBS News how the monitors are trained, the senior official said all of the agency's election monitors have received a training video. It's been made "very clear" to their personnel that they are not to interfere with the voting process. They're there to "observe and report," and if some kind of enforcement action is needed, that would happen after the election, the official said. A man uses a voting machine at the Beverly Hills City Hall voting center in Beverly Hills, California, in 2025. Photo by Daniel Cole/Reuters One new change this year, Young said, is that the DOJ has abandoned a long-held rule to not allow prosecutors to serve as election monitors. "Prosecutors have prosecutorial authority and can be viewed as a more intimidating presence," she said. The senior DOJ official confirmed in the briefing that prosecutors will participate in election monitoring, though they would not personally prosecute a case if they observed some kind of violation of federal law. Defending the prosecutors' participation, the official added: "It's these groups out there that are kind of saber-rattling and fearmongering about prosecutors being monitors that are really doing more to deter voters and make them afraid than our election monitors." The official did not specify which groups were stoking fear. If election monitors observe any violations on Election Day, such as voter intimidation, the DOJ would escalate the issue and work with local law enforcement to address that concern, the official added. Young said that if voters see anything that strikes them as irregular or concerning, they can take action by sharing what happened. They can write down what they witnessed and call their member of Congress, a local official, a voting rights organization or speak with the press. "Voting is core to our democratic system," she said.

12c0aecc6a92.text: By — Jack Brook, Associated Press Jack Brook, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/police-officer-who-shot-and-killed-1-year-old-boy-in-mississippi-has-resigned-mayor-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old boy in Mississippi has resigned, mayor says Nation Oct 23, 2026 3:55 PM EDT The police officer who shot and killed a 1-year-old boy in Mississippi when he fired into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call has resigned, the Senatobia mayor told The Associated Press on Friday. Sgt. Hunter Foster, 33, had been cleared of criminal wrongdoing by the Mississippi Attorney General's office earlier this week after its monthslong probe concluded his use of force had been justified. READ MORE: Mississippi attorney general says officer's force was justified in death of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley On Thursday, the state released videos of the fatal shooting of Kohen Wiley, including Foster's body-worn camera footage of the June 14 encounter in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia, about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis, Tennessee. Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves confirmed Foster's resignation Friday. Foster's attorney Martin Zummach declined to comment when reached Friday. Zummach has said Foster had 'no choice' but to fire his weapon at the vehicle because it was moving at him. Kohen's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, has disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers. Videos show the fatal shooting in a Walmart parking lot Ben Crump, an attorney for Kohen's family, said the footage shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family concluded the same. An image of the vehicle shows its shattered right front passenger window. The family's legal team called for the federal government to investigate the shooting. Van Turner, another attorney representing Kohen's family, has called for Foster to be de-certified as a police officer. "What we need is for him to be de-certified so that he's not able to go to another police department and do the same thing," Van Turner said during a news conference Thursday. The Wiley family and legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Foster's resignation on Friday. Mississippi Department of Public Safety spokesperson Alex Gibert said Friday that Foster remained certified as a police officer. Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday in early November. The group of officers were at the Walmart store in response to an unrelated incident, according to a Mississippi Bureau of Investigation report. A Walmart employee then alerted them of two women running from the store. The videos show Kohen's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, holding Kohen as she and her friend run across the parking lot and enter their vehicle. Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop. The vehicle then accelerates forward as Foster steps toward it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side, where Kohen was seated on his mother's lap. The car continues to drive away. Vellesiya Wiley has denied that she and her friend stole diapers from the store and they have not been charged, according to state and county court records. Former Senatobia officer was sued over alleged civil rights violations Foster has worked for two other agencies in Mississippi since 2019 after becoming certified as a law enforcement officer there. He worked for the police department in Southaven, a city in DeSoto County that's part of the greater Memphis area, for two years and then was employed with the DeSoto County Sheriff's Office until October 2024. About five months later, he was hired by the police department in Senatobia, a city of about 8,000, according to state records obtained by the AP. A lawsuit filed in federal court in Mississippi in 2021 accused Foster and a group of 12 other Southaven police officers of civil rights violations during a 2019 arrest of two Black men outside a Waffle House. The two men said they had been searching for a lost set of keys when they were violently arrested and beaten by several officers. They alleged that Foster submitted a report falsely stating that they tried to run over another officer with their vehicle. Foster and the others officers denied wrongdoing. The Southaven police department agreed to settle the case in 2022 for an undisclosed amount, court records show. Last month, Senatobia Police Chief Harold Vanderford was fired by the city's board of aldermen, after reporting by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News alleged he used racist slurs in private text messages. Nearly all observers agree that Alabama’s new data center policies released this week are an improvement over the state’s old rules, which treat massive, power-hungry data centers like any other large industrial operation.
But several groups say the new rules for contracts between the data centers and Alabama Power, the state’s largest electric utility, don’t go far enough to require transparency and protect other electric customers from paying extra to support data centers.
“The process that was adopted is better than what we had before,” said Jaclyn Brass, an attorney in the Southern Environmental Law Center’s Alabama office.
“But much more needs to be done to ensure that customers aren’t going to foot the bills for the data center build-out,” Brass said. “And more also needs to be done to increase accountability and transparency in Alabama Power regulation across the board.”
The Alabama Public Service Commission issued its final order establishing the new rules this week after commissioners voted 3-0 to approve the framework at a meeting earlier this month. Alabama Power filed a new tariff outlining the process on Wednesday. The new processes will take effect on Nov. 23, according to Alabama Power’s filing.
“Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers,” the company said in an email. “Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers.”
Under the new rules, copies of contracts between Alabama Power and new data center developments must be provided unredacted to the PSC and the Alabama Attorney General’s office, which is the state’s dedicated ratepayer advocate under Alabama law.
These agencies will have 90 days to review the contracts to ensure that they are “consistent with the public interest,” and that the data center customer will cover all the costs of providing electricity, including any new infrastructure and fuel.
Then a redacted copy of the contract is to be provided for the public. The public copy is required to list the location and maximum capacity of the data center, and the company involved, including its parent company. But other key information can still be held back.
Monika Gerhart, executive director of the
Association, said her group filed comments in the PSC docket urging more transparency. The final rule delivered “a good share of it,” she said, but fell short by allowing the information used in the rate impact test to remain confidential.
“The numbers that matter most are still secret,” Gerhart said in an email. “The cost method and the findings stay behind closed doors. Nobody outside the Commission can check that Alabama families and businesses aren’t paying a data center’s bills, or that resources with no fuel bill, like solar, got a fair shot.”
Claire Douglass, senior advisor and spokesperson for Manifest Energy, said it’s crucial for the public to be able to check behind these state agencies and ensure their figures are accurate and that data center contracts really are in the public interest. Manifest Energy is a nonprofit that works with government agencies, utilities and other stakeholders to promote grid modernization, more energy efficiency and lower costs.
“We want to see the math, we want to see the receipts,” Douglass said in an interview. “Just saying, ‘Trust us, this is going to benefit families,’ isn’t really a good governance model.”
The new rules also state the PSC must publicly vote to approve or reject each contract within 90 days of receiving the application, but there is a loophole. The final order includes a “deemed approval” provision, meaning that the contracts are considered approved if the commission takes no action within the provided review period.
Advocates worry this provision could allow the commission to avoid voting publicly on controversial projects, though projects approved by default would be announced at the next commission meeting.

A spokesman for the Alabama Public Service Commission said the agency had considered many public comments in deciding to keep the deemed-approval provision in place.
“The final approved process retains that ‘deemed approved’ provision while making clear the Commission intends to vote on each contract within the 90-day review period,” the spokesman said. “The provision does not eliminate the Commission’s commitment to greater accountability and regulatory oversight or change the public interest standards that must guide these decisions.”
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said the group was glad that the new rules will require a vote, but disappointed about the deemed-approval provision.
“We commend the Commission for identifying what it will review before voting on the contract but are disappointed the actual details of what will be required are not made public,” Tait said in an email. “We wanted more, and we’ll keep making that case.”

House Democrats are making a play for a red seat in Kansas, but Republicans are competitive in a California seat â and both are releasing polling to back it up.
Democrat Don Coover is down by three points against incumbent Republican Rep. Derek Schmidt, within the 3.9% margin of error, according to Democratic polling conducted in mid-October and shared with Semafor.
In another warning sign for Republicans, Kansasâ Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cindy Holscher and Senate nominee Adam Hamilton both narrowly led their Republican counterparts, within the pollâs margin of error. The survey showed Trumpâs approval rating is underwater by 11 points in Schmidtâs district, which he won by 20 points in 2024.
Outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly won the district in 2018 and also in 2022, when Schmidt ran for governor. The DCCC named it one of the âdistricts in playâ this month, meaning it could be on the outskirts of the House battlefield. Over in Californiaâs 48th Congressional District, Republicans are releasing polling from mid-October that shows their nominee Jim Desmond trailing Democrat Marni Von Wilpert by just three points, with a 4.9% margin of error.

- Published
Train services have been cancelled and police have warned against unnecessary road journeys as Scotland prepares for the arrival of Storm Boelo.
Heavy rain and strong winds are expected during the second named storm to hit in two days, with gusts of up to 80mph forecast.
Most of the country is covered by a yellow Met Office warning from midday on Saturday, while a more severe amber alert takes effect from 21:00 on Saturday until 21:00 on Sunday, covering the mainland and Western Isles.
Forecasters say the storm, which is the second named storm in two days, could result in injury, flying debris, power cuts and damage to trees and buildings.
Although the 24-hour amber warning is not unprecedented, it is unusual because of the length of time it will be in place over such a wide geographical area.
On Friday the forecast triggered a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room which ensures the country is prepared for severe weather events.
How bad will the weather be?
Storm Boelo will bring very strong westerly winds with widespread gusts of 60-70mph (96.6-112.7km/h), and gusts up to 80mph (128.7km/h) in exposed coastal areas.
The strongest winds will initially affect western Scotland and the far north of Northern Ireland on Saturday evening and then spread eastwards overnight and through Sunday.
This will be accompanied by periods of heavy rain and frequent showers.
Forecasters warned that flying debris could cause injuries and danger to life, with a good chance of power cuts and an impact on phone coverage.
The Met Office also warned of damage to trees and buildings, bridge closures and transport disruption.
Winds will gradually ease from the west through Sunday.
Can I travel during the storm?
Public transport is still running, though ScotRail has confirmed that some train services will be cancelled:
- Glasgow Central â Ayr line will close between Kilwinning and Ayr from 21:00 on Saturday
- Glasgow Queen Street â Oban / Mallaig line will close between Fort William and Mallaig and between Crianlarich and Oban from around 22:00
- Inverness â Kyle of Lochalsh line will close between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach from the start of service on Sunday
- Inverness â Wick / Thurso line will close between Helmsdale and Wick / Thurso from the start of service on Sunday
Network Rail said trains will also run at reduced speeds across large parts of Scotland from Saturday night into Sunday.
Passengers are advised to expect significant disruption and longer journeys, and are should check services before they travel.
Supt Andy Barclay, deputy head of road policing for Police Scotland, warned drivers that conditions may be hazardous and urged them to consider whether journeys were "really necessary" over the weekend.
He warned:
- Stopping distances can be at least double on wet roads compared to dry conditions, and spray can reduce driver visibility
- HGV and bus drivers should drive with extreme caution and be aware you may be asked to park at a suitable position by the police
- If you need to travel, please drive to the conditions and allow extra time for your journey
- Stay tuned to media outlets for further updates and consult the Traffic Scotland website and social media channels for information relating to affected roads
As for coastal areas, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) said that weather conditions pose a safety risk to visitors and advised "extreme caution" if people are near the shoreline, especially along exposed cliffs, seafronts and piers.
The charity's water safety lead, Michael Avril, urged people to keep a safe distance from the water as conditions "could knock you off your feet or wash you into the sea".
CalMac cancelled a number of sailings on Friday and has amended the Saturday timetable for MV Isle of Mull - which runs between the mainland, South Uist and Barra.
Will events be cancelled?
It may be that some events are postponed during stormy conditions. Friday's Scottish Cup tie between Penicuik Athletic and Clyde was among the first to be delayed because of heavy rain.
Western Isles Council said events including church services should be aware of strong winds throughout Sunday and advised they "plan accordingly".
Paisley's popular Halloween festival is due to take place this weekend, which includes a parade, street theatre and outdoor light installations.
Renfrewshire Council said Friday's programme would go ahead as planned, but that an update on Saturday's events would be provided closer to the time.
And a Halloween family fun day at Dean Park Castle and Country Park in Kilmarnock, scheduled for Sunday, has been postponed due to the weather warning.

32d53f500b2e.text: Progressive House members and candidates are taking a stark turn away from what they describe as "performative" efforts to impeach President Trump . Why it matters: This is a drastic shift in tone from Trump's first term, when progressives were some of the loudest voices in favor of impeachment. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) famously said of Trump in 2019, " We're gonna impeach the motherfucker ," a line Republicans have routinely dredged up to dismiss impeachment efforts against the president as premeditated. On Thursday, she told Axios in a statement: "No matter what happens in November, we'll still have a Trump administration for the next two years to hold accountable." Driving the news: Likely incoming Democratic House members Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Melat Kiros of Colorado struck a similar tone in a recent podcast interview when asked about impeaching Trump. "I support accountability, but ... that is something that Trump himself seems to want," Avila Chevalier said. "My question is: Is that actually going to be meaningful accountability for the Trump administration?" Said Kiros: "The accountability has to actually lead to some material changes." What we're hearing: Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), who has advocated a day-one impeachment, told Axios in an interview, "Impeachment can't just be a political messaging strategy." "I think what Melat and Darializa are getting to is that people want to see justice and real accountability. ... We can't just tell people things that some would feel like is fluff," Ramirez said. "I think the American people are tired of theater," said Adam Hamawy, another likely Democratic House member from New Jersey. He told Axios any impeachment proceedings need to be "a real process with substance, rather than just getting up there and just making a show of it." Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) said Democrats "should investigate the heads of these departments and bad actors across the board," but she is "less inclined to the performative and more inclined to identify what's impactful." "The performative may feel nice, but in the end will not bear the kind of fruit that the American people deserve," she added. Tlaib said the House Oversight Committee "must continue pressing for real accountability and consequences for this corrupt administration's crimes and abuses of taxpayers' dollars against our neighbors, public health, environment, safety and democracy." The big picture: Democrats have had a tortured relationship with impeachment since Trump returned to office in 2025. After impeaching the president twice in his first term only to see him acquitted both times by the Senate and then reelected in 2024, even the most ardently anti-Trump Democrats came into last year recoiling at the mere mention of another impeachment. But they were buffeted by a grassroots base furious about the second Trump administration's precedent-shattering moves and demanding Democrats use every tool at their disposal to fight back. By the numbers: When Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) tried to force a vote on impeaching Trump in June 2025, 128 of his fellow House Democrats voted with Republicans to block it. By December, only 23 Democrats voted to block it . When Green did it a third time last month, 18 Democrats voted to block it, while 147 voted with him to force the vote and 46, including party leaders, voted "present." Yes, but: Green and Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), who similarly championed impeaching Trump in his second term, have both lost their reelection bids this year. Their losses came as the party base has turned away from anti-Trump #resistance crusaders in favor of more broadly anti-establishment, left-wing ideologues, as Axios previously reported . These incoming progressives are expressing a view more in line with Democratic leaders like House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.): That impeachment shouldn't be a fait accompli. What's next: While Trump may be off the board for now, his Cabinet certainly isn't. The House could soon vote on an impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggered by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) just before lawmakers left for October recess. "I do think that holding Pete Hegseth [accountable] and looking into the ways in which our governing bodies have failed to meet the standards, the laws ... is all part of holding this government accountable," said Mejia.

506cfc8d091e.text: U.S. intelligence finds Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and beyond, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages," according to an Oct. 23 memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio obtained by Axios. Why it matters: U.S. officials say the intelligence is one reason the State Department is drawing down personnel at several American embassies across the Middle East, amid mounting fears of a broader regional conflict. U.S. officials also fear that Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen could expand their attacks beyond Saudi Arabia to other countries in the region. Adding to the volatile security environment is the prospect of renewed U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran, potentially after the midterm elections. What they're saying: "We may do another little Operation Epic Fury, or [the Iranians] will agree [to a deal]," President Trump said at a rally in Florida on Friday. "If they're smart, they will just say, 'Let's get down to business,' but I doubt they will do that because perhaps they're not smart." Driving the news: In the one-page, unclassified memo obtained by Axios, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Rubio that intelligence about Iranian assassination plots needs to reach more U.S. personnel than are currently authorized to receive it. The memo does not identify specific targets, countries outside the Middle East or the nature of the plots, but says the underlying intelligence has already been shared with senior State Department officials. Clayton offered to downgrade as much of the sensitive intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it more widely with personnel potentially at risk. State of play: Earlier this week, the State Department ordered family members and nonessential personnel to leave the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh and consulates in Jeddah and Dhahran. On Friday, the department also ordered reductions in U.S. diplomatic and government personnel at embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar and Jordan, a U.S. official said. "We decided that due to the threat of Houthi attacks and Iranian terror plots we need to reduce our footprint and keep only essential staff," the official said. CNN first reported on the reduction in staffing at the four embassies. Read the full memo .

95edad54a9cf.text: By — Matthew Brown, Associated Press Matthew Brown, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/rollins-says-usda-is-full-bore-ahead-on-forest-service-reorganization Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rollins says USDA is 'full-bore ahead' on Forest Service reorganization Politics Oct 23, 2026 7:52 PM EDT BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Thursday that the Trump administration remains "full-bore ahead" with a sweeping reorganization of the Forest Service and other agencies after a judge blocked the changes last week. WATCH: U.S. Forest Service cuts raise concerns on protecting public lands and fighting wildfires The administration wants to move Forest Service headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City, shutter 23 research stations, and close many regional offices and replace them with state offices. It's part of a broader realignment at the Agriculture Department that also would change programs for food and nutrition, rural development and other services. For now the plan is stalled under court order. But that's already under appeal, and Rollins made clear Thursday that the administration hasn't given up. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "We are full-bore ahead in the reorganization," Rollins said during a conference call with reporters following an announcement on fertilizer production. "We believe in it more today than we ever have — taking the USDA to our constituents, which is rural America, the Forest Service out West." Administration officials say the reorganization will trim costs and further concentrate resources in Western states that are home to nearly 90% of national forest lands. Federal employee unions, environmental groups and local officials, including in California, Maryland and Washington state, are trying to quash the plan. They say the shuffling of employees is a ploy to achieve the administration's goal of deep cuts in the workforce. U.S. District Judge Vince Chhabria in California sided with those arguments in an Oct. 13 order halting the reorganization while a lawsuit from opponents works its way through the courts. "If implemented, the planned reorganization activities will likely put thousands of USDA employees to the choice of relocating far from their current home — often to a different state — or losing their job," Chhabria wrote. He said the administration "almost certainly" violated congressional restrictions on using money on the reorganization that was intended for other purposes. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has been eliminating layers of management as part of President Donald Trump's push to slim the federal workforce and make it more efficient. Trump also wants to take away one of the Forest Service's most prominent roles — fighting wildfires — and transfer responsibility to the new federal Wildland Fire Service. Congress so far has blocked that move. With wildfires getting worse in recent decades due to climate change, battling them has consumed a greater share of the Forest Service budget. That's forced officials to look for cost savings elsewhere. WATCH: Wildland firefighters feel increasing strain amid funding and staffing shortages It's not clear how much the reorganization will actually save, said Chris Iverson, who spent almost three decades at the Forest Service before retiring from a leadership position during Trump's first term. Yet Iverson said the changes could result in the loss of personnel with extensive experience, including battling wildfires. He added that the elimination of regional offices and creation of state offices could open the door to more influence by governors pushing the interests of the timber, oil and gas and grazing industries. "It's just going to be a closer alignment of Forest Service leadership with state government priorities," Iverson said. Gov. Spencer Cox in Utah has described the Forest Service reorganization, including a new headquarters in Salt Lake City, as "a big win for Utah and the West." GOP lawmakers said it would ensure agency officials get more local input. The administration last month scaled back part of its plan and said 41 research facilities across the country that faced possible closure would remain open. Almost two dozen research stations still are slated to close. The Forest Service workforce has been cut about 16% under Trump, from more than 39,000 employees to 33,000, according to government data. During his first term, Trump moved the Bureau of Land Management to Colorado, citing many of the same reasons — including a desire to put top officials closer to the public lands they oversee. The Biden administration reversed course, moving BLM headquarters back to Washington, D.C., after two years. The National Federation of Federal Employees union said a survey of Forest Service workers showed a large majority opposed the pending reorganization plan and most were unwilling to relocate. 0f6e30fb13eb.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/signs-of-fraying-loyalty-emerge-in-netanyahu-stronghold-before-israeli-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Signs of fraying loyalty emerge in Netanyahu stronghold before Israeli election World Oct 23, 2026 7:31 PM EDT KIRYAT SHMONA, Israel (AP) — Kiryat Shmona has long been a bastion of support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party. But that loyalty is no longer ironclad. Once a bustling commercial center, Israel's northernmost city was temporarily evacuated three years ago after being battered by rockets from nearby Lebanon, and it still feels half-empty even though the attacks have mostly subsided. Although the town remains staunchly conservative, there are rumblings of displeasure with Netanyahu's handling of the latest war against the militant group Hezbollah, and that could bode poorly for him in Israel's election Tuesday. READ MORE: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Vowing to stop Hezbollah's attacks, Netanyahu led a bombing campaign in Lebanon and invaded the country twice since 2023. More than 4,000 Lebanese have been killed, and Israeli troops have occupied a swath of southern Lebanon, leveling multiple towns and displacing an estimated 1 million people. Still, Hezbollah remains active. Some in Kiryat Shmona say Israel should have been even tougher; others say they no longer trust that Netanyahu cares about them. Eti Ben Shabat, 64, says in previous elections she had always followed her family in voting for Likud, almost without thinking. But in recent years, she said, something snapped. She pointed in part to Netanyahu's broken promises to bring security to the north and dismantle Hezbollah. "I don't want the lies to continue," she said. In previous elections, support went heavy for Netanyahu Netanyahu is unlikely to lose Kiryat Shmona entirely. But even a small dip in its support — and that of other traditional strongholds — could spell trouble for him. It could tip a very tight election to the man aiming to replace him, Gadi Eisenkot. Or it could strengthen far-right parties, which would likely back Netanyahu to remain prime minister but would then have even greater power in a ruling coalition. Kiryat Shmona has always supported right-wing parties, particularly Likud. In the last elections held in 2021 and 2022, around 50% of voters there chose Likud, compared to a quarter of voters nationwide, according to the Central Elections Committee. "Kiryat Shmona, the way the city is socioeconomically and religion-wise, it is made for the right and specifically Likud," said Sami Malul, 72, a retired Likud city councilor who served as the town's acting mayor in 2008. But the town is reeling from the war. The government evacuated Kiryat Shmona and dozens of other towns and villages along the Lebanese border for more than a year – from the time Hezbollah began firing on Israel after Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel until a ceasefire with Hezbollah was reached in late 2024. Netanyahu claimed to have subdued Hezbollah. So trust in him shattered among some in Kiryat Shmona when Hezbollah missiles again started hitting in March after Israel and the U.S. launched their war on Iran. Israel's subsequent occupation of southern Lebanon has reduced but not stopped Hezbollah fire. Efforts by the Lebanese army to remove Hezbollah from southern Lebanon have made little progress. Kiryat Shmona claims that nearly 80% of its 22,000 residents have returned, but locals say the real figure is closer to 50%. Streets feel empty and abandoned. On the main commercial drags, several shops remain shuttered. Others are open but devoid of customers. Malul insists the government handled the war and the evacuation well, prioritizing residents' safety. He argued Kiryat Shmona has faced attacks since its founding and Netanyahu isn't to blame for the current situation. Many others feel the same. "We really love Bibi, and we can't choose anyone else, but he should see the needs of his people," said Maimon Amsalem, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Keeping our security is the most important thing, we don't want anything else." For some, three years of war triggers a dramatic shift Nissan Zeevi, a third-generation resident of northern Israel who lives in a town adjacent to Kiryat Shmona, has voted for Likud as long as he can remember. But this year he is running for a seat in parliament with the Beyachad opposition party, furious over what he calls Netanyahu's "abandonment of the north." During the most recent war with Hezbollah, Zeevi founded Lobby 1701, an activist group advocating for better security in the north. He wants the Israeli military to increase its attacks against Hezbollah and maintain its buffer zone in southern Lebanon until the Lebanese government identifies Hezbollah as a terror organization. "Residents in the north have been in a war for three years that hasn't ended," said Zeevi. "You can see the people's great frustration and great disappointment in Netanyahu." "Netanyahu still has his base here, who will go with him through fire and water. But people have much more political awareness now," said Zeevi. "After 20 years, he needs to make way for new leadership." In a small town, voting along family lines Around town, there's little evidence that elections are just days away, and little outward excitement for Likud or Netanyahu. A few scattered campaign posters for the smaller right-wing parties flutter at intersections or are glued onto mobile bomb shelters. Few residents wanted to speak about politics, citing a general feeling of hopelessness and frustration. No candidates have offered a concrete plan for the conflict with Hezbollah, beyond offering vague promises of "strong defense." 90ec80047af2.text: By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press By — Didi Tang, Associated Press Didi Tang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/treasury-proposes-rule-to-curb-high-tech-investments-in-china-and-other-adversaries Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Treasury proposes rule to curb high-tech investments in China and other adversaries Politics Oct 23, 2026 7:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other "countries of concern." The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power. That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program. In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia. The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin. REAAD MORE: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump's favored term for AI, "superintelligence" or SI. The proposed rule "sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build," said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies. The screening of outbound investments "recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can," Singleton said. Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule "will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk." Treasury's rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases. Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule. "It's just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program," said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm. In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses. Asked about Washington's proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that "Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one's interests." She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests. Since Trump's first term, the United States and China — the world's two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They've restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China's rare earth minerals and America's advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other's products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January. But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries. 0c9a48bd2c49.text: President Trump is making a final push to help Republicans maintain control of Congress as some of the most closely watched races remain competitive. But the battle for the Senate is also playing out in court. In Alaska, the Trump administration sued to potentially block certification of the election if the Republican incumbent loses. White House correspondent Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: President Trump is making a final campaign push to help Republicans maintain control of Congress, as some of the country's most closely watched races remain competitive. But the battle for the U.S. Senate is also playing out in court. In Alaska, the Trump administration has filed a lawsuit seeking to potentially block certification of the election if the Republican incumbent loses. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, has been following both developments and joins us now. So, Liz, let's start in Alaska, where the Justice Department has filed this unusual lawsuit. Why is the DOJ getting involved? Liz Landers: The Department of Justice has taken a series of potentially political actions really close to Election Day now. What was filed here in Alaska is, they're trying to block the certification of the vote there, but only if the Democrat, Mary Peltola, wins and beats the incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The issue here is that there is a-another candidate named Dan J. Sullivan, who's also on that ballot. And Republicans are worried that voters could get confused by this. But this has already been litigated by the Alaska Supreme Court, who said that Dan J. Sullivan could stay on this ballot. Department of Justice is bringing this lawsuit, they say, to protect the integrity of the Senate election there. They say in their lawsuit that the federal government could be harmed by this election certification if it is -- quote -- "tainted by a frivolous candidacy because that undermines confidence in the makeup and workings of the federal government." President Trump was asked about this earlier today. President Donald Trump: I'm the one that said do it. They have two guys run -- named Dan Sullivan running. So the Democrats put up a guy. I don't think he ever voted before. All of a sudden, he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S. One is Daniel J. The Daniel J. is the fake. Liz Landers: Daniel J. Sullivan has voted in Alaska races before, just to be clear. But I asked the former Department of Justice civil rights attorney David Becker, who's also an election expert about this, and he said this is purely a matter of state law, and the Department of Justice has no authority and no role here. He said that this kind of litigation is unprecedented to try to block the certification of an election 11 days before the vote. Geoff Bennett: The Justice Department also announced charges today against two former FBI officials over their testimony about Hunter Biden's laptop. What are they accused of doing? Liz Landers: The Department of Justice is claiming that these two FBI officials lied in congressional testimony that they gave in 2023. And this was about their involvement in a specialized foreign influence task force in these investigations into Hunter Biden's laptop and that they knew about the laptop. The attorneys for one of the former FBI officials who was charged here, Nikki Flores, said in a statement to the "News Hour" that: "The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust to push a false narrative for a shot at political points." Hunter Biden's laptop story broke just a few weeks before the 2020 election. I'm sure you remember covering this. The laptop contained e-mails that appeared to show discussions of Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings. And at the time, Democrats questioned whether that was Russian mis- and dis-information. Geoff Bennett: And so finally, with Election Day approaching, you have got some of the biggest names in politics, to include President Trump, hitting the campaign trail. Who's heading where? Liz Landers: President Trump goes to Georgia tomorrow to help in that Senate race there. Also, he's headed to Michigan on Sunday. Mike Rogers is in a tough election there, the Republican against the Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed. Also, former President Barack Obama will be in Michigan as well tomorrow campaigning with Abdul El-Sayed, and he will also be going to Ohio as well. The former president has also cut a bunch of radio ads for other downballot candidates. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers, a busy week for you. Next week's going to be busier. Liz Landers: Indeed, yes. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: Thanks, as always. Liz Landers: Of course.

70cbcb36a7d9.text: In our news wrap Friday, the White House says Melania Trump brokered a localized ceasefire deal in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky, Romania's president blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship in the Black Sea and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered the army there to prepare for a full closure of the occupied West Bank. Geoff Bennett: We start the day's other headlines with the latest on the war in Ukraine. The White House says first lady Melania Trump has brokered a localized cease-fire deal in Oleshky, the Ukrainian city captured by Russia early on in the war. The cease-fire would allow for humanitarian aid and evacuations from the town, which Mrs. Trump said is -- quote -- "on the brink of disaster." Following today's announcement, officials on both sides welcomed the agreement. President Trump told reporters today it was the first lady's initiative. President Donald Trump: What she wants to do is save children. And that's her focus. And both sides are cooperating with her, so doing a very good job. Geoff Bennett: The cease-fire is set to begin next week. Meantime, Romania's president has blamed Russia for a drone strike today that sank this cargo ship off its coast in the Black Sea, calling it a new example of Russian aggression beyond Ukraine. At least one sailor was killed. Three others were missing. That's as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his military's access to Starlink satellite systems is still being interrupted, despite U.S. assurances that it's running again at full speed. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: This is a real problem for us because the Russians attack us almost every day. Geoff Bennett: Zelenskyy also said negotiators from the U.S., Ukraine and Russia have agreed to hold technical level talks in Abu Dhabi in early November. Those would not involve political leaders. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army there to prepare for a full closure of the occupied West Bank after suspected gunmen shot and killed two Israeli soldiers. Video from the Israeli army showed the firefight at a military checkpoint. The two attackers, both Palestinian, were killed in the exchange of gunfire. The army said it prevented the men from advancing towards civilians. Following the shoot-out, Netanyahu blamed Hamas for the attack and vowed that Israel would retaliate. Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister (through translator): We will act, first of all, to demolish this place, to change it completely. We will evacuate the residents. We will go house by house. We will also remove the weapons there, and all the terror infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed. Geoff Bennett: After his comments, construction equipment could be seen starting to demolish homes near the site of the shooting. All of this comes just days before Israeli elections, when voters will decide whether to give Netanyahu another term in office. In China's Tibet region, first responders are racing to rescue survivors after a magnitude-7 earthquake struck the remote city of Nagqu. State media says at least 16 people are dead and more than 50 others were injured. Security camera footage showed the moment the quake struck as people fled into the streets. Hundreds of homes were destroyed, leaving many people there displaced. Local officials said multiple rounds of search-and-rescue have been complicated by the region's high altitude, low temperatures, and concern about further building collapses from aftershocks. Here at home, a police officer in Mississippi has resigned days after state authorities cleared him in the fatal shooting of a 1-year-old boy during a suspected shoplifting incident. Newly released body camera footage shows officers approaching a car in a Walmart parking lot in June guns drawn. As the vehicle moved forward, Sergeant Hunter Foster fired into it, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was sitting on his mother's lap. Mississippi's attorney general ruled this week that the shooting was justified because the vehicle had moved toward an officer. But Wiley's family disputes that finding and is calling for a federal investigation. Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday on November 1. President Trump signed an order today removing 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods, including those in agriculture and forestry. The move is a bid to help Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is facing a tough reelection race. Many of Mr. Trump's tariffs have put particular strain on businesses in Maine. The changes become effective next Friday. Meantime, stocks ended the week down as oil prices rose to their highest level since 2022. The Dow Jones industrial average tumbled more than 600 points. The Nasdaq had a more modest drop, and the S&P 500 slipped by half-a-percent.

2c37848f6fa5.text: Kaylub Giamanco is the father who stopped a school shooter in Bend, Oregon, a week ago. The teen gunman entered the school and killed three students and a teacher before Giamanco stopped him. In a new interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting, Giamanco describes the moments leading up to his heroic actions, how he felt after he took down the shooter and that day's larger tragedy. Geoff Bennett: There's a new interview today with the first detailed comments from the man who stopped a school shooter in Bend, Oregon, one week ago. Three students and a teacher were killed before the suspect was shot and killed by a father who has children of his own at the Silver Rail Elementary School. That man is Kaylub Giamanco, who is a carpenter. He told our colleagues at Oregon Public Broadcasting in this exclusive interview that he was heading home for lunch and driving by the school when he saw the shooter carrying a shotgun. Kaylub Giamanco, Stopped School Gunman: And then I proceeded into the parking lot, and I saw him walking all the way across the school, and I just was in full panic. Like, no, there's children, there's babies in there. And I told my Siri to call 911. And the dispatch had picked up. And I was reporting the incident. But she was asking questions that they frustrated me, and I understand there's protocol, but she was asking me, do I know the person, all these things. And I said: "I'm sorry. I have to go in. People are going to die." And then I peeked through the window, and, at this point, I found my opportunity, and I seen a teacher on the left struggling with the gunman on the right with the rifle. And I knew that they were -- they were both side to me, and I knew that he did not know that I was there. And so at that point, I swung the door out and open, and I stepped in and I fired. And they dropped to the ground, and the teacher sprang out of the building, thinking that I was a second shooter, and I could see the fear in her eyes, and that did hurt a lot. But I could see the fear in her eyes. She left the room, and this happens in seconds. And then I looked down at the gunman, and he was scrambling for his weapon. And I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else. Geoff Bennett: Giamanco also spoke of how he felt after he took down the shooter and of that day's larger tragedy. Kaylub Giamanco: Felt like I was having a heart attack almost the entire time. I have never had so much chest pain. I mean, I can't tell you what it feels like to take a life. It's really not -- that's not how I thought that my Thursday was going to go. But I can tell you that I genuinely feel like I was supposed to be there. And if I wasn't there, I just don't know what would have happened. The teacher that was wrestling with the gun with the gunman, I just -- I want to recognize her. She gave me the opportunity to make my shot without losing my life. I saw a clear shot to where I did not have to take her life. Without her and that little spur-of-the-moment delay, I very much feel like I would have been facing the shooter head on, and we could have both died, or I could have died, and I felt like I was the last line of defense between me and the rest of the children in the school. I don't know her name. I would love to know her name. I would love to give her a hug, because that's a real true hero to not have a weapon and to put yourself in between your babies and a firearm. It's a lot, you know? I really did want to speak with the families and the victims and just cry with them and hold them. I want to apologize for not saving their babies. That's probably the biggest thing for me right now, because the gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there's ones that I didn't save, and that's probably the hardest thing for me right now. Geoff Bennett: Thank you again to our colleagues at Oregon Public Broadcasting for that interview.

de9ef8c251a6.text: By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/seeking-to-help-collins-in-maine-trump-exempts-some-canadian-imports-from-his-50-tariffs Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Seeking to help Collins in Maine, Trump exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs Politics Oct 23, 2026 6:48 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30. The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.'' Collins, locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, issued a statement saying she'd spoken with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "about the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.'' WATCH: What Maine voters are saying about the Collins-Jackson Senate race "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said. She said she asked for tariff relief for such products "and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Collins said she'd seek "additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner." Trump started a trade war with America's longstanding ally and northern neighbor, reaching back to a Depression-era trade law to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. He charged that Canada discriminates against U.S. dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly lashed back with tariffs of 15% to 50% on American products, matching Trump's import taxes dollar for dollar. Trump ratcheted the dispute up from there last month by imposing a flat-out ban on $1 billion worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles. The U.S. president has claimed that foreign countries pay his tariffs. In fact, U.S. importers do. And they often face the tough choice of having to pass along the higher costs to their customers or absorb them. As the Nov. 3 midterm elections approach, many Americans are furious about the cost of living. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll of 2,140 U.S. adults, conducted Sept. 24-28, found that 65% now blame Trump's policies for persistently high prices more than factors outside of his control, signaling weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and unhappiness with the war with Iran, which has driven up the price of gasoline. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement, "Trump's desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins' political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies." Collins complained that Trump's levies were hurting Maine farms and businesses that rely on Canadian imports when U.S.-made alternatives are not available. Her office cited the example of Maine wild blueberry growers who need specialized harvesting boxes from Canada that work with their processing equipment.
