Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.
Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.
Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.
Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.
They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

0af470896459.text: The speed of the Elon Musk-owned satellite system used by the Ukrainian military has been fully restored after two weeks of restrictions, the country's ministry of defense said in a statement on Saturday. Why it matters: The restrictions limited the Ukrainian military from using drones to intercept Russian attack drones, and from using its own drones to send supplies to soldiers on the front lines. The restrictions were at the center of the recent crisis between the Trump administration and the Ukrainian government. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky saw the restrictions as retaliation by President Trump and Musk for his refusal to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries. The crisis led to bipartisan criticism and pressure and generated a blame game between the White House and SpaceX founder and CEO Musk. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. President Trump denied that the White House was involved in restricting the system and for several days claimed it was fully back on. On Friday Trump denied reports that he spoke to Musk, but said that if the system was still restricted he would speak to Musk about it. What they are saying: "Our monitoring systems are detecting a restoration of Starlink/Starshield speeds. We are recording speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour, with stable connectivity," the Ukrainian ministry of defense said. The ministry said the restrictions were lifted as a result of "direct dialogue" and "firm stance at the highest level" by Zelensky.

A woman has died after attempting to rescue her two sons when they were swept away while snorkelling in the Bahamas.
The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of a 36-year-old British woman on Tuesday.
The force said it believed the woman - believed to be from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire - was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
In an attempt to rescue her sons, "the woman was also swept away", police said. The children were subsequently rescued from the water.
Foul play 'not suspected'
In a statement, posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said: "According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.
"Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
"Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
"In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
"She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered.
"Foul play is not suspected at this time.
"An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death."
A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.
Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.
The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.
Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.
Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.
Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper.
Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.
Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.
Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.
He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".
Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

b7579173ae4e.text: Washington has always viewed Silicon Valley as culturally strange, but the current crop of AI leaders is becoming a political liability, sources close to the White House and Congress tell Axios. Why it matters : Lawmakers, hill staffers and Washington insiders in both parties wish AI founders would do what every other major industry chief does: put a sock in it and just build their products — safely. By centering the conversation around digital sentience and global catastrophe, AI leaders are turning an already complicated regulatory debate into an impossible moral panic. State of play : Rather than leading the charge to persuade Americans about the benefits of AI, and the potential for shared prosperity — the core elements of any winning political campaign — industry leaders are constantly warning of its existential dangers. What they're saying: Lawmakers say the message from AI execs too often alternates between prosperity and doom, sometimes in the same public appearances. The whiplash creates adds to political instability in the face of an already powerful public backlash, lawmakers and regulators say. "It's obvious that they're tripping over their own shoelaces in trying to sell the value of this to the public," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) told Axios. "It's very hard to imagine a group right now that operates more in a vacuum, more out of touch with everyday Americans, than the AI industry." "CEOs like Sam Altman are saying the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology," Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Axios. "You cannot trust billionaires to make decisions to keep us safe." "Your instinct is to wreak havoc on the public SI discourse," Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month, complaining about Amodei's "panic-inducing commentary." Democrats also have paid close attention to just how much top AI and tech leaders have cozied up to President Trump. Many see opportunity in turning AI gaffes into an easy political win. "The American people hate that Donald Trump is cozying up to tech billionaires, while AI threatens our jobs and livelihoods," Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) told Axios. "Democrats need to make the AI industry's political money an issue, data centers an issue, and go on offense to protect workers and kids." The big picture: Friday night news dumps and consequential weekend blog posts have become Anthropic and OpenAI's bread and butter. Regulators are left wondering whether that's a feature or a bug: deliberate attempts to quietly course-correct damaging narratives ahead of IPOs, or the work of inexperienced teams struggling to navigate Washington. "We can all speculate on what's going on, but all it does is have everybody wake up Monday morning and say 'these guys are awful, we've had enough,'" one source citing conversations with Hill offices said. Behind the scenes: Administration officials are once again disgruntled with Anthropic, for two reasons. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei attended a late September gathering with Trump but didn't disclose safety incidents involving Anthropic models that affected government web sites. The company told U.S. officials on Thursday, Oct. 8, then published a Friday evening blog post about it. "They were hiding the ball," one official told Axios. Then the company added to the confusion with an AI safety bill that included something the company has broadly opposed: federal preemption of state AI laws. It also defined a catastrophic incident related to AI as causing 50 deaths or more, drawing backlash. Anthropic's Head of Public Affairs has since walked back parts of the bill, prompting growing distrust from Washington given the topsy-turvy nature of the company's advocacy. Anthropic says it briefed the White House and affected agencies on the safety incidents once their reviews were complete, and it is working with the Super Intelligence Force as it develops an incident reporting process. The industry is pushing for more clarity on incident reporting, and AI companies don't see the administration's process as straightforward. Provisions defining AI catastrophe in terms of deaths have been a part of landmark state regulations in California and elsewhere , according to Politico. Zoom in: Washington's headaches with AI execs also extend to OpenAI, and both companies are targets of a developing FTC investigation. OpenAI's legislative strategy has also raised eyebrows on the Hill and in state legislatures. In response to a blog post from Chris Lehane, the company's chief lobbyist, New York state assemblymember Alex Bores said OpenAI's policy proposals are vague and the company ultimately wants to block states from regulating. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company has engaged with both parties, the administration and statehouses across the country. The company is "talking with people around the country" about the benefits of AI. Reality check : Those efforts have so far failed to win hearts and minds, with another recent poll showing a majority of Americans see AI as bad for society. The bottom line: For AI CEOs, the lesson is increasingly clear: do less. Axios' Stef W. Kight contributed reporting.

A few days before Christmas in 2023, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency received a complaint through its National Response Center: “There has been a horrible smell in the air for almost a week,” the caller said, according to state records. “It’s so bad it’s making people throw up.”
The caller thought the odor was emanating from Smithfield’s enormous hog slaughterhouse in Tarheel. But the rendering plant wasn’t the culprit. The stench instead came from poultry manure that farmers were slathering on agricultural fields throughout Bladen County, an investigation by the North Carolina Division of Air Quality found.
Spreading dry poultry feces on fields is legal, as is the secrecy underpinning North Carolina’s poultry industry.
With a few exceptions, state law allows poultry CAFOs, or concentrated animal feeding operations, to operate without a permit. 
Many poultry CAFOs raise millions of birds each year, in as many as 48 barns per farm. The law also keeps their locations confidential, known only to the N.C. Department of Agriculture.
Now three environmental nonprofits, CleanAIRE Carolina, Rural Empowerment Association for Community Help and the N.C. Environmental Justice Network, have launched a community science project—E-I-E-I-O No!—to identify and monitor poultry CAFOs and swine biogas projects. The project relies on state government satellite imagery, analyzed by volunteers and then verified by “ground truthing”—driving to the sites themselves.
Several universities are assisting with the project, which aims to provide a public accounting of the CAFOs and their potential harms to air and water quality.
“People are inundated” with the waste, said Chris Lamont Brown, director of research and education with NCEJN. “There are real public health issues.”
An Alternative to Doomscrolling
An aerial photo of three long, narrow barns displayed on a large screen.
“Raise your hand if you think this is a swine CAFO,” Brown asked the crowd of 200-plus people.
No one did.
“Raise your hand if you think it’s poultry.”
Every hand went up.
“Look at you–you’re ready,” Brown said.
The N.C. Environmental Justice summit is held every October at the Franklinton Center at Bricks, a former school for previously enslaved people after the Civil War. Here, project leaders Brown and Z Strawderman, AirKeeper Dashboard & GIS manager for CleanAIRE Carolina, publicly debuted E-I-E-I-O-No, which launched in late July.
Throughout the summer, more than 1,600 volunteers logged on to Zooniverse, an online platform for community research. The task was simple, if tedious: Scan satellite images of every land parcel in Sampson County and identify whether it contained a poultry CAFO, a swine CAFO, both or neither.
Volunteers also scrutinized the images for covered swine lagoons that could indicate the presence of biogas anaerobic digesters. For quality control, 20 people reviewed each image.
“People said that instead of doomscrolling, they would work on this project,” Brown explained. “They wanted to do something bigger than themselves.”

Project leaders estimated it would take a month to review the images. It took 24 hours.
Since the summer, volunteers have analyzed six counties and identified 2,011 swine and 2,349 poultry CAFOs.
Project leaders intentionally refrained from using artificial intelligence to scan the imagery. Not only would it be less accurate than a human review, but data centers that power AI consume vast amounts of energy and water, create heat islands and noise, and inflict other social and economic harms.
“We want to bring more people into the environmental justice movement,” Brown said. “And we want to use a method that aligns with our values.”
For the past 20 years, a permanent swine CAFO moratorium has been in effect in North Carolina, which prohibits new or expanded operations unless they install “environmentally superior technology” to manage the billions of gallons of hog waste currently stored in open-air lagoons.
Poultry CAFOs have filled the gap, Strawderman said, and the number of operations have doubled or even tripled in some North Carolina counties in just five years.
In 2022, about 1 billion chickens, broilers and turkeys were sold in North Carolina both export and consumption according to federal Department of Agriculture data. The state ranks fourth in the U.S. in chicken production and first in turkeys.
From the air, poultry CAFOs look different from their swine counterparts. Poultry barns are long and narrow. Instead of enormous lagoons to hold slurried waste, such as those used in swine CAFOs, poultry operations mound dry feces and store it in a barn.
Swine CAFOs spray millions of gallons of reeking waste onto agricultural fields. From there, it seeps into the groundwater or can run off into streams and contaminate drinking water.
Poultry waste can also contaminate air and water. Companies haul the material off and pile it in fields, sometimes for up to 15 days, as state law allows. If it rains during that time, the piles become tides of waste. Even when it is spread as dry manure for fertilizer, it can seep into the drinking water supplies much like swine waste.
“We don’t know where the waste is going,” Strawderman said, “or whether there is enough land to apply it responsibly.”
It’s difficult to pinpoint all the poultry operations in North Carolina, but every five years the USDA conducts a census of CAFOs and birds sold per county and publishes the information online.
Strawderman analyzed county-level data from 2017 to 2022. Sampson County, already home to 2.1 million hogs, reported sales of 47 million poultry in 2017.
Five years later, the number had doubled to 95 million.

From our collaborating partner Living on Earth, public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by Paloma Beltran with Tzeporah Berman, the founder of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative.
As the United Nations gears up for the COP31 climate session in mid-November, nearly three decades after the Kyoto Protocol, there’s a newer set of international climate negotiations intended to close the yawning gap between discussion and action.
The first Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was held this April in Santa Marta, Colombia. It’s known to proponents as the “coalition of the willing.” The conference was co-hosted by then-Colombian President Gustavo Petro and the government of the Netherlands, with the global campaign led by Tzeporah Berman through the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, which she founded. The event brought together 57 countries and the European Union as well as civil society organizations, scientists, Indigenous leaders and more.
Born out of frustration with fossil-fuel friendly nations and the oil and gas lobbyists involved in the COP process, this fossil fuel treaty effort is kickstarting an alternative approach to international cooperation on climate. The second conference is coming up in just a few months.
Berman is the founder and chairperson of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
PALOMA BELTRAN: Six months after the first conference, what is the energy like from the countries who are interested in transitioning away from fossil fuels?
TZEPORAH BERMAN: In some ways, we’re starting to see groupings of countries within the process. There were 57 countries that came. I think at the next international conference, which will be co-hosted by Ireland and Tuvalu in 2027, there’s going to be even more, because I’ve been talking to a lot of countries that are like, “Wow, it happened really quick.” I think the broad coalition of countries that are committed to a fossil-fuel phaseout will grow, and that’s exciting.
There are also specific conversations that began in Santa Marta that are now deepening—conversations on specific solutions. There is a group of countries which I think of as the high-ambition coalition on fossil-fuel phaseout that are at the table starting to design a fossil-fuel treaty. There are 25 or so countries that are at the table working on this, and these are countries that are really committed to new global governance on the fossil fuel phaseout—legal strategies so that they can be binding, not just voluntary, and cooperative mechanisms.
There are a lot of countries that are digging for more oil, fracking for more gas because they feel like they have to, like they’re being pushed into it because of crushing debt, because of financial architecture and tax agreements and trade agreements that have existed historically to prop up the fossil fuel industry and push fossil fuel production. These are countries that want to cooperate on some of those big-picture solutions like debt. Those countries are hard at work looking at different legal mechanisms and mechanisms of international cooperation. There’s a group of countries that are working specifically on fossil fuel subsidies and encouraging countries to get rid of subsidizing the oil and gas industry. And there’s a number of countries that are now doing national roadmaps, which are great, and that’s increasing ambition within the UNFCCC and COP spaces as well.
There’s not one answer to phasing out the most powerful industry on Earth. It’s going to take multiple initiatives, and I think these conferences have really sparked a lot of new bilateral and plurilateral convenings and cooperations.
BELTRAN: How does a potential fossil fuel treaty exist in relation to the United Nations and the Paris Agreement?
BERMAN: A lot of people don’t realize that any issue that we work on within the U.N. has multiple agreements, multiple treaties associated with it. It’s not uncommon to have different agreements and treaties on different aspects of a big problem: landmines, nuclear weapons, chemical weapons. So what we are proposing is that the fossil fuel treaty would be a companion to the Paris Agreement. It would be international agreements on helping phase out the production of fossil fuels in a way that is equitable and fair.
We don’t have that. For 30 years our countries have been negotiating on emissions reductions—so, how much each country gets to pollute—but not on reducing the supply and production of fossil fuels. An economist would say it’s like trying to cut with one half of the scissors—only the demand, but not the supply. Every year we negotiate new emissions-reduction targets, and then every year we grow new projects and new development, and then we fail to meet our targets. But it’s not rocket science. What we build today will be what we use tomorrow.
BELTRAN: This fossil fuel treaty we’re talking about was not initiated by the United Nations. It was spearheaded by you, with a formal campaign launching in 2020. How is it different from U.N. processes and conventions?
BERMAN: It is likely that the fossil fuel treaty will become a U.N. process. It’s not right now, and that historically is what we’ve seen with a lot of tricky, intransigent issues: landmines, chemical weapons, nuclear. These are treaties that were created initially outside the U.N. process, especially landmines.
We got the idea of the Santa Marta conference from landmines, because land mines were an issue that was really not moving forward in the U.N. space, because there are vested interests who were adamant not to have the conversation. They wanted to expand landmines. Ottawa created the Ottawa Convention, which was the precursor to the landmine agreement, and it was again a coalition of the willing: “Fine, you don’t want to talk about it? Don’t come, because you’re holding back the conversation.” That process outside the U.N. sp

Climate pollutant concentrations in the Beijing region of northern China have plateaued or begun to decline—except for the world’s most potent greenhouse gas, new research concludes.
The findings, published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology, suggest a decades-long effort to clean Beijing’s air is beginning to pay off. But while it cites progress, the research also highlights a growing climate challenge, driven by the region’s surging electricity demand and the explosive growth of semiconductor manufacturing amid the AI boom.
Sulfur hexafluoride—known as SF6—is 24,300 times more effective at warming Earth’s atmosphere, pound for pound, than carbon dioxide, the leading driver of climate change. The synthetic gas is widely used as an electrical insulator in high-voltage equipment, making the power sector a key source of concern as electricity infrastructure expands. While SF6 emissions are declining in other parts of the world, they are rapidly rising in China, which accounts for more than half of global releases.
The country’s state-owned electric power companies recycle only about 30 percent of the gas they discard each year, with the remainder likely released into the atmosphere, a recent Inside Climate News analysis concluded.
The study, by researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Atmospheric Physics in Beijing, examined greenhouse gas concentrations in the region between 1993 and 2024 to assess the effectiveness of the city’s energy transition.
The researchers found that semiconductor manufacturing, where the gas is used for etching and cleaning, is another fast-growing source of SF6 emissions in the Beijing region.
The scientists, who did not respond to interview requests or declined to comment, found that carbon dioxide concentrations have begun to decrease in China’s capital. The study attributed the shift to local policies introduced around 2008, when Beijing hosted the Summer Olympics, that promoted natural gas and electricity while discouraging or banning coal use.
Growth in atmospheric concentrations of methane and nitrous oxide, the second and third leading drivers of climate change, has slowed. The study attributes the change in methane levels to capturing landfill emissions and reusing the gas for power generation or incinerating waste before it can decompose. Increased electric-vehicle use and stricter pollution controls for gas-powered automobiles hit the brakes on growth in nitrous oxide concentrations, the researchers found.
However, SF6 concentrations are accelerating.
“These findings underscore the power and semiconductor sectors as critical domains for targeted SF6 emission control,” the study concluded.
The electric power sector is China’s leading national source of the climate pollutant, accounting for about 70 percent of all SF6 emissions, according to the study. However, emissions from semiconductor manufacturing in Beijing have grown rapidly for more than a decade and are now the pollutant’s primary local source, the study found.
Martin Vojta, an atmospheric scientist at the University of Vienna, noted that Beijing’s increase in semiconductor manufacturing correlated with rising SF6 emissions. However, other factors, such as changes in production practices, could affect the industry’s emissions, Vojta said.
Atmospheric modeling that traces SF6 emissions back to their sources would more definitively link the increase in emissions to the semiconductor industry, Vojta said.
The research results were compiled into a policy report, “Beware of Sulfur Hexafluoride Emissions Behind AI Industry Development,” which was quickly adopted by the Beijing Municipal Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, according to an Aug. 19 press release from the Institute of Atmospheric Physics.

Donate Now
Artificial Intelligence, or AI, could fuel rising SF6 emissions by increasing semiconductor chip manufacturing and continuing the region’s power-grid buildout. The Beijing Municipal Committee is a government advisory body overseen by the Chinese Communist Party. The institute’s press release announcing the policy report’s adoption came less than a week after the study was published.
Members of the committee visited the institute shortly before publication for briefings. Tang Guiqian, one of the study’s co-authors, was among those speaking to the group, according to the institute.
Tang declined to comment, citing institute policies. The Beijing Municipal Committee did not respond to a request for additional information.
SF6 supplies fluorine for the semiconductor industry, where it is used to carve channels into silicon or other materials to help build circuitry in computer chips, liquid crystal display panels—better known as LCD—and other electronic devices. The gas can also clean deposition chambers where chips and other electronics are fabricated. In both processes, some sulfur hexafluoride passes through without reacting and, unless properly abated, is released into the atmosphere.
The semiconductor industry can rein that in. Among the options: optimizing production, using alternative fluorine sources and destroying waste gas.
From 1996 to 2010, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency partnered with manufacturers in a voluntary effort to reduce emissions of SF6 and other fluorinated greenhouse gases.
Scott Bartos, a former EPA official and program manager on the partnership, said any effort to reduce climate pollution as a result of the current study and subsequent policy report would be good news as China ramps up semiconductor manufacturing and electrifies its economy.

Six Flags has announced it will be adding seat belts to some of its rollercoasters after a man fell to his death on the Goliath ride in the US state of Georgia earlier this month.
The company's CEO John Reilly said in a letter to customers late on Friday that the company is reinforcing safety measure across its parks, including adding seat belts to Goliath and similar rides, which already feature lap bar restraints.
The chain of amusement parks has 34 locations across North America, with over 220 rollercoasters in total.
Georgia's Goliath ride will remain closed pending safety reviews and out of an abundance of caution, so will eight other rides at five other parks, Reilly added.
The CEO also said the company has hired independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review safety procedures across all its amusement parks. The company is committed to taking action based on the experts' findings and will share progress updates, he said.
On 12 October, a 42-year-old man named Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed at Six Flags Over Georgia after being ejected from the Goliath, police have said. Four other passengers were injured as he fell.
An investigation into the incident is ongoing.
"Our hearts remain with the family and loved ones of Hassan Kariem, those injured, and everyone impacted by the tragic incident," Reilly said in his letter.
"What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags," he added.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five
Over 28 million guests visit Six Flags locations every year, according to the company's website.
October's fatal incident was not the first time a passenger has been hurt at one of the parks.
An Iraq War veteran died in 2011 after being ejected from a ride in New York. In 2013, a woman died after slipping from her restraints and falling 75 feet from a coaster in Texas.
In 2022, a 22-year-old man died from a brain injury after riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California. His family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August.
The following month, the California park announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.

80dfa1b69af0.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press By — Elise Morton, Associated Press Elise Morton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ukraines-starlink-satellite-speeds-restored-after-a-week-of-front-line-disruption Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ukraine's Starlink satellite speeds restored after a week of front-line disruption World Oct 24, 2026 12:05 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday. "The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. WATCH: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication — alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications." Zelenskyy on Friday said Ukraine was still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed limits. Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks. Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement. Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday. Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks. Ukraine's General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city. Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Morton reported from London. Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, known as the Eagle's Nest, was engulfed in flames on Friday night while police arrested a 33-year-old male suspect.
The residence, called the Kehlsteinhaus, is above the town of Berchtesgaden. It was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed", with the public urged to avoid the area.

In a memo sent Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said his teams "have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel." Please check your inbox to confirm. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote. The memo was obtained by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Axios. Three U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, confirmed that the memo was sent to Rubio in his capacity as secretary of state and national security adviser. The memo emerged shortly after the State Department announced it is reducing staff at the U.S. embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The three officials said the threats from Iran and Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels are related to the staffing changes. WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open. However, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where nonessential U.S. personnel and their families were ordered Wednesday to leave the country, staff in the other four countries are not compelled to depart. In announcing the staffing drawdowns this week, the State Department pointed specifically to increased threats from Yemen's Houthi rebels and did not mention threats to U.S. personnel directly from Iran. There has been a resurgence of fighting between a Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis, with the militant group launching missile and drone strikes against Saudi Arabia. U.S. officials have adamantly denied the drawdowns are tied to any potential new U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran. The unpopular war has spiked energy costs for Americans and posed political problems for President Donald Trump and Republicans, who are trying to keep control of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Trump, speaking at a rally Friday in Florida, touted the U.S. military operations in Iran, which were dubbed "Operation Epic Fury," and said that "we may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree. If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business.'" Mediators have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks as the war has reached a stalemate. According to Iranian state television, the Revolutionary Guard navy this week again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the United States keeps helping guide commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the global energy trade. "Any further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the region will put civilian lives and the well-being of all regional states and the global economy at great risk," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote in an opinion column in the Financial Times this week. d40de761d73b.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/doj-orders-some-california-counties-to-set-aside-ballots-from-suspected-noncitizens Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DOJ orders some California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens Politics Oct 24, 2026 10:49 AM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press. The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Donald Trump's Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. READ MORE: DOJ has monitored elections for decades. Here's why some state officials are concerned this year Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday. The Trump administration asked the 9th Circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday. Now, according to the LA County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48 hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified. "Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli. The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more. WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county. California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens. Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted. The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.
Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free".
The video, posted on Friday, teases the release of a longer YouTube video to come on Saturday, in which Vanessa and Kai Trump will discuss breast cancer awareness and prevention, Kai wrote in the caption.
Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.
"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.
"I sat down with my mom and Dr. Nicole Saphier to talk about my mom's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection," she continued.
Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from American singer and media personality Mary Millben.
In Friday's video, Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.
According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, according to the group.
Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some disease remains, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.
Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

e0c4dbfc751c.text: By — Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press By — Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/north-korean-leader-kim-jong-un-visits-china-to-inaugurate-a-new-cross-border-bridge Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visits China to inaugurate a new cross-border bridge World Oct 24, 2026 10:30 AM EDT SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hoped to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbor. READ MORE: North Korea threatens to restart propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy more weapons at South Korea border Kim's visit to China is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a "new Cold War." It's his first visit in a year. Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China's official Xinhua News Agency. Both sides promised to strengthen cooperation He met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China's Communist Party. The two toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship. Kim said his country "stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries," Xinhua said. Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to Xinhua. North Korean state media did not immediately report on Kim's visit. New bridge was built to help expand trade between the countries Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge this month was a key symbol of strengthening ties between North Korea and China and reflected their intent to expand trade, as it is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks. Kim has recently sought to strengthen ties with China, the North's traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. He sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance. Kim's visit timed to key battle anniversary in Korean War with China Kim's latest visit to China is his sixth since taking power in late 2011 following the death of his father. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of his ties with Beijing ahead of the Oct. 25 anniversary of China's first major victory in the Korean War, which was days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950. The war began with North Korea's surprise attack on the South in June 1950, prompting a U.N.-led coalition headed by the United States to intervene and push back the offensive. North Korea was backed primarily by Chinese forces, with assistance from the then-Soviet Union's air force, before fighting ended with a 1953 armistice that left the peninsula technically at war. Kim said his visit on Saturday was also to memorialize those killed in the war, according to Xinhua. Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing's willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority. READ MORE: In a relatively mild speech, North Korea uses UN platform to lament 'mutual distrust' and tension Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders. Kim has maintained a hard line toward Seoul and has so far rebuffed a proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019 during Trump's first term. Kim's government has called for Washington to abandon its "hostile policy" and drop demands for the North's denuclearization as a precondition for renewed talks. South Korea's liberal government, which favors engagement with the North, hopes renewed talks between Washington and Pyongyang will thaw inter-Korean relations, and has also urged China to play a "constructive" role in resolving the standoff. Seoul's spy agency told lawmakers last month that it saw a 50% possibility of a meeting between Trump and Kim on the sidelines of next month's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit in Shenzhen, China. "From Seoul's perspective, if North Korea focuses more on economic development than military buildup and threats, that would be positive for diplomacy and security," said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. "But if Kim can extract ever more benefits from China and Russia, it is unclear what Seoul could offer that would be worth the political risks Pyongyang attaches to exchanges with a more prosperous, globalized, and free Korea." Wu reported from Bangkok. AP video journalist Mayuko Ono in Tokyo contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 4852e8a86e6c.text: President Trump has endorsed Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday's Israeli election, but some of his advisers see opportunity for his Middle East agenda in a government led by someone else, U.S. officials tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump has never worked with an Israeli prime minister other than Netanyahu, and doesn't personally know any of the other candidates. The two have forged a close but often turbulent relationship. "He's the devil he knows," one Trump adviser said, describing the president's view of Netanyahu. Driving the news: After weeks of hesitation, Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday — and even suggested his defeat would have consequences for U.S.-Israel relations. One U.S. official described the endorsement as a win-win for Trump, regardless of the outcome. If Netanyahu wins — or remains in power as caretaker prime minister — Trump could claim credit for rescuing him politically and use that leverage to press for concessions. If Netanyahu loses and his opponents form a government, Israel's new leaders would still have every incentive to cultivate good relations with Trump. His endorsement of their rival would quickly become a footnote. Behind the scenes: Many of Trump's closest advisers opposed his decision to endorse Netanyahu, believing the president should stay out of the Israeli election, according to sources familiar with the discussions. Vice President Vance notably declined to follow Trump's lead when asked about the election this week, amid growing hostility toward Netanyahu in parts of the MAGA movement. "I'm not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I'm not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu. I think the president's endorsement is ultimately what matters," Vance told reporters. Zoom in: Vance, who endorsed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán days before his election defeat in April , said he would no longer get involved in foreign elections. The vice president is among the senior Trump officials who became disillusioned with Netanyahu during the war with Iran, according to sources familiar with their thinking. Vance and other top aides believe Netanyahu's pre-war assessments to the White House were mistaken, deepening questions about whether he remains the best partner for achieving Trump's regional ambitions. The big picture: Once the Israeli election and U.S. midterms are over, Trump will face a defining choice for his Middle East agenda: whether to join Netanyahu in another major military operation against Iran. Netanyahu is eager to move forward. But the election results could influence Trump's decision, or at least the timing of any renewed large-scale fighting. Trump also wants to move beyond the Iran war and pursue an ambitious diplomatic agenda that includes implementing his Gaza peace plan , brokering deals between Israel and Lebanon and Syria , and ultimately securing a historic Israeli-Saudi peace agreement . Whether Trump can make progress on those goals will depend in part on who governs Israel — and what kind of coalition emerges from Tuesday's vote. The intrigue: Behind the scenes over the last six months, several of Trump's top advisers have grown dissatisfied with Netanyahu on key regional priorities. Gaza: Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have expressed frustration with Netanyahu's reluctance to advance implementation of the president's peace plan. Syria: Trump's envoy Tom Barrack has similar concerns about the Netanyahu government's approach to Damascus and continued Israeli military operations in Syria. Lebanon and the West Bank: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his team have a better relationship with Netanyahu, but believe Israel could do more to strengthen Lebanon's government. They are also frustrated by Netanyahu's failure to do more to curb settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. Between the lines: Some U.S. officials say a new Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners could be easier to work with. White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly declined to comment, referring Axios to Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu on Truth Social . State of play: Three major Israeli television networks released their final pre-election polls Friday, all showing Netanyahu's coalition falling well short of a parliamentary majority. All three projected just 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc in the 120-member Knesset — 17 fewer than his current coalition holds. His Likud party, which currently holds 32 seats, was projected to win just 20. The polls gave former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc between 52 and 56 seats, with another 14 to 16 going to two Arab Israeli parties. Channel 11 also projected four seats for a reservists party unaffiliated with either bloc. Pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 was the major outlier, projecting 60 seats for his bloc and 30 for Likud in a poll earlier this week. What to watch: The polls point to a potential political deadlock: Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot appears to have a clear path to the 61 seats needed to form a government. Eisenkot would need to bring Arab Israeli parties into his coalition, which he has ruled out, or form a minority government with their outside support — an arrangement some of his potential partners oppose. A unity government between Netanyahu and his rivals is considered highly unlikely. If neither side can assemble a governing majority, Israel could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining in power as caretaker prime minister. The bottom line: Rather than ushering in a new government more receptive to Trump's agenda, Tuesday's election could leave the president dealing with a weakened Netanyahu and an Israeli political system consumed by another prolonged crisis.

Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target US personnel" in the Middle East and other areas, the US national intelligence director has warned in a memo seen by the BBC.
Jay Clayton's assessment come as the US State Department makes adjustments to staffing at diplomatic posts in the region, including the ordered departure earlier this week of non-emergency US embassy staff from Saudi Arabia.
The order came in response to escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia in the past month.
Clayton's memo was marked unclassified and sent to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.
It said: "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries."
Clayton said he was making every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so Rubio could share it with US State Department personnel.
A US official told the BBC: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment.
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others â the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
The Houthis say the attacks on Saudi Arabia are in retaliation to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport they blame on the kingdom.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks. Some 155 civilians have been killed in Yemen since, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.
This particular conflict has re-emerged on the backdrop of a wider conflict in the Middle East.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has seen oil prices surge, exacerbated by the Houthis' "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia.

a98bb2af1667.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/republican-billionaire-rick-jackson-is-walking-a-trump-tightrope-in-his-quest-to-lead-georgia Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Republican billionaire Rick Jackson is walking a Trump tightrope in his quest to lead Georgia Politics Oct 24, 2026 3:04 PM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — He's hardly the first billionaire to promise working-class voters he'll fight for them in public office. Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, has even compared himself to the real estate mogul who reached the Oval Office. But Jackson's path differs from Donald Trump's, and the 72-year-old healthcare magnate and investor brings a vastly different persona to his first campaign. Unlike Trump, who was born to wealth, Jackson spent his early years bouncing through foster homes before launching his first company as a young man. Now, he wants to leverage both his similarities and contrasts with the president, a challenge he's tackling with buckets of his own campaign cash and a personal story that anchors his appeal to voters. Please check your inbox to confirm. "I have lived in poverty," Jackson says. "When you have not eaten, you never forget that, and you don't forget the people that are struggling." Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, disputes Jackson's altruistic pitch, setting up the Nov. 3 election as a test of whether an alternate, softer version of conservative billionaire politics can complement or even counter Trump's pugilistic populism in a key swing state. Jackson planned to join Trump at a rally Saturday in Perry, in what would be his second appearance with the president in the closing stretch of the campaign. 'From foster care to billionaire' "My father left me at nine months old. My mother was a sixth-grade educated waitress with a severe alcohol problem," Jackson said in the only debate of their general election campaign. "I had seven stepfathers before I was 12. I lived in the projects, went to 13 different schools, and lived in five different foster homes." He left college to start a business at 21. That led to Jackson Healthcare, a behemoth company that provides contract nurses and other workers to hospitals and health systems, including public entities that have helped fuel Jackson's fortunes with taxpayer money. At events with supporters, Jackson gets more personal. "I have, because of my background, severe abandonment issues," he told hundreds of voters in Cleveland, a conservative enclave in the north Georgia mountains. He turns that acknowledgment into a promise: "Let me tell you one thing: I will never abandon you." READ MORE: Trump will rally Georgia Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state Rags-to-riches themes are not uncommon in politics, and it's yielded Jackson's campaign motto: "From foster care to billionaire." But the scale is eye-popping, illuminated by the nearly $200 million Jackson has spent personally on the campaign. That puts him among the largest self-funding candidates in the history of American elections. But on that score, too, Jackson tries to soften the caricature of the billionaire executive. "It's not my money," he said in a northern suburb of Atlanta. Jackson calls his fortune "God's money" and says that "my job is to have kingdom impact" with it. "The reason I have spent so much money to do this," he said, is to "help 11 million Georgians, to keep them from struggling." A range of images over a long campaign Jackson launched his bid as a relative unknown, though Capitol insiders knew him because of Jackson Healthcare, its lucrative state contracts and his lobbying interest in healthcare, business and tax policy. The Republican primary field featured a trio of statewide elected officials, including Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who won Trump's endorsement in August 2025, before Jackson got in. During the primary, Jackson embraced the president even though he wasn't Trump's choice. Jackson sometimes promised to "be like Trump, but with Southern tone." He pledged to "deliver for Georgia the same type of business solutions that President Trump is bringing to our country." Largely aligning himself with Trump on immigration, Jackson promised to make Georgia a national leader in deportations. "I don't care if you're Muslim or Mongolian, you don't have the right to force your culture on our country," he said in one ad. "Criminal illegals" who "commit sick, violent crimes" would "end up deported or departed," he promised. Soon after defeating Jones in a runoff, Jackson shelved the immigration ad, but not before using it as part of a spot featuring his grandchildren. "Granddad, why do you look so mean in these ads?" one asks after watching the "deported or departed" clip on her phone. The children and teenagers then tell their grandfather how he can "look cool" with a pickup truck, a dog and a hipper wardrobe. "Let's make Georgia better together," the redressed Jackson concludes. He has since circulated an ad with several young adults who benefited from the millions he spent helping foster children who age out of the Georgia system when they turn 18. "I am so proud of you," he tells them as he chokes up. On policy, Republican fare and centrist appeals As he softens his image, Jackson maintains traditional Republican positions, pledging to cut taxes, regulation and what he describes as waste. If he cannot halve the state income tax in four years, he promises not to seek a second term. He wants a balanced budget and full audits of state spending, without saying state law requires a balanced budget and audits of state agencies have long been standard practice. He says he will

6edf0296fbfb.text: By — Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Philip Marcelo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/new-york-state-woman-charged-with-voting-illegally-says-she-recently-learned-she-wasnt-a-citizen Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New York state woman charged with voting illegally says she recently learned she wasn't a citizen Politics Oct 24, 2026 2:07 PM EDT An upstate New York woman who says she only recently learned she wasn't born in the U.S. has been charged with voting illegally, one of the latest arrests touted by the Trump administration as it hunts for noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections. Marva Cook was adopted as a toddler and had always assumed she was a U.S. citizen, she told Homeland Security investigators earlier this month, according to the criminal complaint. READ MORE: DOJ orders some California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens But in searching for her biological mother, the 66-year-old Syracuse resident, who starred on Syracuse University's women's basketball team decades ago, said she discovered she had a German birth certificate. Federal prosecutors say Cook has had a green card for several years now, but she still cast ballots in recent elections despite not having citizenship. She faces a single federal charge of voting by an alien stemming from her vote in the 2022 midterms. The misdemeanor offense carries a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a fine up to $100,000, if convicted. Cook can also face deportation, under federal law. Cook says she has faith in God and support from community Reached by phone Friday, Cook declined to discuss the criminal case, her voting record or her past efforts at becoming a citizen. But she said she was "not thrilled" by her court appearance Wednesday as she was placed in shackles despite having voluntarily turned herself in just hours earlier. "It was a difficult time," Cook said. "I'm about kindness and service and doing for others as I want to be treated." WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting She also said she appreciated the outpouring of support of community members, a number of whom accompanied her to court Wednesday. "The prayers and the support is a big part of how I will get through this," Cook said. "I have a deep faith that God will get me through it." Cook's lawyer, Paul Tuck, also declined to discuss details of the criminal case Friday other than to say there are no upcoming hearings or filing deadlines. There are no pending immigration proceedings, he added, but Cook has an immigration lawyer in the event that changes. Spokespersons for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn't immediately respond to emails seeking comment. Cook is latest arrest in Trump's nationwide crackdown on noncitizen voting First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, whose upstate New York office is prosecuting the case, said Cook's arrest showed "voter fraud is rampant" in the state. Other federal agencies amplified the statement on social media, even as the administration's own investigations have demonstrated that such instances are incredibly rare and been shown not to change the outcome of elections. "We cannot and will not allow the votes of American citizens to be canceled out by noncitizens illegally voting in our elections," the Homeland Security wrote in a post on X that included Sarcone's statement. In California, federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents with illegally casting ballots or registering to vote. Weeks earlier, 10 people were charged in Minnesota with illegally voting over the last three elections. Supporters say Cook is a valuable member of the community Cook's supporters, meanwhile, described her as a vital part of the local community where she had lived nearly all of her life and had starred in college basketball. The Syracuse University athletics department confirmed Cook was the team's leading scorer in the 1979-80 season, averaging 15 points per game. She also holds the school record for most steals in a single season. READ MORE: DOJ has monitored elections for decades. Here's why some state officials are concerned this year Fred Daley, pastor at All Saints Church, said Cook is an active member of the parish who for years has been the church's go-to Easter Bunny, decked out in full costume during the spring holiday season. "If the government wanted to make a case, they chose the wrong person," he said. "She's a poster child of an amazing person. She's highly respected throughout the community." Dale Avers, a parishioner who has known Cook for almost 20 years, described her as a "person of service" who "never sought limelight." She said Cook supports low-income families and youth as the YMCA's community school program director. "I'm in total shock that they're putting this much effort into this," Avers said. "They understood the story. There was no intent. There's no malice. There was no deception involved." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 9b0bd02376f3.text: By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/six-flags-says-it-will-install-seat-belts-on-georgia-roller-coaster-after-riders-death Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider's death Nation Oct 24, 2026 1:32 PM EDT The chief executive of Six Flags says the company will install seat belts on the Georgia roller coaster from which a rider fell to his death earlier this month. The company's rides with similar restraints will also get the safety upgrade. The theme park operator announced the extra safeguard less than two weeks after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta died after being ejected from his seat on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. READ MORE: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park "We are reinforcing safety precautions at our parks and taking additional measures, including adding seat belts on Goliath and other coasters with a similar restraint," John Reilly, president and CEO of Six Flags Entertainment Corporation, said in a statement Friday. Goliath remains shut down while state and local officials investigate the Oct. 12 death. Reilly didn't specify which other Six Flags coasters will get seat belts. But it has temporarily closed eight additional roller coasters at five other parks in the U.S. and Canada. Those rides all share the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system. Six Flags hasn't said when those coasters are expected to reopen. Reilly's statement said Six Flags has enlisted independent engineers and inspectors to review safety procedures for all rides at its theme parks. Investigators haven't said what went wrong on the Georgia coaster. Witnesses said they saw Kariem rise up out of his seat and fall headfirst back into the cart before being ejected. Some people who rode Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints. All nine of the Six Flags coasters taken offline were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard. They also feature similar clamshell restraints that sit at the top of a vertical bar between each rider's knees. The bar locks a padded restraint into place over the rider's lap and upper legs. The U.S. patent granted to Bolliger & Mabillard for the restraint system in 2001 says it's designed to make each rider feel "that he is seated on a flying carpet or that he is at the controls of a kind of flying scooter, while still guaranteeing optimum security." Following the death in Georgia, non-Six Flags theme parks SeaWorld Orlando in Florida and La Ronde in Montreal, Canada, also temporarily closed one roller coaster apiece that use clamshell restraints. SeaWorld reopened its Mako coaster Tuesday after it had been offline for a week. The Associated Press emailed the company Saturday asking if seat belts or other safety upgrades were planned for the coaster. The AP also emailed a spokesperson for La Ronde seeking an update on its shuttered coaster. In addition to Goliath in Georgia, eight coasters remain closed at Six Flags parks in Gurnee, Illinois; Jackson Township, New Jersey; Charlotte, North Carolina; Mason, Ohio; and Vaughan, Ontario. Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
